The Sodium Struggle Hypothesis: Autism as a Manifestation of Compensatory Physiology in Coupled Osmotic–Volume Defence

Kathleen Roberta Bell
Independent Researcher

Revised 1 November 2026

Markdown edition: The complete parent manuscript is reproduced below. Each figure is replaced by a text description; its original caption is retained.

A concise conceptual summary of this hypothesis is available as:

The Sodium-Struggle Hypothesis of Autism: A Sodium–Volume Defence Systems Physiology Framework (Summary of a Larger Hypothesis)
https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31885234

Abstract

The Sodium Struggle Hypothesis proposes that diverse initiating conditions contribute to later features of autism through impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery during sensitive development. This narrative synthesis evaluates the proposed connection through compensatory physiology in coupled osmotic–volume defence. Maternal, placental, renal and vascular disturbances can provide systemic entry. Genetic, immune and environmental influences may act systemically, directly on local cellular capacity or demand, or both. Clinical hyponatraemia and a preceding systemic disturbance are not required.

Systemic routes can recruit vasopressin (AVP), renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, cortisol, autonomic and renal responses. Sensing or regulatory errors can alter their recruitment, strength or timing. These responses support tonicity, circulation and delivery. Successful restoration is the comparator; the proposed developmental cost requires impaired local recovery, not defence or pumping work alone. Normal serum sodium does not establish intact local recovery.

Candidate mechanisms involve chloride regulation, cell-volume control and glial support; their proposed developmental consequences concern inhibitory maturation and circuit refinement. Redox-dependent vascular dysfunction may initiate or amplify recovery difficulty through impaired delivery or altered filling signals. Separate metabolic proposals concern temporary osmotic support from glucose and insulin-associated changes in peripheral AVP clearance.

Hypothalamic and local AVP signalling could alter autonomic and neuroendocrine responses, favouring AVP-linked recruitment or weaker oxytocin modulation in specified circuits without a uniform circulating hormone pattern. Repeated defence could imprint controller thresholds or recovery kinetics; resulting circuit changes might persist after physiological restoration. Later orthostatic, metabolic or sensorimotor demands could reveal or modify those consequences. Exposure, recovery and later expression therefore need not coincide.

The selected evidence is strongest for physiological components and directly measured recovery in experimental preparations. The central developmental inference remains unresolved: impaired local recovery must carry a defined developmental effect, beyond altered resting values or increased regulatory effort. Universal participation across autistic trajectories is an unestablished conjecture, and no particular exposure or hormonal direction is compulsory. A credible developmental route bypassing the required recovery disturbance would challenge universal scope; an unmeasured intermediary establishes neither a bypass nor support.

Part A Claim and physiological logic

1 Introduction

Autism research has identified substantial genetic liability alongside synaptic, immune, metabolic, endocrine and vascular differences. This manuscript brings together empirical findings from clinical, experimental and post-mortem studies to evaluate a hypothesis about compensatory physiology in coupled osmotic–volume defence. Its central question is how immediate protection and incomplete local restoration during a sensitive developmental window could shape later development. The proposed interpretation distinguishes continuing or renewed compensation, changes retained from an earlier response, and further downstream consequences that need not themselves be compensatory (Section 21).

The framework began as The Sodium Struggle: Autism as a Manifestation of Compensatory Measures Against Hyponatraemia and Hypovolaemia. Hyponatraemia, hypo-osmolality and hypovolaemia remain central working examples. The author’s working expectation is that low extracellular tonicity and inadequate effective filling predominate among the proposed systemic initiating routes; their relative frequency has not been established. The broader designation also accommodates hypertonic exposure, genuine volume expansion and direct cellular constraints. Hypertonic, expansion and direct cellular routes need not involve an impending low state.

The conjecture is that impaired local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery carries a developmental effect across autistic trajectories. Systemic sodium–volume disturbance can initiate the process, but an intrinsic genetic or cellular constraint can enter locally without maternal exposure or preceding circulatory instability. Participation across all autism remains the hypothesis’s ambition, not an established result. The required connection is specific: restoration must be slower, less complete or less stable than in an appropriate developmental comparator, and that disturbance must change development. Increased regulatory work with adequate recovery does not satisfy the claim.

This proposal builds on existing accounts. Good (2011) proposed a link between low blood sodium, loss of brain taurine and glutamine, and autistic features. Genetic, synaptic, excitatory–inhibitory and neuroimmune mechanisms can initiate, modify or bypass the proposed recovery process. Ben-Ari, Tyzio and colleagues already linked perinatal oxytocin signalling, chloride regulation and lasting neural outcomes in valproate-exposed rats and fragile-X mice (Tyzio et al., 2014). Tang et al. (2019) measured chloride-recovery kinetics in human Rett-syndrome neurons. Naviaux’s cell danger response and three-hit metabolic-signalling model likewise address protective signalling, developmental costs, delayed chloride maturation and renewed challenge before recovery is complete (Naviaux, 2026a,b). The additional claim here is convergence on the specified local recovery intermediary across different initiating routes. Sections 23.13 and 26.7 develop those relationships.

Diagnosed prevalence does not establish this mechanism. Swedish birth cohorts from 1993–2002 showed a stable measured autism symptom phenotype while registered diagnoses increased (Lundström et al., 2015). In Danish cohorts born during 1980–1991, diagnostic and reporting changes were estimated to explain 60% of the observed increase (95% confidence interval 33–87%; Hansen et al., 2015). These findings constrain interpretation of those trends without showing that every increase is administrative or excluding environmental contributions. The hypothesis rests on physiological and developmental evidence, not an assumed epidemic mechanism.

1.1 The Sodium–Volume Survival Axis

Coupled osmotic–volume defence, shortened here to sodium–volume defence, is a compact label for coordinated renal, vascular, endocrine, autonomic and cellular regulation that supports extracellular tonicity, effective circulating volume, vascular tone or containment, and local ionic or cell-volume recovery. Sodium gradients support neural signalling, transport and regulatory volume change, but normal serum sodium does not establish intact local recovery. Preserved arterial pressure does not establish adequate regional delivery. The systemic account distinguishes an actual filling or delivery deficit from an error in sensing or regulating circulation. Sensing is a control layer, not an additional defended variable. Either route belongs to the developmental hypothesis only if impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carries its effect (§2).

Here, compensatory physiology means biological responses that maintain or restore physiological function, distinct from behavioural or cognitive compensation and from masking or camouflaging autistic characteristics. It includes acute, recurrent or sustained regulation; its developmental consequences may persist after the initiating response ends. Within the proposed low-direction routes, defence may limit an emerging disturbance before overt hyponatraemia, hypo-osmolality or hypovolaemia develops. Cellular responses may also limit swelling and threats to structural integrity. Normal measurements can therefore be compatible with successful prevention, but do not by themselves establish that history or continuing compensatory effort.

Different sensors contribute different information. Osmoregulatory circuits respond to effective osmolality and tonicity; cardiovascular controls respond to pressure, filling and perfusion; renal signalling includes NaCl delivery at the macula densa. Their inputs can diverge under stress (Bourque, 2008; Castrop et al., 2010). Schrier’s functional view of circulatory adequacy explains why water-conserving and vasomotor responses may accompany normal or increased total body fluid when effective filling is inadequate (Schrier, 1979). The distinction is central to the systemic branch of this hypothesis.

Six explanatory roles organise the account: initiation, compensation, recovery, developmental conversion, persistence and later expression. Initiation creates a disturbance or recovery constraint; compensation protects immediate function; recovery restores the affected compartment and withdraws responses no longer needed. Developmental conversion is the point at which this physiological history changes maturation or circuit refinement. Persistence may reside in altered regulation, enduring circuit organisation or both. Later expression reflects interaction with subsequent demands. These roles can overlap and feed back on one another; they are not six compulsory sequential stages.

Part A introduces the physical variables, successful restoration and the proposed recovery problem. Part B places genetic and direct cellular entry alongside developmental anatomy, maternal–placental–fetal transformation and intergenerational susceptibility. Part C pairs catalogues of candidate disturbances with their mechanisms, interacting routes and evidence maps. Part D distinguishes ongoing disturbance, persistent regulation and lasting developmental change.

Part E develops local neural and glial recovery and its proposed developmental consequences before Part F examines renal, endocrine, receptor, controller and vascular regulation. Part G considers sex and other stage-specific modifiers, current physiological demands and later expression. Part H uses wider disease comparisons before the Discussion evaluates the complete argument and the conclusion states its remaining commitments. This order explains the relationships; it does not make organ mechanisms exclusively upstream or downstream. The more detailed roadmap in Section 22 introduces Parts E–H.

This manuscript presents a narrative hypothesis synthesis with a mechanistic scope. Clinical, experimental and post-mortem findings are selected for their relevance to particular initiating disturbances, protective responses, recovery trajectories, developmental consequences or alternative explanations. The selection is illustrative, not an exhaustive or systematic review of autism research. Species, developmental stage, compartment, exposure and measured endpoint delimit each comparison; contrary and null findings remain attached to the claims they test. Evidence for a physiological component, directly measured recovery and a recovery-mediated developmental effect serves different purposes. A measured initiating disturbance can merit inclusion without demonstrating the complete route to autism. The [E], [S] and [H] labels identify claim roles rather than evidence strength. The fixed genetic classification in Section 6 has its own scope and limitations. Compatible observations motivate the proposed connections; they do not establish their prevalence or universal participation.

1.2 Clinical Hyponatraemia and Low-Effective-Sodium Pressure

Clinical hyponatraemia retains its standard meaning: a measured low serum sodium concentration interpreted with tonicity and clinical context (Verbalis et al., 2013; Spasovski et al., 2014). Hypotonic dilution, hypertonic translocational sodium lowering and analytical pseudohyponatraemia are different states. Hyperglycaemia, for example, can draw water out of cells and lower extracellular sodium concentration while raising effective tonicity. Low-mineral water contributes to dilution only when the balance of retained water, solute and excretory capacity produces it. Barrier leak can reduce effective filling without a total-body fluid deficit.

Low-effective-sodium pressure is the manuscript’s heuristic for specified instability in sodium-dependent support of extracellular tonicity, effective filling or local perfusion, including a demonstrated error in sensing those conditions. This heuristic covers specified routes within the broader coupled framework; it is not a synonym for every initiating condition. It is neither a new analyte nor hidden hyponatraemia, and it does not imply a dedicated “effective sodium” receptor. The relevant evidence is the physiological relationship among solute, water, delivery and regulatory response. Normal routine chemistry alone neither demonstrates this state nor excludes an earlier disturbance. Tables 13.2 and 15.2 distinguish conditional response patterns. The two contributor maps use a shared structure: Table 13.1 covers cellular osmotic and ionic routes; Table 15.1 separates actual filling/delivery disturbances (Panel A) from sensing/regulation disturbances (Panel B). Table 16.1 supplies subordinate component evidence, and Table 20.1 records claim-specific evidence roles.

The systemic and local claims remain separate. A circulatory or osmotic disturbance may constrain cellular recovery through altered delivery, transport conditions or continuing defence. A direct neuronal or glial lesion may begin with the recovery constraint itself. Evidence for local recovery mediation does not establish an earlier systemic sodium deficit, and the common-process conjecture requires neither excess intracellular sodium nor simultaneous sodium and chloride accumulation in every route. “Anti-hyponatraemia” and “anti-hypovolaemia” describe parts of this defence problem without changing their clinical definitions.

1.3 Sodium–Volume Defence Physiology

The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad names three protective, context-dependent arms: arginine vasopressin (AVP) regulates free water and supports circulatory defence; the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) supports sodium conservation and effective filling; glucocorticoid action helps sustain circulation under constraint. Autonomic vasomotor responses redistribute flow, and renal and cellular responses restore local conditions. The arms need not rise together. Their recruitment and effects depend on stimulus, compartment, phase and locally regulated hormone action (Chapman et al., 2013). Hypotonicity may suppress AVP, whereas hypertonicity or circulatory threat may recruit it. This architecture predicts changing combinations of protection, not one obligatory hormone profile.

Metabolic responses could initiate or modify osmotic–volume disturbance. Section 19.7 develops two separable proposals: temporary extracellular osmotic support through glucose mobilisation or reduced disposal, and insulin-associated peripheral AVP clearance influencing water handling. The latter could operate without a preceding protective glucose rise. Their possible coordination, GSH-sensitive processing and inflammatory feedback are further conditional questions, allowing successful compensation as well as prolonged disturbance.

Successful compensation restores filling, tonicity and transport conditions and permits withdrawal of responses no longer needed. Increased pump turnover can be met by increased energy supply without ATP depletion. The developmental concern is slower, less complete or less stable local neural or glial recovery that changes a defined developmental process. Redox-dependent vascular dysfunction may amplify this constraint through reduced delivery, while successful metabolic and vascular compensation may interrupt the sequence. The vascular and cellular explanations are developed in Sections 16.8, 23, and 26.

A hypothalamic branch connects these systemic responses to neural regulation. Recruitment of magnocellular AVP neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei may, through dendritic signalling, modulate nearby autonomic and neuroendocrine circuits. The proposed developmental effect concerns a lasting change in controller weighting or responsiveness, not AVP elevation alone. Circulating, local neural and portal hormone signals remain distinct, as do hormone production, release, clearance and receptor action. Sections 21, 36, and 37 develop that distributed controller account.

Vasopressin escape retains its specific renal meaning: partial escape from antidiuresis during persistent AVP exposure (Verbalis, 2006). It is distinct from withdrawal of the hormone signal or complete recovery of the wider system.

1.4 Developmental Relevance and Evidentiary Boundaries

Timing gives the proposal its developmental force. Rapid survival responses and slower maturation unfold on different timescales. A transient disturbance may therefore end before its developmental consequence becomes visible. During a susceptible window, incomplete restoration could alter neural differentiation, inhibitory maturation, synaptic stabilisation or pruning. Repeated recruitment may also change thresholds, receptor responsiveness or recovery dynamics across hypothalamic, autonomic, vascular, renal and cellular systems. This proposed distributed imprinting follows the developmental-programming question of how early conditions become biologically embedded (Gluckman et al., 2010); it is not established by repetition alone.

Prospective MRI found greater extra-axial CSF volume at six months in high-familial-risk infants later diagnosed with autism (Shen et al., 2017; Section 30). This is an early fluid-space association, distinct from brain growth or cell swelling; it does not establish sodium–volume mediation or impaired local recovery.

Genetic and immune entry preserve that temporal logic without requiring the same upstream event. Genetic influences may alter systemic regulation, local transport, cytoskeletal organisation or energetic support, or more than one of these. Maternal immune activation can operate through transferred molecules, placental relay or altered vascular function; local neural and glial effects can also occur without a systemic sodium–volume deficit. Maternal conditions, fetal exposure and the fetus’s own response are distinct steps. Sections 6, 7, 18.5, and 18.6 explain these routes and their alternatives.

Persistence and later expression need not reproduce the initiating state. Altered circuit organisation may remain after blood chemistry and hormone levels normalise. Later illness, sensory activity or upright locomotion could reveal a consequence that was partly compensated earlier; the walking window is one possible source of added demand, not a universal initiating event. The central explanatory task is to connect the earlier recovery disturbance to a defined developmental change. A developmental route that preserves the relevant local recovery would challenge the common-process conjecture. Section 2 states this commitment; the chapters that follow develop the positive physiological account and the evidence that supports or limits its component links.

2 Core Physiological Claim

The common-process conjecture is that diverse genetic and physiological initiating conditions converge on difficulty restoring sodium-dependent ionic gradients or cellular volume during sensitive neural development. Within the proposed routes, this local neural or glial disturbance is the required intermediary. Recovery is assessed through the specified variable’s time to restoration, residual deviation and stability under matched or explicitly modelled initial disturbance, ongoing load and developmental conditions. Successful restoration is the comparator, including when it requires increased transport or metabolic support. To meet the developmental claim, recovery must be slower, less complete or less stable than in an appropriate comparator, and that difference must carry a defined developmental effect. Whether this process participates across all autistic trajectories remains a conjecture.

Increased inward NKCC1 flux can bring sodium with chloride and raise Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase work where the measured ion gradients support that flux (Brumback and Staley, 2008). Impaired KCC2-mediated chloride extrusion provides a distinct route to delayed restoration. Increased work with adequate recovery is insufficient, and increased ATP turnover need not deplete ATP. Extracellular ATP release, oxidative stress and loss of BH4–nitric-oxide support are additional, conditional links. Redox-dependent vascular dysfunction could initiate or amplify a recovery problem through impaired delivery or altered filling signals (Sections 16.8, 16.9, and 23).

Intrinsic cellular routes begin with constraints on local transport, energetic support or recovery capacity, without requiring preceding systemic sodium–volume instability. Here, intrinsic identifies the site of the constraint, not an exclusively genetic origin. Genetic influences can also act through systemic physiology or both levels. A variant or synaptic phenotype belongs within the common-process account when the recovery disturbance carries its developmental effect; ordinary neuronal dependence on sodium does not establish that connection (Sections 6 and 7).

Immune exposures provide another route to local initiation. Maternal inflammation, placental signalling and specific brain-reactive antibodies can change developmental conditions through different mechanisms. Sections 18.5 and 18.6 distinguish their measured effects from proposed recovery mediation, including routes without a preceding systemic sodium or circulating-volume deficit.

Systemic entry can recruit the protective AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad, autonomic vasomotor support and renal sodium–water responses. A hypothalamic branch may couple magnocellular AVP recruitment to dendritic modulation of neighbouring autonomic circuits (Son et al., 2013). The proposed balance shift is greater AVP-linked recruitment or weaker oxytocin-linked modulation in a specified circuit under comparable developmental demand. Peripheral, local brain and portal signalling remain distinct (Caraty et al., 1990), as do neuron abundance, release, clearance and receptor responsiveness. Restored filling and transport conditions normally permit withdrawal and recovery; continued disturbance requires renewed challenge, delayed withdrawal or failure of restoration.

The proposed enduring consequence is distributed imprinting: altered thresholds, structures or recovery responses in vascular, renal, autonomic, hypothalamic or cellular systems, or a lasting circuit change after physiology normalises. Co-occurrence alone does not establish that recovery carries a developmental effect. Normal routine chemistry neither excludes an earlier disturbance nor establishes hidden compensation, and an unsupported earlier episode cannot rescue an informative negative result. Section 23.13 develops these interpretive limits.

Impaired chloride recovery could alter GABA signalling and the timing of inhibitory maturation, although depolarising GABA can retain inhibitory function. Swelling, increased NKCC1 and an astrocyte-first sequence remain conditional. Later orthostatic, metabolic or sensorimotor demands may reveal or modify an enduring developmental consequence; walking is one possible challenge, not a required initiating event. A credible developmental bypass of the required local recovery disturbance would challenge universal scope. An intermediary that was simply not measured establishes neither a bypass nor support.

Table 2.1. Comparative tests of the proposed developmental recovery route

Claim Required comparison Supportive result Limiting result
A relevant local recovery disturbance is present (Sections 2 and 23.13.1). Compare recovery under matched developmental conditions with an appropriate comparator, alongside a separately assessed developmental endpoint. Slower, less complete or less stable recovery preceding or accompanying the specified developmental change identifies the proposed phenotype. Co-occurrence alone leaves mediation unresolved. A developmental effect despite adequately demonstrated preservation of the relevant recovery counts against this route. Normal serum sodium, a resting value or an inconclusive null is not that demonstration.
The recovery disturbance carries a developmental effect (Sections 23.13 and 50). Timely, sufficiently selective prevention or correction of the specified disturbance, with prevention or correction verified during the claimed causal interval and development assessed separately. Preventing the recovery disturbance reduces the developmental effect, with alternative direct developmental effects of the intervention addressed. This supports mediation in the specified route. The developmental effect persists despite timely, verified prevention of its proposed necessary disturbance. A credible bypass challenges universal participation while allowing contributions elsewhere. Broad upstream improvement or failed late reversal is not decisive.
A specified systemic disturbance initiates the route (Sections 1.2 and 23.13). Compare timely correction of the systemic exposure with timely correction of the local intermediary, verifying removal of the claimed upstream disturbance and what each correction changes. Systemic correction restores the local recovery process and its linked developmental outcome under the specified conditions, supporting that proposed sequence when direct intervention effects are addressed. Verified, timely systemic correction fails to restore local recovery when timely local correction succeeds. This weakens the specified systemic intermediary; direct genetic or immune entry remains possible. Correction after developmental conversion is not decisive.
A lasting response change reflects prior recovery history (Sections 9, 21.3, and 42). After exposure and the relevant ionic or cellular-volume disturbance resolve, compare later responses under matched current physiology, developmental stage and challenge. Assess correction during the earlier recovery interval. A history-dependent response difference remains under matched conditions and is reduced by correcting the earlier recovery disturbance, consistent with a recovery-dependent persistent change. Its developmental consequence remains a separate claim. Differences fully explained by current exposure or ordinary maturation weaken this persistent-calibration branch. Normal later physiology alone does not disprove an earlier developmental consequence.

Reading note. These comparisons concern the proposed ASD developmental route. Specify the relevant neural/glial compartment, developmental interval and required disturbance in advance; do not reassign them after an informative negative result. Compare recovery time, residual deviation and stability as appropriate, with the initial disturbance, ongoing load and developmental conditions matched or explicitly modelled. A resting value or larger initial perturbation cannot substitute for measuring the recovery trajectory. Positive results in selected routes do not establish universal participation. Skeletal effects may be parallel systemic consequences without neural mediation (Section 48). Sections 23.13 and 23.13.1 develop the interpretation.

Text description of Figure 2.1

The diagram, titled ‘Compensatory physiology and developmental recovery’, presents proposed systemic and local routes in the Sodium Struggle hypothesis. A top box identifies genetic, immune and environmental influences that may act at systemic sites, local sites or both. Dashed arrows lead to two parallel boxes, which are also joined by a dashed connection labelled ‘Conditional systemic–local interaction’.

The systemic-regulation box identifies protection of cell volume and integrity against hypo-osmotic swelling, and maintenance of effective circulation through filling, delivery, vascular tone and containment. Its inset describes early physiological defence involving AVP, RAAS, cortisol, sympathetic and renal responses. Recruitment is context-dependent, may be heightened or prolonged, and can involve conservation or corrective disposal. The local neural/glial capacity-and-demand box identifies ion transport and gradients, energy supply and delivery, and membrane and cytoskeletal support. It states that direct cellular constraints can occur without systemic disturbance, with Na⁺/K⁺ pumps, NKCC1/KCC2 and Kir4.1/AQP4 as examples.

Dashed arrows from both boxes converge on a requirement to measure local ionic or cell-volume recovery in neurons and glia during a sensitive developmental interval, comparing speed, completeness and stability after a load. A separate dashed arrow from systemic regulation leads to candidate parallel peripheral effects, listed as renal, vascular or skeletal changes.

From the recovery-measurement box, a solid, unarrowed fork compares two outcomes: adequate recovery preserved throughout the relevant interval; and slower, incomplete or unstable recovery relative to an appropriate comparator. Only the impaired-recovery outcome has a dashed arrow to proposed developmental effects, specified as altered circuit development or function. The accompanying test condition refers to Table 2.1: a developmental effect despite preserved local recovery throughout the causal interval limits this proposed route.

The legend distinguishes dashed arrows for proposed contribution or mediation from solid lines for recovery comparison. A final note includes acute, recurrent, sustained and mixed histories, with timing and spacing considered relative to recovery. The diagram supplies no numerical measurements or calibrated durations.

Figure 2.1. Compensatory physiology and proposed developmental recovery routes. Genetic, immune and environmental influences may act at systemic and local sites. Early defence can limit emerging low states; normal values alone cannot establish hidden compensation. Underfilling can sustain AVP. AVP-mediated water retention can create dilutional pressure when water becomes disproportionate to effective solute, whereas low tonicity ordinarily suppresses AVP. Dashed arrows show proposed contributions or mediation; the solid fork compares recovery outcomes. The developmental route requires impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carrying a defined developmental effect. Peripheral effects branch separately. Preserved relevant recovery throughout the causal interval limits this route (Table 2.1); later recovery can follow an earlier developmental effect.

3 The Physical Constraint

Text description of Figure 3.1

The diagram, titled ‘Three coupled physical constraints’, arranges three regulatory components in a triangle. At the top is extracellular tonicity, described in terms of effective solutes and water. At the lower left is effective circulating volume, described in terms of filling and delivery. At the lower right is vascular tone and containment, described in terms of resistance and distribution.

Solid double-headed arrows connect every pair: tonicity with circulating volume, tonicity with vascular tone and containment, and circulating volume with vascular tone and containment. The central label is ‘Coupled regulation’. These links depict physiological coupling rather than a sequence or an obligatory failure of simultaneous regulation.

A dashed downward arrow leads from the coupled system to a conditional statement: if a specified demand exceeds available reserve, competing costs may limit local delivery or recovery. This dashed link marks the proposed cost under that condition, distinct from the solid coupling arrows. The closing note states that successful simultaneous regulation remains possible, with no obligatory trade-off and no fixed hormone profile. No numerical values, thresholds or measured outcomes are plotted.

Figure 3.1. The Tri-Axial Constraint. Solid double arrows indicate physiological coupling, not an inability to regulate all three variables successfully. The dashed link marks the proposed cost under a specified limitation of reserve. Local delivery and ionic or volume recovery must be measured; intrinsic cellular routes need not pass through this systemic geometry.

Sodium–water balance, effective circulation and vascular containment form a coupled physical system in which successful simultaneous regulation remains possible. Developmental exposure and response histories unfold within this system; Section 10 develops their maternal–fetal transformation.

The central constraint is conditional: when demand exceeds available reserve, stabilising extracellular tonicity, effective circulating volume, and vascular tone or containment can impose competing costs. The developmental question is which trade-off becomes limiting, in which compartment and for how long.

Instability in one axis can change the work required from the others, and vascular tone and containment can independently fail or be recruited as compensation even when measured sodium or total water appear acceptable.

3.1 The Tri-Axial Constraint

Hyponatraemia and hypovolaemia remain distinct clinical states; hypertonic exposure and genuine volume expansion can also perturb the coupled developmental control problem. Extracellular tonicity, effective circulating volume, and vascular tone or containment are three interacting constraints. Tonicity concerns effective extracellular solute relative to water and its influence on cellular water distribution. Vascular tone alters resistance and blood distribution; containment concerns retention of circulating fluid. Adequate arterial pressure need not guarantee regional delivery. Here, effective sodium is the manuscript’s shorthand for sodium-dependent support of extracellular stability, not a separately sensed analyte. Effective filling concerns circulatory adequacy rather than total body water. The proposed tri-axial constraint arises when a specified limitation prevents compensation from preserving both local delivery and cellular conditions without additional cost. Water-first and volume-first disturbances can enter that problem through different mechanisms; their convergence must be measured. These physical constraints are distinct from the AVP–RAAS–cortisol response triad (§1.3). Their sensory and regulatory control is treated in Table 15.1 Panel B, not as another physical axis.

3.2 Trade-Offs Within the Constraint

Protective responses can recruit water conservation, sodium conservation and vascular support together. Vasopressin rapidly increases collecting-duct water permeability, but it also activates ENaC-mediated sodium transport within minutes (Wall et al., 1992; Bugaj et al., 2009). These findings establish rapid responses in separate preparations, not a universal sequence in which water conservation precedes sodium conservation. Their separation is nevertheless possible: in an adult human experiment, amiloride prevented the sodium-retaining response to dDAVP while substantial antidiuresis remained (Blanchard et al., 2011).

The proposed trade-off arises when available supply, ongoing losses or impaired transport prevent water and effective-solute balance from remaining matched. Conserving the sodium that remains is different from replacing sodium already lost. Maturity-dependent neonatal sodium handling provides one measured constraint on net sodium balance (Al-Dahhan et al., 1983; §14.4). Under such a constraint, relatively greater water retention can lower extracellular tonicity while helping conserve fluid. The relevant quantities are net water and solute balance over the same interval, rather than a hormone concentration or channel response alone.

Compensation can also act by disposal. When effective filling is genuinely expanded, reduced sodium-conserving drive and increased sodium excretion can help restore balance; this differs from fluid excess accompanied by underfilling (§15). Sodium and water responses need not move together. During continuing antidiuresis, natriuresis can offset expansion while leaving the water–solute relation incompletely corrected (§14.3.3). Successful disposal that restores filling and tonicity without a local recovery deficit remains the compensatory comparator.

The hypothesis locates the cost at the point where these protective adjustments leave a residual problem for circulation or cellular recovery. Limited fluid availability may increase reliance on vascular support; dilution may increase the work of restoring cellular conditions. Successful combined regulation remains possible. A trade-off is therefore specified by the limiting reserve, affected compartment and residual disturbance.

3.3 Microperfusion and Endothelial Ion Transport

Microperfusion provides a possible link between systemic compensation and local cellular restoration. A change in tonicity, vascular regulation or fluid distribution can alter delivery without reducing total body water. The relevant question is whether compensatory responses preserve flow in the tissue and interval that require it.

Acute water intoxication in adult mice disturbed cerebral capillary flow, and Aqp4 deletion modified flow distribution and the accompanying reduction in microvessel diameter (Bordoni et al., 2023). This supports a local vascular consequence of acute oedema, although the large water challenge and raised intracranial pressure limit extrapolation to ordinary developmental fluctuations. Endfoot expansion and altered vasoactive signalling were not isolated as competing explanations. Vascular regulation also provides a distinct route. Low sodium dilated isolated rat middle cerebral arteries through an endothelium-dependent response that reversed under NO/cGMP inhibition (Klapczyńska et al., 2023). In smaller parenchymal arterioles exposed to low sodium with AVP, constriction and impaired ATP-evoked dilation occurred; correcting osmolality restored the ATP response without reversing constriction (Aleksandrowicz, 2025). Thus, protective dilation, osmotic effects and sodium-dependent regulation can contribute differently according to the vascular compartment and available reserve.

Flow disturbance must also be distinguished from barrier leakage and systemic underfilling. Acute experimental hyponatraemia produced brain oedema without increased sodium-fluorescein permeability in a rat study (Aleksandrowicz et al., 2025). Swelling therefore does not establish plasma escape. The proposed developmental link is that insufficient local delivery could constrain neural or glial ionic or cell-volume restoration (§2); a further claim of renewed systemic volume defence requires independent evidence of altered effective filling. Microperfusion remains a candidate bottleneck for these systemic routes, not a requirement imposed on intrinsic cellular entry.

The blood–brain endothelium provides a further candidate interface between systemic compensation and local recovery. A circulating signal could alter transport at that interface without itself entering the brain or causing generalised barrier leakage. The proposed sequence is altered endothelial transport, changed conditions for neural or glial ionic or cell-volume restoration, and a developmental effect only where restoration becomes inadequate.

Primary experiments identify responsive transport machinery. Lam et al. (2009) located NHE1 and NHE2 predominantly on the blood-facing membrane of rat brain microvascular endothelium. In cultured bovine endothelial cells, AVP increased sodium-dependent hydrogen extrusion through a V1-sensitive, calcium-dependent mechanism; V2 blockade did not prevent the response. Yuen et al. (2014) found that hypoxia, aglycaemia and 100 nM AVP increased exchange activity over 1–5 hours, with selective increases in total-cell NHE1 abundance and no significant increase in NHE2 abundance. ERK inhibition suppressed acute stimulation. These measurements concern cellular exchange and intracellular-pH recovery after acid loading, rather than net transport across a complete barrier.

Complementary evidence concerns NKCC1 and brain sodium entry. AVP increased bumetanide-sensitive rubidium uptake, a cotransport assay, in human and bovine cerebral endothelial cells and freshly isolated microvessels, with V1- and calcium-dependent signalling (O’Donnell et al., 2005). In rats subjected to permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, predominantly luminal cotransporter localisation and reduced oedema after intravenous bumetanide supported an endothelial contribution (O’Donnell et al., 2004). A later study from the same group measured reduced accumulation of total and extravascular brain sodium with intravenous HOE-642 or bumetanide, alongside less oedema (O’Donnell et al., 2013). Separate small control experiments found no significant differences in plasma electrolytes or mean arterial pressure. The early-ischaemia design and prior permeability evidence support transport before expected barrier breakdown; the pharmacological effects do not exclusively isolate endothelial transport from all other actions.

For the developmental hypothesis, these findings supply a conditional transport route alongside the microperfusion route above. Luminal sodium entry would have to be coupled to transport toward the brain, and altered extracellular conditions would have to exceed local compensatory capacity or prolong recovery. The decisive extension is whether developmentally relevant exposures produce that sequence, with endothelial transport, perfusion, permeability and neural or glial recovery measured separately. Cell-culture AVP concentrations and severe rodent ischaemia are not measured infant exposure conditions. Successful regulation remains the comparator, and normal serum chemistry alone neither establishes nor excludes the proposed local disturbance (Sections 2 and 23.13).

4 The Cost of Defence

Defence is protective. Under limited reserve, one response can increase the cost of another, creating a feedback problem whose persistence depends on the effectiveness and timing of recovery.

The proposed developmental cost arises when impaired local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery changes the development of transporter responses, osmolyte handling, receptor sensitivity or structural reserve. Additional work with adequate recovery remains successful compensation.

Systemic entry: an oxygen-delivery example. A proposed systemic route is reduced tissue delivery that limits neuronal oxygen supply. Its local recovery step is experimentally measurable: after five minutes of chemically induced anoxia with glucose available, cultured postnatal rat hippocampal neurons returned intracellular sodium concentration to baseline after reoxygenation; inhibiting the sodium pump prevented recovery (Sheldon et al., 2004). The measured variable is the sodium trajectory, and uninhibited restoration is the successful comparator. The developmental hypothesis is that a specified delivery constraint prolongs recovery during a susceptible developmental interval sufficiently to alter circuit maturation. Systemic initiation and recovery-mediated developmental change remain separate proposed links; this culture experiment established neither (Section 14.7).

Intrinsic entry: chloride recovery. A genetic constraint can alter local recovery without a preceding systemic episode. In human stem-cell-derived, MECP2-deficient Rett-model neurons, KW-2449 shortened the SuperClomeleon chloride-signal recovery time constant towards the isogenic wild-type value, compared with vehicle treatment (Tang et al., 2019). The local variable is intracellular chloride restoration, rather than transporter abundance alone. The developmental test is whether selective correction of this recovery phenotype, under comparable loading, changes inhibitory maturation or synapse development. The measured drug response does not establish that mediation, because KCC2 and the drug have other actions. Sections 6.4 and 23 retain the full evidence and causal tests.

The proposed feedback begins when protective recruitment changes the conditions under which local recovery must occur. With water and effective-solute balance incompletely matched (§3.2), conservation can preserve fluid while leaving a dilutional challenge. In fetal life, that challenge may originate outside the fetal kidney: maternal dDAVP-induced dilution lowered fetal plasma sodium concentration despite increased fetal urine output in sheep (Roberts et al., 1999). Maternal antidiuresis, fetal exposure and fetal renal compensation are therefore distinct steps. The developmental question is whether the resulting disturbance impairs local neural or glial recovery during a susceptible window.

A fall in extracellular tonicity can drive cellular water entry. Swelling can also recruit protective responses. Regulatory volume decrease exports intracellular osmoles through coordinated ion and organic-solute pathways, allowing water to leave. LRRC8A knockdown slowed and reduced tested volume recovery in cultured rat cortical astrocytes, identifying a VRAC-dependent component in that preparation (Formaggio et al., 2019; Section 24). Recovery of cell size need not restore the previous solute composition. Conversely, incomplete solute restitution does not establish continuing swelling. Each endpoint requires its own measurement.

Successful compensation restores filling while cellular volume regulation and subsequent solute recovery resolve the local disturbance. If restoration is incomplete, the proposed feedback can take different forms. Local flow or vascular regulation may remain impaired during recovery (§3.3), limiting delivery without any additional loss of circulating volume. Alternatively, a separately demonstrated permeability or redistribution disturbance may reduce effective filling and sustain antidiuretic or vasomotor recruitment. That second branch requires evidence of altered filling and regulatory output; local swelling or reduced flow alone does not establish it.

Both routes retain restoring brakes: recovery of pressure and filling reduces conservation signals, renal water and solute handling re-equilibrate, and local cellular restoration proceeds. The hypothesis concerns a measured residual disturbance that persists into a subsequent challenge or a susceptible developmental interval. Repeated exposure, positive feedback and unequal recovery times do not themselves demonstrate oscillation, accumulating injury or developmental harm; the relevant local recovery deficit and its developmental consequence remain separate requirements (§2).

4.1 Energetic Cost

The proposed energetic cost arises when restoration demands exceed the supply available to developing neurons or glia. Water movement and downhill channel-mediated efflux do not directly consume ATP. Re-establishing ionic gradients requires active transport, including Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity; cotransporters such as NKCC1 depend on the gradients that pumping maintains. The relevant burden is the additional restoration work relative to metabolic and delivery reserve, rather than every movement of water or osmoles.

In cultured embryonic mouse cortical neurons subjected to oxygen–glucose deprivation and reoxygenation, NKCC1 inhibition or deletion preserved ATP and sodium homeostasis (Chen et al., 2010b). This supports a connection between ion loading and energetic vulnerability under injury conditions, although reduced pump work was not isolated from other protection. Neonatal recordings also show that pump activity can shift the chloride equilibrium without establishing continuously increased pump work thereafter (Brumback & Staley, 2008). The preparation- and timing-dependent mechanisms are developed in Section 23.

Under the hypothesis, restricted local delivery could prolong ionic or cell-volume recovery if ATP resupply and other compensatory routes cannot meet restoration demand. Increased transport, altered chloride or reduced perfusion alone does not establish that limitation. The developmental claim requires a measured local recovery deficit and its consequence for a defined neural or glial process; successful energetic compensation remains possible.

4.2 Timing Cost

The timing cost concerns the overlap of three intervals: the initiating disturbance, restoration of the affected cellular variable, and the developmental process occurring during that interval. These intervals need not coincide. Serum sodium, tissue water, ionic gradients and organic-solute pools are distinct recovery endpoints. If renewed challenge arrives while a relevant residual remains, separate episodes could produce sustained local difficulty during a susceptible developmental window. Recurrence alone does not establish that residual or its consequence.

An initiating disturbance may be a single episode with prolonged recovery, recurrent challenges before restitution, a sustained exposure, or a mixture. Severity, duration, challenge spacing, developmental stage, affected tissue or circuit and intrinsic reserve are separate candidate determinants. These patterns are not diagnosis-specific, and neither a diagnosis nor episode count reconstructs the physiological history. The proposed mechanism requires the specified recovery disturbance to carry a developmental effect; complete restoration without that effect remains successful adaptation.

Text description of Figure 4.1

The diagram, titled ‘Defence and recovery can run on different clocks’, explicitly presents conceptual timing only, with no calibrated durations or measured traces. Its upper row contains three boxes joined from left to right by solid arrows: ‘Challenge’, ‘Protective defence’ and ‘Restoration begins’.

A dashed downward arrow from protective defence leads to a separate measurement box. This calls for restitution to be measured through ionic and volume recovery, osmolyte replenishment, transporter/aquaporin localisation and response withdrawal. The placement distinguishes the protective response and the beginning of restoration from the separate assessment of recovery processes.

Two dashed arrows then lead to contrasting branches. In the left branch, restitution completes and recovery occurs before rechallenge. In the right branch, rechallenge arrives early and residual disturbance may persist. The latter is conditional: the diagram does not report that a residual was measured or that it necessarily persists. Neither branch is assigned a numerical duration, frequency or recovery rate.

The closing statement identifies the Osmotic Pendulum as a dynamics proposal and states that unequal response times alone do not demonstrate oscillation. The branches therefore organise a comparison of recovery relative to rechallenge without displaying an observed oscillatory trajectory.

Figure 4.1. The Osmotic Pendulum as a time-scale mismatch proposal. Protective defence and the relevant recovery processes must be measured separately. The branches distinguish complete restitution from rechallenge before restitution. Neither their ordering nor unequal kinetics proves oscillation, persistent gain or developmental harm; those outcomes require their own time-resolved measurements.

Adult rats with severe chronic hyponatraemia illustrate unequal restoration: after rapid correction, brain sodium and chloride overshot, tissue water fell, and organic-solute replenishment lagged (Lien et al., 1991). By day seven, tissue water was near normal while myo-inositol remained reduced in the rapid-correction group. This establishes different recovery trajectories, not persistent swelling or a fetal recovery timetable. The severity and correction injury limit developmental extrapolation. Conversely, neuronal and astrocytic swelling in mouse slices largely reversed after normal medium was restored, including with repeated challenges (Murphy et al., 2017). Such washout recovery differs from volume regulation during continuing hypotonicity.

For the proposed timing mechanism, the residual must therefore be identified in the relevant neural or glial compartment and, where recurrence is proposed, measured before the next challenge. Its duration must overlap a specified process, such as migration or maturation, and alter that process through impaired local ionic or cell-volume recovery (Sections 2, 23, and 24). Fetal restoration also remains coupled to maternal and placental exchange. The hypothesis concerns this demonstrable overlap, rather than a universal recovery clock or inevitable accumulation of osmolyte debt. Neonatal sodium associations provide developmental context, but do not measure this intermediary (Section 12). Recurrently exposed adult rats also showed an attenuated imaging response to a later water challenge, although complete physiological restitution was not established (Tejedor et al., 2026; §23.6).

4.3 Imprinting Cost

Repeated conditions during development could leave a changed regulatory starting state, including altered transporter responsiveness, osmolyte regulation or receptor sensitivity. Three outcomes must be separated: residual disturbance before restitution; altered responsiveness after relevant current conditions have normalised; and a developmental effect that remains after the acute physiology resolves. They can interact, but none establishes the others. An imprint need not be irreversible or require a permanently abnormal sodium concentration.

Experimental precedents show how later regulation can change. After prenatal water restriction, lambs had altered AVP-release thresholds, although hypertonicity and hypertension persisted at assessment and maternal nutritional restriction accompanied dehydration (Desai et al., 2003b). Early stress in mice left sustained hypothalamic Avp expression and altered regulatory-region methylation (Murgatroyd et al., 2009). These findings identify regulatory plasticity without establishing sodium–volume mediation. For the present hypothesis, impaired local recovery must carry a defined developmental effect. Later physiological normalisation may leave that consequence intact; adequate recovery without the predicted effect remains successful adaptation. Sections 21.4.3 and 36.3 develop the component precedents, while Section 23.13 distinguishes a retained recovery defect from a consequence of an earlier disturbance.

5 Divergent Defence Geometries

Text description of Figure 5.1

The diagram, titled ‘Protective defence can use different weightings’, begins with the shared aim of protecting effective filling and extracellular stability. Two dashed downward arrows lead from this aim to proposed ‘wet’ and ‘dry’ weightings.

The wet weighting gives relatively greater reliance to antidiuretic water conservation. Its conditional cost is stated as dilution and volume-recovery load if water outpaces solute. The dry weighting gives relatively greater reliance to solute conservation and tone. Its conditional cost is stated as delivery and distribution load if the filling margin narrows. The two columns thus identify different proposed allocations and different conditions under which a load may arise. They do not supply measured hormone concentrations, sodium values or volume changes.

A solid double-headed horizontal arrow beneath both columns is labelled ‘Continuous allocation’, ‘mixed responses’ and ‘changes over time’. It presents the weightings as a continuum that permits mixtures and temporal changes. The closing notes identify them as proposed physiological weightings rather than diagnostic categories, and state that history dependence requires matched current inputs and measured responses. The figure contains no quantitative scale or measured response trajectories.

Figure 5.1. Wet and dry defence geometries as continuous response weightings. Both seek protective stabilisation; conditional costs fall on different constraints. These are proposed combinations, not diagnostic groups or obligatory AVP concentrations. The illustrated solute-conservation/tone pairing is conditional; sodium balance, AVP activity and actual volume must be measured separately. Hysteresis requires different responses under matched current inputs after different histories. Local neural or glial recovery remains a separate developmental endpoint.

The physiological and genetic reserve constraints considered in Sections 3, 4, and 6 may favour different combinations of water conservation, solute handling and vascular support. Figure 5.1 organises these combinations as continuous response weightings. Their physiological components have experimental support; their grouping into developmental defence geometries remains a hypothesis. A response can preserve immediate stability without generating either a residual disturbance or a developmental cost.

5.1 Defence Weighted Towards Water Conservation

A “wet” weighting gives relatively greater emphasis to antidiuretic water conservation during a filling challenge. This can support fluid availability, but does not establish volume expansion: the result depends on intake, ongoing losses, solute balance and redistribution. In fetal sheep, three days of elevated AVP reduced extracellular volume while increasing the plasma-to-interstitial volume ratio (Gibson and Lumbers, 1997). The ratio alone does not show that plasma volume increased. AVP concentration also cannot specify the allocation: V1a-null mice had altered circulating volume and baroreflex function despite normal plasma AVP (Koshimizu et al., 2006).

The proposed cost arises if water retention is disproportionate to effective-solute retention, lowering extracellular tonicity. Cells then face an additional volume-regulatory and recovery task (§4). Its developmental relevance depends on the local disturbance, compensatory capacity and recovery interval; antidiuresis alone demonstrates neither swelling nor failed recovery. Successful water conservation with maintained tonicity remains ordinary protection.

5.2 Defence Weighted Towards Vascular Support

A “dry” weighting gives relatively greater emphasis to vascular support. Solute conservation could accompany this response, as illustrated in Figure 5.1, but sodium balance, AVP activity and actual circulating volume are separate measurements. Low-renin hypertension is not intrinsically AVP-sparing: plasma AVP was higher in 48 untreated men with low-renin hypertension than in 29 normotensive comparisons (Os et al., 1986). These adult findings neither identify a developmental subgroup nor invalidate a possible low-AVP response under other conditions.

Resistance and regional capacitance also have different consequences. In healthy adults, lower-body negative pressure and upright tilt both reduced thoracic volume and increased regional resistance, but changed splanchnic volume in opposite directions (Taneja et al., 2007; §16.5). Thus greater resistance does not establish a smaller circulating volume or the absence of pooling. A conditional cost arises where the recruited vascular response preserves pressure while local delivery or recruitment reserve remains inadequate. The affected tissue and its actual supply must be identified.

Such underdelivery could constrain biosynthesis, but a selective “dry” vulnerability of heparan sulphate scaffolding or cholesterol-dependent construction is unproven. Hypoxia reduced sulphate incorporation into cell-associated heparan sulphate in bovine endothelial cultures, without reducing measured heparin-like activity (Karlinsky et al., 1992). In cultured hepatoma cells, hypoxia reduced final cholesterol synthesis despite an adaptive response that preserved squalene monooxygenase activity (Coates et al., 2023). These findings support oxygen-sensitive components, not the complete developmental chain. The proposed link is that underdelivery constrains local biosynthesis and thereby makes ionic or cell-volume recovery harder. Its developmental relevance requires impaired neural or glial recovery carrying a defined developmental effect (§§2 and 35); either response weighting could encounter such limitations.

5.3 Shared Constraint, Divergent Weightings

“Wet” and “dry” are descriptive weights that can coexist and change over time. Water availability, renal responsiveness, vascular mechanics and cellular recovery reserve could alter their balance. A hormone snapshot, urinary concentration or normal cuff pressure cannot identify the proposed allocation or its cost. Low CSF AVP does not establish a systemic dry state (§36.5).

History dependence is a separate claim. Human baroreflex responses differ during falling and rising pressure, but vary between trials (Studinger et al., 2007); depressed baroreceptor gain after chronic renal hypertension in rats recovered within 90–120 minutes of pressure reversal (Moreira et al., 1990; §16.9). These comparisons motivate measurements under matched current conditions, including relevant volume and vascular mechanics. They do not establish developmental imprinting. The developmental endpoint remains impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery, with its subsequent consequence measured separately.

Part B Developmental context and routes of entry

6 Genetic Initiation and Recovery Bandwidth

Genetic variation can initiate the proposed physiological burden as well as modify its cost. Section 4 explains the local restoration tasks and the comparison with successful recovery relevant to the proposed developmental connection. Direct disruption of ion transport, energy supply or cellular organisation may constrain developing neural or glial tissue without a preceding maternal or peripheral disturbance (Section 7). Other variants may reduce structural reserve, amplify defence recruitment or limit restoration after a challenge. The hypothesis therefore treats genetic initiation, susceptibility and recovery capacity as distinct causal roles. None follows solely from an autism association, and a gene’s established developmental effect may also operate through a route that bypasses the proposed intermediary.

Autism’s substantial heritability is compatible with a physiological mediator but does not identify one. Bai et al. (2019) reported a median country-specific heritability estimate of 80.8% and maternal-effect estimates of 0.4–1.6%. Their maternal component concerns maternal genetic influences beyond offspring inheritance; it is not a ceiling on all pregnancy-specific exposures. These results constrain proposals in which stable maternal traits account for a large share of autism liability independently of inherited offspring susceptibility. A fetal genetic effect could operate through physiological regulation or through a direct neural route. Distinguishing those routes requires measuring the intermediary, not assigning the inherited variance to sodium–volume defence by interpretation.

FOXP1 provides a candidate intrinsic route into altered hypothalamic neuropeptide-system composition. In postnatal-day-10 male Foxp1+/− mice, Berkhout et al. (2026) found fewer oxytocin- and vasopressin-labelled neurons in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei than in wild-type littermates, with a greater oxytocin reduction and a lower OXT/AVP labelled-cell ratio. Whether this altered composition changes the functional balance of hypothalamic signalling, water regulation or recovery remains to be tested. These counts describe labelled-cell composition, not hormone output or the AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad; an intrinsic genetic route need not involve prior osmotic stress.

6.1 Structural Reserve

Structural reserve is one such constraint. Nephron endowment is established during a limited developmental window and can constrain later renal responses, but it does not by itself specify whole-kidney filtration, sodium–water handling or hormonal gain. The proposed gain amplifier is conditional: where fewer functioning nephrons reduce the relevant reserve, a matched challenge may require greater or more prolonged regulatory work. Structural endowment and successful physiological compensation must therefore be measured separately (Section 32).

6.2 Genetic Routes into Physiological Demand and Defence Execution

Molecular resilience and response capacity determine what a genetic constraint does under demand. Tables 6.1 and 6.2 bring selected measured examples from Bell's frozen Satterstrom-102 classification into the proposed architecture (Bell, 2026c). Table 6.1 concerns sodium conservation, neuropeptide deployment, respiratory control and vascular or lymphatic support; Table 6.2 concerns local ionic regulation and cellular organisation. These are physiological roles, not a primary–secondary causal hierarchy. An intrinsic neural or glial route can initiate the proposed process without a preceding maternal or systemic sodium–volume disturbance.

Selection key: ‘102; counted’ identifies membership in the fixed Satterstrom-102 set and a Yes/1 qualifying component in the frozen v46.20 audit. It does not mean that impaired local recovery or its developmental mediation was demonstrated. Ten selected genes have that status; KCNJ10 and SLC12A5 are external mechanistic benchmarks and do not enter the frozen 42/102 numerator. TCF7L2's counted component is separate from its astrocyte example below. Selection favours a defined model, informative measured physiology and a testable missing connection; it is neither a ranking of autism risk nor an enrichment analysis. The exact variant, dosage, tissue and developmental stage remain part of each claim.

Table 6.1. Selected genetic routes into physiological demand and defence execution

Gene and selection Measured variant or model finding Proposed connection and boundary

NR3C2

102; counted

 Heterozygous loss-of-function variants causing renal pseudohypoaldosteronism impair mineralocorticoid-receptor execution of sodium conservation despite increased renin and aldosterone. Adult carriers can maintain normal extracellular water and blood pressure with increased salt appetite (Escoubet et al., 2013). Conservation can be constrained while compensation succeeds. An ASD-associated allele’s functional direction and effects on reserve or local recovery remain unresolved; obligatory underfilling does not follow from the gene label.

FOXP1

102; counted

 Postnatal-day-10 male Foxp1+/− mice had fewer AVP- and OXT-labelled hypothalamic neurons, with OXT disproportionately affected (Berkhout et al., 2026). Labelled-cell abundance does not measure hormone secretion. Altered neuropeptide-system composition could change response capacity. Challenge-evoked release and water regulation remain unresolved. Systemic and local developmental FOXP1 effects are distinct; neither requires prior osmotic stress.

STXBP1

102; counted

 Heterozygous Munc18-1 reduction in cultured mouse hippocampal neurons impaired activity-evoked dense-core-vesicle secretion, especially its initial high-demand phase; vesicle abundance was preserved (Puntman et al., 2021). Secretory deployment capacity may constrain response to demand. The reporters were not AVP/OXT assays; direct synaptic or trophic effects and systemic peptide output remain separate possibilities.

TCF4

102; counted

 Heterozygous Tcf4-truncation mice showed unstable breathing, prolonged post-sigh apnoea and markedly blunted ventilation during CO₂ challenge, despite similar average resting ventilation (Cleary et al., 2021). Respiratory-controller reserve could constrain physiological support during demand. Neither sodium loss nor deficient brain perfusion was demonstrated; direct neural TCF4 effects remain an alternative.

VEZF1

102; counted

 Heterozygous Vezf1 loss in mouse embryos produced incompletely penetrant lymphatic hypervascularisation with local jugular oedema and haemorrhage (Kuhnert et al., 2005). Altered vascular or lymphatic development could limit fluid-return or delivery reserve. Local embryonic oedema does not establish generalised leakage, chronic hypovolaemia or a particular ASD-associated variant’s physiology.
6.2.1 Additional candidates for physiological response and reserve

Further pathway candidates remain worth testing, with cohort membership and functional qualification assessed separately:

REN: renin synthesis and availability provide a candidate source of variation in sodium–volume recruitment; altered thresholds or persistence require functional measurement.

HSD11B2: cortisol–mineralocorticoid receptor specificity provides a candidate route by which a variant could shift sodium defence towards cortisol-mediated substitution.

WNK / KLHL3 pathway components: candidate links between chloride-sensitive regulation and renal transport. The proposed proxy-signal bias requires variant- and tissue-specific testing. Section 23.7 distinguishes normal replenishment from altered recovery in defined neural models; renal and neural effects of the same variant require separate measurement.

AQP4: Controls astrocytic water flux and extracellular space dynamics, potentially influencing the initiation and resolution of osmotic stress signals.

AGT / ACE: candidate RAAS-related influences on defence gain and recovery kinetics under matched upstream inputs; the variant-specific functional effect and direction require measurement.

6.3 Genetic Constraints on Local Ionic Regulation and Developmental Reserve

Table 6.2 makes the local entry route explicit through channel function, structural adaptation, astrocytic responses and a direct chloride-recovery assay. A changed current, cell size or resting value is distinct from impaired post-challenge restoration; the proposed developmental connection is considered in Sections 6.4 and 23.13.

Table 6.2. Selected genetic constraints on local ionic regulation and developmental reserve

Gene and selection Measured variant or model finding Proposed connection and boundary

SCN2A

102; counted

 Autism-associated SCN2A variants expressed in HEK293 cells reduced or abolished NaV1.2 currents or altered gating towards loss of function (Ben-Shalom et al., 2017). This directly connects autism-ascertained variants with channel physiology. Altered channel function could change activity-related ionic recovery; reduced current alone implies neither excess sodium loading nor impaired recovery. Adequate recovery would constrain this connection.

ANK2

102; counted

 CRISPR-engineered heterozygous p.Arg1225* human iPSC-derived excitatory neurons had hyperactive, desynchronised networks and failed to adjust axon-initial-segment length appropriately during sustained activity suppression or stimulation (Teunissen et al., 2023). Impaired structural adaptation could alter subsequent ionic demand or restoration. The measured endpoint is homeostatic structural plasticity, not sodium, chloride or volume-recovery kinetics.

SHANK3

102; counted

 In Shank3+/ΔC mice, targeting actin regulators rescued reduced prefrontal F-actin and NMDAR synaptic function (Duffney et al., 2015). Shank3B-null mice retained GABA driving force and inhibition at the tested ages (Chiesa et al., 2019). The scaffold–receptor route is experimentally modifiable; recovery effects remain allele-, circuit- and stage-specific. The Shank3B counterexample prevents one SHANK3 model from standing for another (Section 23.7).

TCF7L2

102; counted

 Postnatal astrocyte-specific biallelic deletion enlarged astrocytes, altered extracellular amino acids and lowered extracellular potassium at one sampled post-pulse endpoint (Popek et al., 2026). These observations do not establish slower clearance or volume-recovery kinetics. Altered astrocyte structure and extracellular ions could change neuronal support; recovery mediation remains unresolved. The frozen count rests on separate beta-cell physiology. Rare neurodevelopmental alleles, common diabetes variants and conditional deletion are distinct contexts.

GFAP

102; counted

 Gfap-null mice showed slower astrocytic swelling and less challenge-induced extracellular-space narrowing during high potassium, hypotonic exposure or spreading depression than controls (Anderová et al., 2001). Slower swelling is not impaired recovery. Null and toxic mutant models are distinct; a filament-dependent volume response does not specify recovery direction or developmental cost.

SLC12A5

KCC2

External benchmark

 R952H and R1049C slowed chloride-sensor recovery after a three-minute KCl/glycine load in transfected Neuro2a cells in an epilepsy study (Kahle et al., 2014). Both variants were later detected in ASD (Merner et al., 2015); association limits are detailed below. Direct variant-to-recovery component evidence; developmental mediation in ASD and persistent swelling remain unestablished. A positive GABAA reversal shift does not itself abolish inhibition (Sections 23 and 26).

KCNJ10

Kir4.1

External benchmark

 In selected ASD-cohort variants, R18Q increased membrane expression and current in U251 astrocytoma cells; R348H reduced pH-dependent inhibition in oocytes (Sicca et al., 2016). These gain-of-function effects differ from EAST-syndrome loss of function (Reichold et al., 2010). Allele-specific glial potassium handling could change local recovery. Neither reduced buffering nor greater swelling follows automatically from KCNJ10 association.

The SLC12A5 benchmark also requires an association boundary. Merner et al. (2015) found no enrichment in the initial targeted ASD screen; combined datasets showed a nominal signal for all coding C-terminal regulatory-domain variants (P = 0.03), but not nonsynonymous variants alone (P = 0.31), with different sequencing pipelines limiting interpretation. This does not remove the measured chloride-clearance defect, but keeps its experimental origin and autism relevance distinct.

6.3.1 Additional candidates for local recovery and developmental reserve

The receptor, sterol, matrix and metabolic examples developed in the later mechanism-specific sections remain relevant beyond the fixed-cohort selection. Further pathway candidates for membrane stability, ion–water handling and recovery reserve are listed below; they are not additions to the frozen 42/102 count:

Sterol trafficking and membrane reserve: NPC1 and NPC2 (intracellular cholesterol mobilisation), ABCA1 (cholesterol export), APOE (lipid delivery), and CAV1 (membrane organisation). Table 35.1 separates measured variant effects from pathway candidates.

Astrocytic ion–water coupling: AQP4 (water flux speed), GJA1 (Connexin-43 spatial buffering), SNTA1/DTNA (anchoring of perivascular end-feet).

Osmolyte recovery: SLC6A6 (taurine), SLC6A12 (betaine), SLC5A3 (myo-inositol), LRRC8A (volume-regulated anion channel [VRAC]-mediated loss).

Barrier integrity: CLDN5, OCLN (tight-junction resilience), MFSD2A (lipid support).

Mitochondrial and autonomic reserve: PPARGC1A (recovery capacity), SOD2 (redox buffering), ADRA2A (sympathetic termination).

6.4 Interpretive Conclusion

Genetic variation can therefore determine where instability begins and which restorative step becomes limiting. The hypothesis considers intrinsic neural or glial disruption alongside reduced renal, vascular and energetic reserve. These are possible causal entry points, not merely modifiers of a prior maternal disturbance. The proposed shared contribution is a local ionic or volume-recovery disturbance that alters neural development. Convergence remains subject to the causal boundary in Section 2.

Bell's frozen phenotype-first classification makes these candidate entry points explicit: 42 of the externally fixed Satterstrom-102 genes each cleared one strict primary gate across ten heterogeneous endpoint families (Bell, 2026c). Fifteen qualify through current, receptor or GABA-related endpoints: 12 in direct ion transport and excitability and three in chloride/GABA-related function. Their neuronal location is consistent with an ionic mechanism, but neither identifies its developmental cost nor establishes altered chloride gradients in all 15. The remaining families concern physiological support, control and recovery. This is component evidence within the proposed architecture. Classification asks whether an endpoint meets the stated rule; enrichment asks whether such endpoints occur more often than in comparable genes; mediation asks whether the specified local recovery disturbance carries a developmental effect. Universality is a further question. No matched-set enrichment or shared developmental mediation was demonstrated, and the classification paper's subset formulation cannot establish the parent's universal conjecture.

Two examples show both the signal and the next missing measurement. In Celf4+/− mouse cortical layer-V pyramidal neurons, persistent sodium current and axon-initial-segment NaV1.6 abundance were increased (Sun et al., 2013). This is a measured sodium-current endpoint in a heterozygous model, not merely a functional annotation. Whether it increases pump work, delays sodium or chloride recovery, or changes maturation through those costs remains unmeasured. In HEK293 receptor-expression experiments, the human de novo GRIA2 A643V variant slowed AMPAR deactivation and reduced desensitisation; deactivation was approximately sevenfold longer in homomeric GluA2(Q) receptors (Coombs et al., 2022). Prolonged cation entry supplies a concrete test of duration-dependent recovery demand, although neuronal ATP use and recovery were not measured. The variant was identified in a child with epilepsy and developmental delay; it cannot stand for every GRIA2 allele or the exact variants ascertained by Satterstrom. These examples preserve the proposal that altered signalling can become altered restoration work, while locating the untested joint precisely.

Genetic routes into developmental chloride regulation are experimentally concrete. In male Fmr1-null mice, He et al. (2014) found delayed chloride-reversal maturation in layer-IV somatosensory neurons and increased cortical NKCC1 protein at postnatal day 10; KCC2 protein was unchanged at the sampled ages, and the reversal-potential difference was no longer detected at day 15. In human neurons derived from Rett patients carrying MECP2 Q83X or N126I variants, Tang et al. (2016) found deficient KCC2 and a delayed hyperpolarising GABA-reversal shift during 1–3 months of culture. IGF1 treatment increased KCC2 and restored that electrophysiological endpoint. These findings support direct genetic entry into chloride regulation without requiring a preceding maternal sodium–volume episode. They identify distinct candidate import and extrusion routes, rather than a requirement that every lesion increases NKCC1. Neither study measured restoration after a matched chloride load, and reversal-potential rescue is not a complete behavioural or clinical rescue.

The intrinsic worked example in Section 4 draws on dynamic recovery measured in a defined genetic model. Tang et al.
