(2019) reported that the KCC2-expression enhancer KW-2449 accelerated chloride extrusion in human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons, shortening the SuperClomeleon recovery time constant towards the isogenic wild-type value. This supplies a positive precedent for measuring local recovery beyond a resting chloride value or transporter abundance. It does not establish osmotic initiation, impaired cell-volume recovery or a common mechanism across autism. KCC2 also has structural functions in synapse development, and the drug acts on other signalling processes; improved recovery and morphology under the same treatment do not by themselves identify chloride recovery as the developmental mediator.

WNK3 adds a human genetic example of an intrinsic developmental route into cation–chloride regulation. Küry et al. (2022) identified six maternally inherited hemizygous variants in 14 males from six families with intellectual disability/developmental delay; autistic features were reported in one individual. An earlier report of two brothers with autism and intellectual disability involved a deletion encompassing PHF8, FAM120C and WNK3, so it could not attribute autism specifically to WNK3 (Qiao et al., 2008). The single-gene evidence supports a rare X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, rather than an explanation of autism’s population sex ratio. Section 23.7 considers the direction-specific functional findings and the proposed recovery question. WNK3 is discussed outside the frozen 42/102 analysis, whose membership and classifications remain unchanged.

The Shank3B counterexample and negative human bumetanide trials constrain generalisation (Section 23.7), which also distinguishes normal WNK-dependent restoration from delayed recovery. Sections 29 and 31 connect recovery to developmental protein production and the relative timing of interacting cell populations. Section 23.13 compares the recovery claim with immune, metabolic and developmental-signalling explanations. A shared endpoint does not decide which causal route produced it.

Calibration of the map remains incomplete. In the frozen companion audit, review was not blind to the hypothesis, an independent matched comparison set was not analysed, and background phenotype extraction was unfinished (Bell, 2026c). One intended no-change control retained a strict count of zero while generating additional non-counting routes, leaving the specificity of route generation unresolved. A second control and an equal-depth IMPC comparison had not been completed. These limitations affect calibration of the classification; they do not erase the reported component findings.

Enrichment depends on comparable evidence-search depth and assay coverage; untested endpoints are not negative findings. Even demonstrated enrichment would leave developmental mediation unresolved (Section 7).

7 Intrinsic and Direct Molecular Entry into Sodium-Handling Burden

Intrinsic molecular initiation provides another possible local entry into the recovery problem introduced in Section 4, without preceding systemic sodium–volume disturbance. The functional examples below complement the genetic evidence in Section 6. No majority allocation to systemic or maternal routes across autism is assumed.

Reduced gradient-maintenance or energetic capacity could lower the demand at which recovery fails; altered channels or receptors could instead increase demand. A direct developmental effect with preserved relevant recovery remains an alternative, not an instance of the common process by definition.

One route is insufficient mitochondrial support for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase during actual demand. If compensation meets that demand, reduced reserve need not impair extrusion or deplete ATP. Otherwise sodium recovery could fail locally, with developmental significance only if that recovery constraint carries an effect.

A substrate-specific energetic constraint is demonstrated in AGC1 deficiency. Homozygous SLC25A12 Gln590Arg abolished AGC1 transport in reconstituted liposomes and accompanied severe developmental disease with hypomyelination. Muscle-mitochondrial ATP production was markedly reduced with glutamate-based substrate pairs, while respiratory-chain enzyme activities were normal (Wibom et al., 2009). This preserves a substrate-dependent energetic route alongside aspartate/N-acetylaspartate supply. It does not equate biallelic AGC1 disease with ASD association or establish deficient neural recovery reserve.

Direct pump dysfunction is distinct from inadequate ATP production. In cultured rat hippocampal neurons, α3-preferring ouabain inhibition slowed dendritic sodium clearance after transient potassium-free loading; separate pump-current recordings supplied excess ATP (Azarias et al., 2013). In COS cells expressing the neurological-disease-associated ATP1A3 D923N variant, reduced sodium affinity accompanied higher intracellular sodium than with wild-type α3 (Toustrup-Jensen et al., 2014). These findings make intrinsic transport limitation a concrete local entry route, without implying that every variant lowers transport or causes ATP depletion. Its proposed developmental role still requires impaired neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery to mediate the specified developmental change.

A third route is impaired chloride extrusion through reduced KCC2 (SLC12A5) function, arising from genetic variation, altered developmental regulation or changes in membrane organisation. Reduced effective extrusion can constrain restoration of an age-appropriate chloride state during repeated loading; Table 6.2 supplies variant-specific recovery findings. This does not by itself establish increased NKCC1 inward flux, sodium accumulation or additional pump work; those quantities require separate measurements under the prevailing gradients (Section 23.2).

Membrane scaffolding supplies a measured component of this route. In mature rat hippocampal cultures, gephyrin knockdown reduced KCC2 clustering and weakened chloride extrusion assessed from the somatodendritic GABA-reversal gradient during an imposed chloride load. The surface-to-total ratio of recombinant KCC2 did not change significantly (Al Awabdh et al., 2022). This connects a scaffold perturbation with functional chloride handling. KCC2 also has structural effects on excitatory synapses that are separable from its transport function (Gauvain et al., 2011; Section 28). The proposed developmental extension requires the specified molecular change to impair local chloride recovery and that difficulty to alter circuit development. Such an intrinsic entry need not begin with a systemic sodium–volume disturbance.

Environmental compounds can also act directly: §14.8 and Table 20.1 include increased neuronal sodium influx and impaired astrocytic volume recovery. Whether these effects occur at relevant developmental exposures and mediate lasting change is distinct from exposure–ASD association or an effect on pumps or actin.

Intrinsic initiation may bypass systemic stress while still acting through recovery. A well-characterised recovery-independent route to the neurodevelopmental features of autism would challenge universal scope. The intermediary cannot be reassigned after the result, and peripheral findings cannot substitute for a failed neuronal prediction.

8 Developmental Anatomy and Endocrine Regulation

Primary developmental abnormalities can alter endocrine and water-regulatory capacity. In a holoprosencephaly cohort, diabetes-insipidus severity was associated with hypothalamic non-separation (Hahn et al., 2005). This illustrates a possible causal direction from developmental anatomy to water-regulatory dysfunction; it does not establish a sodium-mediated cause of the anatomical abnormality.

Human OTX2 variants are associated with variable pituitary phenotypes, and patient-derived organoids demonstrate a role for hypothalamic OTX2 in pituitary development (Gregory et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2020). These primary developmental mechanisms should be distinguished from the later extracellular OTX2 signalling discussed in Sections 30 and 30.4. They do not demonstrate sodium–volume mediation, and craniofacial morphology is not used here as supporting evidence for the hypothesis.

9 Calibration Inputs to the Sodium–Volume Defence Axis During Fetal and Early Perinatal Development

During fetal life and the early perinatal transition, repeated defence and recovery may shape later sodium–volume regulation. Persistent recalibration here means an exposure-related change in threshold, gain or recovery that remains after the initiating conditions resolve, assessed under comparable current physiology and developmental stage. Ordinary recruitment supports the current challenge and subsides as conditions recover (Sections 4.3 and 39.3). Maternal physiology contributes through placental fluid, perfusion, nutrient and endocrine conditions; the developmental input is the fetal exposure and response history that results, rather than a single maternal analyte.

In Guyton’s systems physiology framework, total body sodium and extracellular fluid volume are coupled through renal–vascular feedback: changes in sodium balance affect volume, pressure and renal excretion. Plasma tonicity instead describes effective extracellular osmoles, chiefly sodium salts, relative to water and governs transcellular water distribution. These distinct variables interact, linking circulatory filling, tissue perfusion, renal handling and cellular hydration.

At birth, placental exchange ends, pulmonary flow increases with lung aeration and sodium–volume regulation shifts towards autonomous neonatal control. The hypothesis proposes that demand across fetal life and this transition can alter receptor responsiveness, transporter regulation or neural thresholds. Maternal regulatory activity is not transmitted intact: placental transformation and the fetus’s own response connect maternal conditions to any persistent recalibration.

The fetal regulatory environment includes its own tonicity trajectory, perfusion and oxygen delivery, renal handling and endocrine responsiveness. Maternal and placental inputs interact with intrinsic fetal capacity; maternal sodium alone cannot describe that environment.

During fetal and early perinatal development, calibration inputs arise through multiple interacting domains. The inventory below separates the variables and signals involved; Section 10 then follows the maternal contribution through placental transformation and the fetus’s own regulation.

A. Osmotic and Electrolyte Inputs

• Maternal extracellular sodium relative to water, chloride availability and other contributors to tonicity
• Maternal osmoreceptor recruitment and the resulting changes in water balance
• Fetal extracellular composition after placental exchange
• Placental and fetal cellular osmolyte handling, measured separately from maternal osmotic signalling

B. Volume, Pressure, and Perfusion Inputs

• Maternal effective arterial blood volume, assessed alongside maternal RAAS and AVP recruitment
• Maternal arterial pressure, vascular tone and uteroplacental perfusion
• Fetal pressure, filling and oxygen delivery after placental exchange
• Fetal regional redistribution, including brain-sparing responses during circulatory stress

C. Endocrine and Receptor–Ligand Inputs

• Maternal AVP recruitment and water balance as indirect inputs to fetal exposure and endogenous fetal defence, including fetal AVP pulsatility and V1a/V1b/V2 responsiveness (Section 10.3)
• Maternal RAAS-dependent sodium conservation and vascular effects, distinguished from local placental and fetal angiotensin signalling and AGTR1 response gain
• Fetal cortisol exposure after placental metabolism, interpreted with fetal mineralocorticoid/glucocorticoid receptor (MR/GR) expression, enzymatic gating and coupling
• Maternal thyroid status and resulting fetal hormone exposure as possible influences on metabolic and transport development, including thyroid support of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase

D. Stress, Cytokine, and Sympathetic Inputs

• Maternal inflammatory signals acting on placental metabolism and vascular function
• Maternal sympathetic activity influencing maternal resistance, renin recruitment and adrenal output
• Fetal autonomic and endocrine responses to the resulting changes in oxygenation, perfusion and composition, with any lasting threshold change tested in the fetus; metabolic and mitochondrial activity are additional determinants of tissue response capacity

E. Neural and Vascular Threat-Interpretation Inputs

• Maternal arterial and cardiopulmonary afferents regulating the maternal circulation
• Candidate fetal arterial and cardiopulmonary afferent inputs, distinguished from local endothelial flow responses
• Fetal brainstem and hypothalamic integration of circulatory and chemical inputs
• Candidate afferent routes through the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), with their contribution defined by stimulus, species and gestational stage

Fetal integration permits coordinated defence without one afferent route carrying every response. In late-gestation fetal sheep, bilateral cervical vagosympathetic section altered circulation during slow haemorrhage without significantly changing AVP, ACTH, cortisol or plasma renin activity increases (Wood et al., 1989). Repeated fetal integration, rather than transfer of maternal neural traffic, is the proposed calibration input.

These inputs interact. Water handling, membrane transport, barrier permeability or inflammation may first disturb tonicity; underfilling or impaired delivery may initiate a circulatory route. Where pooling or containment failure demonstrably reduces central filling, defence can respond to a real deficit despite adequate sodium intake; this is distinct from a sensing error. Sensory or regulatory disturbances can instead exaggerate, blunt or mistime defence, so impaired sensing implies no uniform AVP or RAAS direction. Disproportionate free-water retention can lower sodium concentration. Table 15.1 separates actual filling/delivery disturbances from sensing/regulation disturbances while allowing their interaction.

Hormone concentration alone does not define signalling strength. For AVP, RAAS ligands, cortisol, oxytocin and FGF-23, available ligand, receptor abundance and downstream coupling influence the response at a specified tissue. Steroid-specific controls act at additional steps: adrenal zonation and steroidogenic programmes shape production, while 11β-HSD-dependent metabolism modifies local glucocorticoid availability (Sections 10.1 and 34). Production, local metabolism and receptor responsiveness therefore require separate interpretation.

Cortisol-biased signalling could involve glucocorticoid responsiveness, MR/GR balance, local 11β-HSD activity or adrenal architecture (§34). Normal or low serum cortisol neither excludes nor establishes that state. The proposal requires a greater specified response at comparable exposure, or independently demonstrated prolonged exposure, with the proposed developmental consequence.

Stable osmotic, volume and autonomic inputs permit calibration under relatively consistent conditions. Maternal dehydration or inflammation, placental perfusion instability and intrinsic fetal transport or receptor variation can instead impose competing cues. The hypothesis is that repeated adjustment under those constraints leaves shifted thresholds, receptor balance, endocrine recruitment or cellular recovery kinetics.

10 Maternal-Fetal Signal Transformation and Calibration of the Sodium-Volume Defence Axis

Placental transport, peptide metabolism and vascular regulation transform maternal changes into fetal exposures. The fetus’s endocrine and renal responses then shape its history of defence and recovery. Recirculating fluid compartments could prolong that history, but amplification is a prediction rather than an automatic consequence of circulation through a loop (Section 10.4). The account below follows peptide availability and transport kinetics, fetal endocrine recruitment, renal and amniotic-fluid feedback, and developmental timing.

10.1 Maternal-Fetal Partitioning and Enzymatic Barriers

Within this placental interface, local RAAS balance, endothelial sensing and perfusion modify how maternal sodium–water balance and endocrine activity become fetal exposures. Transport, peptide metabolism and endocrine filtering determine different aspects of that transformation. Water–solute balance, nutrient and oxygen delivery, vascular resistance and glucocorticoid availability therefore require joint interpretation when defining the fetal exposure.

Maternal and fetal fluid and peptide environments are coupled through different processes. Water and small-solute exchange can change fetal osmotic or metabolic stimuli without equivalent transfer of the maternal AVP response. Human placental perfusion experiments support substantial AVP metabolism and limited detectable transfer under the tested conditions, rather than an absolute barrier (Landon et al., 1988). These perfusion findings do not map every gestational stage or define a frequency-specific filter. Placental 11beta-HSD2 separately limits maternal cortisol exposure by converting cortisol to cortisone (Stirrat et al., 2018). Fetal hormone concentrations therefore depend on fetal secretion and removal as well as maternal contributions. This partitioning provides a possible route to different maternal and fetal endocrine states; lower fetal effective tonicity or discordant osmotic and circulatory cues must be established separately. Oxytocin and desmopressin require peptide-specific assessments of transfer and metabolism.

Normal gestation establishes a lower osmotic reference for thirst and AVP release. Longitudinal human studies found lower plasma osmolality and lower osmotic thresholds during pregnancy; basal AVP in late pregnancy could remain similar to postpartum values (Davison et al., 1984, 1988). This coordinated reset is a normal adaptation, distinct from additional hypotonicity, impaired effective circulating filling or glucose-related changes in tonicity. A proposed disturbance must therefore be defined against gestational stage and, where possible, the individual's baseline. Lower osmolality alone does not establish deficient AVP. Lower sodium during hyperglycaemia likewise does not establish lower effective tonicity; the glucose-first and subsequent recovery phases are considered separately in Sections 10.2 and 19.7.

10.1.1 Gestational Peptide Clearance and Compensatory Capacity

Peptide exposure reflects secretion and active removal, while its physiological effect also depends on tissue responsiveness. In five women studied longitudinally, maternal AVP metabolic clearance at 7–8 gestational weeks was similar to the preconception value, and circulating vasopressinase was undetectable. Clearance was approximately 3–4-fold higher at 22–24 and 36–38 weeks, alongside increased plasma vasopressinase. Basal plasma AVP remained similar, so Davison et al. (1989) inferred increased production to offset disposal; secretion was not directly quantified. Similar urine osmolality at matched plasma AVP supported preserved renal responsiveness under the study conditions. Normal hormone concentrations can therefore coexist with substantially increased hormone turnover.

Changes in clearance can be offset by secretion. The proposed disturbance arises when that compensation is insufficient to preserve appropriate exposure or water handling; the normal gestational rise in clearance does not demonstrate failure.

The underlying enzyme is placental leucine aminopeptidase (P-LAP), also called insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP), encoded by LNPEP; vasopressinase and oxytocinase describe its peptide-degrading activities. Purified human placental enzyme can hydrolyse both AVP and oxytocin (Tsujimoto et al., 1992). Tissue expression, access of substrate to membrane enzyme, soluble enzyme released by shedding, and native-peptide degradation are different measurements (Ito et al., 2004; Vear et al., 2023). They should be linked experimentally before a change in one is assigned to altered hormone exposure. Reproducible parity associations could motivate such measurements, but parity is not a measurement of enzyme burden or compensatory capacity. Neither parity nor enzyme abundance alone specifies maternal water balance, fetal dilution or the direction of the fetal AVP response.

Maternal peptide turnover therefore changes across gestation. Undetectable circulating vasopressinase early in pregnancy does not establish absent placental tissue activity or passage of intact maternal AVP into fetal blood. The clearance study did not measure that transfer, and the placental perfusion findings in Section 10.1 do not map it across gestational ages. These observations do not establish a period of maternal AVP supply followed by a discrete fetal takeover. Fetal AVP development follows its own timetable (Section 10.3).

MIA adds molecular passage, placental relay and circulatory routes to this interface (Sections 18.5 and 18.6). Their distinct intermediaries connect maternal conditions to fetal exposure and possible local recovery disturbance. Maternal dependence does not establish molecular transfer, and maternal concentration alone identifies neither fetal dose nor response.

10.2 Placental Transport Asymmetry and Exposure Kinetics

Placental transport asymmetry is kinetic and regulatory rather than absolute. Glucose and water exchange do not imply identical sodium transfer kinetics. In human term placental preparations, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase protein and activity occur in both the maternal-facing microvillous and fetal-facing basal syncytiotrophoblast membranes (Johansson et al., 2000). Na⁺/H⁺ exchange supports trophoblast pH recovery; Speake et al. (2005) found predominantly NHE1-mediated activity on the microvillous side, with no detectable basal-membrane NHE activity under their assay conditions. These are measured components of placental ion handling, not a complete map of net maternal-to-fetal sodium flux. The proposed exposure mechanism is that their regulation, together with water and nutrient exchange, changes the time course of fetal composition after a defined maternal input.

Transport asymmetry does not itself establish fetal hypotonicity, swelling, a fixed equilibration lag or an anti-hyponatraemic response. Recurrent glycaemic excursions and low-solute fluid loading are separate inputs: their fetal gradients, composition and timing determine the proposed sodium–water consequence (Sections 18.2 and 19.7). Maternal and fetal concentrations may change at different rates; sodium concentration must be interpreted alongside glucose and other effective osmoles.

Organic osmolytes add a further layer of placental regulation. Perfused term human placentas actively transferred taurine and sustained a fetal-to-maternal concentration ratio of 1.38 ± 0.14 (SEM) in six preparations (Hibbard et al., 1990). Myo-inositol has a different supply pattern: stable-isotope measurements in seven uncomplicated term pregnancies indicated that less than 10% of fetal plasma inositol came from maternal plasma, consistent with substantial endogenous production (Staat et al., 2012). Nuclear factor of activated T cells 5 (NFAT5/TonEBP) protein and SMIT transcripts are present in term human trophoblasts (Shin et al., 2012). Together these findings support a regulated osmolyte environment, while requiring transfer, local synthesis and intracellular redistribution to be distinguished. The hypothesis proposes that altered regulation of this environment changes fetal buffering and recovery; fetal brain osmolyte restoration is a separate endpoint from placental abundance or cord concentration.

A solid connection labelled “Renal input and fluid feedback” has arrowheads toward both fetal exposure and renal and fluid handling, representing input and return without assuming amplification.

The fetal-response and renal-handling boxes are grouped under “Exposure, defence and recovery history”. This history has two branches:

  • A dashed arrow labelled “If unresolved” leads to persistent or recurrent local ionic or cell-volume recovery disturbance during a sensitive window. A further dashed arrow leads from that disturbance to a specified developmental change.

Figure 10.1. Maternal–fetal signal transformation, defence and recovery. Solid arrows show component exchange, sensing and regulatory pathways; the return arrow denotes fluid feedback without assuming amplification. The fetus responds to its own exposure, maturity and capacity. AVP–RAAS–cortisol names complementary protective roles for arginine vasopressin, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and cortisol, not an obligatory three-hormone rise. 10.3 The Fetal Endocrine Readout: The AVP–RAAS–Cortisol Defence Triad

The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad names complementary protective roles: AVP supports water balance and circulatory defence; RAAS supports sodium conservation and effective circulating volume; cortisol provides stress and metabolic support. Their recruitment has different triggers and timescales, so the architecture does not require all three to rise together. The developmental hypothesis concerns how repeated defence or incomplete recovery during sensitive periods might alter maturation. With sufficient reserve, appropriate withdrawal and recovery, compensation may leave no lasting functional impairment.

Human fetal pituitary samples contained immunoreactive AVP at 11–19 gestational weeks (Skowsky and Fisher, 1977), with continued maturation of hypothalamic and pituitary hormone content (Burford and Robinson, 1982). These ages establish neither first synthesis, mature secretion or renal responsiveness, nor a maternal-to-fetal supply handover. Earlier maternal or placental disturbance could affect neural and endocrine formation before fetal AVP matures; a mechanism requiring fetal AVP persistence instead depends on secretion, clearance and target-organ competence at the relevant stage (Section 36.5).

Osmotic and volume inputs interact within AVP regulation. In unanaesthetised rats, hypovolaemia increased the sensitivity of the osmotic AVP response and, with greater depletion, lowered its threshold (Dunn et al., 1973). This provides a physiological basis for interacting cues; fetal response thresholds and the developmental consequences of repeated defence require their own evidence.

When fetal hypotonicity coexists with a filling, perfusion or oxygen-delivery threat, osmotic suppression of AVP can compete with nonosmotic recruitment. The mixed-cue prediction is delayed recruitment or a smaller response than under a comparable circulatory challenge without hypotonicity. These are distinct predictions: AVP may still rise, and appropriate suppression during uncomplicated dilution is not failed defence. RAAS and cortisol responses need not form a fixed hormonal profile. Adequately demonstrated absence of delay or attenuation would oppose the corresponding prediction; absence of a proposed concurrent RAAS or cortisol response would limit that additional conjunction. A mixed-cue response can reflect appropriate cue integration without harmful mismatch.

In near-term fetal sheep, maternal DDAVP plus water loading shifted the threshold for increased AVP immunoreactivity from 17.5% to 22.5% of estimated blood volume withdrawn during haemorrhage. Plasma immunoreactivity rose in both groups: the published abstract describes similar increases, whereas the full Results and Discussion report differing response slopes and a lower peak in treated fetuses (Desai et al., 2003a). These are withdrawal thresholds, not measurements of the net circulating deficit. Assay cross-reactivity with DDAVP and differing volume restoration limit attribution to osmotic inhibition alone. Renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and cortisol were not measured together to establish the full triad.

The intervention also relatively preserved fetal urine output. At the end of the 60-minute haemorrhage, after withdrawal of 30% of estimated blood volume, urine flow was 0.35 mL/min in treated fetuses versus 0.12 mL/min in controls, approximately 2.9-fold higher. Flow fell in both groups. The authors proposed that preserved output could help sustain amniotic-fluid supply during haemorrhage; benefit to amniotic-fluid volume and later development was not demonstrated by this experiment (Desai et al., 2003a).

Experimental fetal physiology supports protective recruitment and changing endocrine relationships. In anaesthetised sheep, V1 antagonism reduced the hypoxaemia-associated rise in fetal cerebral blood flow (Eisenach et al., 1992). During prolonged reduced uterine flow in another sheep study, AVP rose early and then approached control levels while cortisol remained elevated despite continuing hypoxaemia (Hooper et al., 1990). This is phase separation during a continuing challenge, not complete recovery or evidence that near-control AVP is deficient. Fetal pituitary-adrenal stress responses mature with gestation (Rose et al., 1978); these preparations provide component evidence, not human midgestational thresholds or proof of developmental imprinting.

The corresponding birth-response prediction is lower cord copeptin with lower effective fetal tonicity under comparable nonosmotic stimuli and birth context (Section 18.1.9). A positive association could reflect ordinary protective physiology, without harmful mismatch or developmental programming; an adequately precise null or opposite relation would weaken this prediction.

Table 10.1. AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad: proposed fetal responses to mixed dilution and underfilling cues

Component Candidate fetal response Interpretive meaning
Fetal AVP recruitment Delayed or attenuated relative to a matched challenge (proposed) Osmotic inhibition can oppose nonosmotic recruitment. Compare timing and magnitude with a fetus of matched maturity under the same circulatory challenge without hypotonicity; low AVP during uncomplicated dilution may be appropriate.
Fetal RAAS activity Renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone may rise or diverge The proposed sodium-conserving defence requires separate assessment of renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and renal response; a rise in one does not establish the others (Raff and Wood, 1992; Robillard et al., 1984).
Fetal cortisol recruitment May increase with an adequate stress stimulus; gestational stage and phase matter Recruitment reflects fetal stress-axis and adrenal responsiveness. Duration alone does not determine cortisol direction (Carmichael et al., 1997).

Note: responses depend on stimulus, phase, compartment and maturity. The three arms need not be recruited together. A net AVP rise can coexist with delayed recruitment relative to the comparator; acute hypoxaemia or severe stress may increase fetal AVP. Circulating concentration reflects input and removal and does not itself measure receptor responsiveness. These are conditional responses, not a universal fetal stress signature.

Box 10.1. Pregnancy State Classifier

Initiating state Placental / fetal signal emphasis Predicted fetal interpretation
Electrolyte-free or low-solute fluid loading Maternal water–solute changes may alter fetal tonicity; fetal exposure depends on placental exchange and timing. If fetal hypotonicity coexists with a circulatory challenge, osmotic AVP inhibition may compete with nonosmotic recruitment. The net AVP response and RAAS/cortisol recruitment require separate assessment.
Recurrent gestational hyperglycaemia Maternal glucose and water changes may alter fetal exposure; fetal concentrations and timing require measurement Phase-dependent fetal response unestablished; do not infer hypotonicity or a fixed hormone direction from transport asymmetry (Sections 18.2 and 19.7).
Placental underperfusion Reduced placental delivery may alter fetal oxygenation, pressure or effective filling; establish which fetal disturbance occurs. Fetal hypoxia or hypotension can recruit AVP, with renin, aldosterone and cortisol assessed separately by severity and phase; underperfusion does not predict a fixed low-AVP state (DeVane et al., 1982; Zubrow et al., 1988).
Altered vasopressinase burden (hypothetical) Altered maternal AVP removal may change maternal peptide exposure and water balance, depending on compensatory secretion and tissue response (Davison et al., 1989). Fetal consequences require a measured fluid, perfusion or peptide-transfer intermediary. Maternal clearance differences alone establish neither fetal dilution nor deficient endogenous fetal AVP.

10.4 Fetal Renal Decoding and Amniotic-Fluid Re-exposure

The fetus is not a passive recipient of placental information, and its renal response changes as transport capacity develops. Human MAGED2-related antenatal Bartter syndrome provides direct evidence: impaired NKCC2 (sodium–potassium–2 chloride cotransporter 2) and NCC (sodium–chloride cotransporter) expression and function accompany severe fetal salt loss and polyhydramnios, yet the renal phenotype can resolve after birth (Laghmani et al., 2016). In human fetal kidney specimens, AQP1–3 expression, including collecting-duct AQP2, increased with gestational age while remaining below adult levels (Feng et al., 2019). These findings anchor stage-dependent salt and water handling; they do not establish adult levels of concentrating capacity. Macula densa–renin signalling, epithelial sodium channel (ENaC)–mineralocorticoid responsiveness and natriuretic counter-signals must likewise be assigned to the relevant stage. The hypothesis predicts that the same placental input can therefore produce different urine output, sodium conservation and endocrine recruitment as the fetal kidney matures.

Fetal urine changes amniotic water–solute balance; swallowing with gastrointestinal absorption and intramembranous transfer can return water and solutes to circulation. Fetal-sheep experiments demonstrate systemic osmotic effects after ingested or intraamniotic fluid, followed by recovery and regulatory fluid removal (Smith et al., 1986; Ross et al., 1991; Brace et al., 2004). The developmental extension is that residence and delayed return prolong or repeat a disturbance after a transient input. Direction and duration depend on composition, flows, compartment volumes, placental exchange and renal responses. Recirculation alone establishes neither amplification nor developmental harm. Polyhydramnios identifies neither fetal salt depletion nor hypotonic exposure by itself; urine production, swallowing and intramembranous return require separate assessment.

Text description of Figure 10.2

The diagram maps selected fetal fluid pathways using solid arrows. Its subtitle specifies that an increase in disturbance amplitude is not assumed.

At the top, a two-headed arrow connects ongoing placental exchange of water and solutes with fetal circulation. The circulation box states that composition reflects input, distribution and removal. A downward arrow leads from fetal circulation to fetal renal handling, identified as stage-dependent urinary water and solute output. A further downward arrow carries renal output to amniotic fluid, whose composition and volume reflect inflows and outflows.

Two return routes leave the amniotic-fluid box. One leads to swallowing and gastrointestinal absorption; the other leads to intramembranous transfer. Both connect to a shared pathway labelled “Water and solute return”, which points back to fetal circulation. Together these connections depict exchange and recirculation rather than a quantified balance of all flows.

A separate box with a dashed outline states the proposed re-exposure mechanism: delayed return may prolong or repeat a measured fetal disturbance. The same box states that regulation can restore stability and that recirculation alone establishes neither amplification nor harm. The legend identifies the solid arrows as component pathways and emphasises that only selected fluxes are shown; the diagram is not a complete fluid-balance model. The dashed outline marks a prediction about persistence or recurrence, rather than an established developmental consequence.

Figure 10.2. Fetal fluid exchange and proposed re-exposure. Solid arrows show selected component pathways: placental exchange, renal output to amniotic fluid, swallowing with gastrointestinal absorption, and intramembranous return. The diagram does not quantify net flux or include every fetal-fluid pathway. Exchange and regulation can restore stability. The dashed box marks the prediction that delayed return prolongs or repeats a defined fetal disturbance after a matched transient input. Recirculation alone establishes neither amplification nor developmental harm; persistence, local ionic or cell-volume recovery and developmental effects require separate measurements.

10.5 Temporal Vulnerability: Skin-Barrier Maturation and Proposed NFAT5 Imprinting

Skin-barrier maturation provides a candidate window in which fetal fluid exchange and susceptibility change. Human fetal-skin experiments found lower tracer-water permeability as keratinisation progressed (Parmley and Seeds, 1970). Hardman et al. (1999) reported regionally patterned barrier initiation at 22–26 weeks menstrual age (20–24 weeks in their gestational convention), rather than synchronous whole-skin closure. These findings identify changing routes of exchange; they do not by themselves establish weaker whole-fetus osmotic buffering or larger tonicity excursions. The developmental proposal is that altered exposure kinetics can coincide with limited response or recovery capacity while control thresholds are being set. That prediction requires stage-specific exposure and response measurements, rather than assigning the endocrine behaviour of near-term sheep to a human midgestational window.

NFAT5 provides a candidate molecular connection between osmotic exposure, chloride regulation and endothelial recovery (Section 23). Term placental NFAT5/SMIT localisation identifies an interface component (Shin et al., 2012), not fetal neural imprinting. Intracellular ionic strength, cell volume and extracellular tonicity remain distinct; hypertonic findings do not specify a hypotonic response. The 20–24-week anchor identifies regional skin-barrier initiation, not a measured NFAT5 calibration window.

10.6 Integration with Later Control Systems

Placentally transformed exposure could influence later brainstem threat classification, hypothalamic AVP recruitment and sodium-conserving endocrine behaviour through the fetus’s own defence and recovery history. Repeated or incompletely resolved challenge may alter conditions while regulatory thresholds develop; successful recovery can leave no lasting impairment.

The proposed developmental input is the pattern of defence needed to maintain stability, shaped jointly by maternal physiology, placental processing and intrinsic fetal capacity. A single maternal sodium value cannot reconstruct that history, and compartment separation alone does not establish costly compensation. The core developmental test is whether that exposure impairs local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery, and whether the recovery disturbance carries a specified developmental effect (Section 2).

11 The Intergenerational Sodium Struggle: Inherited Susceptibility and Developmental Programming

The intergenerational proposal connects two distinct routes: inherited susceptibility and developmental exposure. Genetic variants can constrain offspring transport, structural reserve or recovery directly (Section 6), while maternal physiology can influence the gestational environment through the maternal–placental–fetal processes developed in Sections 9, 10, and 18.1. In the latter route, fetal tissues respond to the exposure that reaches them. A maternal receptor pattern is not transferred intact. Structural reserve and receptor responsiveness are candidate offspring outcomes to measure, not interchangeable signs of an inherited defence state.

For the developmental-exposure route, the proposed continuity must be traced from maternal physiology through a measured fetal exposure to a persistent offspring structural or response change. Section 32.6 supplies a specific renal-reserve example to test alongside inherited liability and shared environment. Its place in the common-process account still requires the defined local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty and its developmental effect (Section 2). Adequate gestational compensation and normal offspring recovery remain alternatives. Neither progressive loss of reserve across generations nor transmission of acquired receptor changes is assumed; familial recurrence alone cannot supply the missing links.

Part C Candidate disturbances and evidence

12 Converging Osmotic and Volume Pathways in Autism Contributing Factors

The defence weightings described in Section 5 can arise through different initiating disturbances. The Sodium Struggle concerns both those disturbances and the cost of correcting them when solute, water, circulatory and cellular recovery operate on different timescales. Routes may begin with hypotonic dilution, hypertonic loading, altered renal transport, impaired effective filling or vascular signalling. Their proposed developmental significance depends on magnitude, duration, compensation and its withdrawal, particularly whether recovery finishes before another challenge.

The two contributor maps organise possible entry routes into the coupled physiology of §3: extracellular tonicity, effective circulating volume, and vascular tone or containment. Table 13.1 addresses cellular osmotic, ionic and volume-control difficulties. Table 15.1 addresses circulatory difficulties and altered defence, separating actual filling or delivery disturbances in Panel A from sensing or regulatory disturbances in Panel B. These maps organise overlapping routes; they do not assign a separate defended variable to each panel. Their proposed developmental convergence requires the recovery intermediary specified in §2.

The maps use matching fields to connect a defined disturbance with its mechanism, representative contributors, candidate genes or systems, and claim-specific evidence. Table 20.1 indexes the observed associations, measured components and hypothesized developmental links. Sections 16.8 and 16.9 distinguish actual vascular dysfunction from mechanical transmission, afferent encoding and regulatory interpretation; Table 16.1 supplies supporting component evidence. Sections 18.2 and 19.7 retain the glucose-related redistribution and proposed compensatory roles, distinct from hypotonicity.

12.1 Neonatal Sodium Trajectories and Later Development

Measured neonatal sodium disturbances already have longitudinal developmental associations in humans. The relevant evidence concerns different exposures: a concentration minimum, a maximum, a range across days, or the number of days above a threshold. These measurements bring the question beyond component physiology, while separating an observed sodium history from the proposed cost of defending and recovering from it.

Gervais et al. (2022) studied 147 infants born before 29 weeks who survived the first ten days; 127 had ascertainable death or developmental outcomes. A larger first-ten-day range of glucose-corrected sodium was associated with death or developmental impairment at 18–21 months corrected age after gestational-age adjustment (linear-model coefficient B=2.10, 95% CI 0.16–4.04). With gestational age, neonatal illness score and NSAID use considered together, the estimate was B=2.03 (−0.30 to 4.37; p=.087); uncorrected sodium remained nominally associated (B=2.28, 0.01–4.56; p=.049). These are published linear coefficients, not risk ratios. The range was the maximum minus minimum of daily medians, with missing days interpolated; it did not measure oscillation count or recovery time. Glucose correction changed the analysed quantity but was not necessary to detect an association.

The high-sodium branch has a further human developmental signal. Murakami et al. (2026) analysed 272 followed infants born before 32 weeks. A first-week peak whole-blood sodium above 145 mEq/L was associated with composite neurodevelopmental impairment at 3–4 years (adjusted RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.08–2.84). In a supplementary analysis, sodium above 145 on at least two days was associated with RR 2.37 (1.39–4.02), compared with RR 1.07 (0.50–2.28) for one day, each relative to infants without hypernatraemia. This was not a direct statistical comparison between the two exposure durations. The days need not be consecutive, so persistent and recurrent disturbance remain distinguishable explanations. The composite combined developmental-quotient, motor and sensory impairments. Developmental-quotient impairment alone was not statistically significant in the main adjusted analysis, but was associated in the supplementary two-or-more-day comparison (RR 2.06, 1.17–3.63). Deaths were excluded and developmental data were available for 272 of 418 survivors, making selective follow-up an important limit.

Low sodium has been examined in a different clinical setting. Viitaharju et al. (2026) followed 269 infants born at or after 36 weeks with perinatal asphyxia for a median 11.2 years. A minimum sodium below 125 mmol/L in the first 72 hours was associated with death or a listed neurological or developmental diagnosis (adjusted OR 3.85, 95% CI 1.04–14.22). The below-130 threshold was associated with cerebral-palsy/paralytic, epilepsy and hearing outcomes, but the grouped psychiatric/developmental endpoint was not statistically significant (OR 1.51, 0.69–3.28). That heterogeneous category was not an autism-specific test, and its interval does not establish equivalence. This asphyxia cohort is neither a direct replication nor a refutation of the preterm sodium-range result.

Together, these findings justify testing the developmental consequences of sodium history in both directions. They do not yet establish a shared causal U-shaped curve, a safe middle band, compensatory overshoot from high to low sodium, or the proposed recovery intermediary. Prematurity, hypoxic injury, treatment and sampling can contribute to the associations; none of these cohorts measured the full defence-to-recovery sequence or an autism-specific outcome. The discriminating next step is to connect the timed exposure to independently measured physiological recovery and later development. This preserves the hypothesis’s central question: whether the history of maintaining stability matters beyond the laboratory value observed at one moment.

The maternal posture and gestational-load comparison is developed in Section 16.5, alongside regional filling and venous-return constraints.

13 Osmotic Pathway Catalogue

This catalogue retains nine core routes into water–solute imbalance, altered transport or incomplete cellular recovery. Table 13.1 also maps intergenerational programming, hyperglycaemic translocation and maternal salt loading as interacting contexts. The rows identify initiating disturbances, regulatory responses and recovery constraints at interacting causal levels, rather than mutually exclusive diagnoses. Not every route begins with hypotonicity or low serum sodium. Compensation can change the direction of disturbance; recurrence, overshoot and incomplete recovery are separate possibilities. Endocrine responses depend on phase, compartment and effective filling. The component studies cited below anchor particular steps; §14 and Table 20.1 distinguish those observations from proposed developmental mediation.

13.1 Water-Balance and AVP Pathways

These pathways begin with altered water balance or AVP recruitment. Appropriate early conservation, excessive or persistent antidiuresis, and later dilution are distinguishable phases rather than one obligatory sequence.

13.1.1 True dilution (low-TDS / free-water states)

True dilution reflects water retained in excess of effective solute and excretory capacity. Infant water-intoxication cases demonstrate an acute free-water exposure, not harm from low mineral content alone (CDC, 1994; §14.1). Appropriate AVP suppression favours water excretion; filling, renal function and concurrent stress determine whether that response suffices.

13.1.2 Maternal antidiuresis / excess AVP action

Maternal antidiuresis, altered fetal water–solute exposure and the fetal response are separate steps. Renal drug action need not require maternal AVP excess: sertraline enhanced AQP2 signalling in rat renal preparations (Kim et al., 2021; §14.2). That component does not establish fetal dilution or ASD mediation; maternal peptide transfer is not required for a maternal water-balance change to matter.

13.1.3 Fetal AVP recruitment, persistence and withdrawal

Fetal hypoxia can recruit AVP (Raff and Wood, 1992; §§10.3 and 14.3). A dilutional route additionally requires available water and antidiuretic action sufficient for water retention relative to solute; delayed withdrawal is one proposed mechanism. Acute recruitment does not demonstrate failed termination or developmental recovery impairment.

13.2 Sodium-Balance Failure Pathways

These represent disturbances that weaken sodium retention or mineralocorticoid-mediated sodium conservation.

13.2.1 Salt-wasting phenotypes

Net sodium loss occurs when losses exceed replacement and conservation. Preterm infants can have negative sodium balance despite renin and aldosterone recruitment (Sulyok et al., 1979; Al-Dahhan et al., 1984; §14.4). Sodium concentration and filling also depend on water balance; the neonatal balance findings do not establish the proposed local recovery or ASD connection.

13.2.2 Inadequate RAAS support / possible control reassignment

RAAS support is inadequate only relative to a demonstrated conservation or circulatory need. A low hormone value alone does not show failed support: FGF23-treated mice retained sodium while aldosterone fell (Andrukhova et al., 2014). Where support is deficient, alternative endocrine or vascular contributions may be recruited. Sections 14.5 and 16.10 distinguish hormone direction, renal response and proposed control reassignment.

13.3 Perfusion-Energetic Sodium Stress

These routes concern possible energetic constraints on sodium transport when oxygen delivery or ATP support is inadequate.

13.3.1 High-RAAS impact / angiotensin-dominant constriction

Ang II impaired endothelial redox/NO signalling in cultured cells (Chalupsky and Cai, 2005; §14.6.7). The further route from excessive vascular action to constrained microvascular delivery and ATP-supported ionic recovery remains conditional. High circulating input and excessive tissue responsiveness are distinct possibilities; neither is identified by plasma renin alone.

13.3.2 Hypoxia-induced sodium stress

Hypoxia enters this route when oxygen limitation prevents adequate ATP-supported transport despite available sodium and endocrine compensation. In cultured postnatal rat hippocampal neurons, intracellular sodium returned to baseline after reoxygenation, whereas Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase blockade prevented recovery (Sheldon et al., 2004; §14.7). Fetal hypoxic endocrine recruitment is a separate measured component (Raff and Wood, 1992). The proposed delivery-related transport and developmental effects require their own endpoints. Hypoxia or hormone recruitment alone does not establish progressive hypotonicity.

13.4 Cellular Osmolyte-Control Failure

These routes concern regulatory volume decrease and proposed impairment of osmolyte recovery following cellular swelling.

13.4.1 Cytoskeletal volume-control disruption (actin / osmolyte axis)

Actin perturbation delayed regulatory volume decrease (RVD) in human HT-3 cells (Shen et al., 1999; §14.8). A distinct ionic comparator is methylmercury-induced RVD inhibition in neonatal-rat astrocytes, with recovery restored by extracellular sodium substitution (Vitarella et al., 1996). These findings support cellular volume-control components, not a shared fetal lesion across the listed toxicants or genes. Altered osmolyte recovery and systemic endocrine amplification require additional measurements linking local disturbance to the relevant response.

13.5 Renal Sodium-Redistribution Pathway

This pathway asks whether proximal phosphate disposal and distal sodium conservation become insufficiently coordinated under a specified load.

13.5.1 Dietary inorganic phosphate load

Phosphate loading engages absorption, renal phosphate transport and FGF23/Klotho regulation. A five-day human loading study raised FGF23 without detected changes in serum or urinary sodium, urine volume or weight; sodium matching was imperfect (Scotti Gerber et al., 2025; §14.9). Timing and compensating transport determine balance; phosphaturia alone does not establish salt wasting or developmental recovery failure.

Table 13.1 maps each disturbance to its physiological mechanism, representative contributors, candidate genes or systems, and claim-specific evidence. Contributor cells distinguish ASD-associated exposures from physiological comparators and untested candidates; they do not assign every listed item an ASD association. Volume appearance is phase-dependent. Table 13.2 retains the conditional endocrine patterns; §14 and Table 20.1 provide the fuller evidence and its limits.

Evidence key: [E] marks the stated empirical observation or association; [S], a measured physiological component; [H], a proposed response or mediation, as in Table 20.1. These are claim roles, not a strength ranking. Gene names retain candidate correspondences. ASD genetic relevance and measured variant effects are separate claims, limited to individually sourced findings in §6 and Table 20.1; neither establishes assignment to this row. The proposed local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery link remains [H] unless directly measured. Physiological systems imply no ASD genetic association. This chart does not change the frozen genetic classification.

 [E] Maternal diabetes–ASD associations (Xiang et al., 2018) and acute human redistribution (Hillier et al., 1999; Table 20.1). [H] Compensation and developmental recovery mediation. The studies do not establish a salt-deficient fetus or protective hyperglycaemia (§§18.2 and 19.7).

Transient gestational hypertension is a distinct clinical context, not proof of a sodium load.

Table 13.2 separates the initiating state from conditional maternal and fetal responses. Its entries are working physiological predictions, not validated diagnostic signatures or obligatory stages. Renin, angiotensin action and aldosterone are not interchangeable measurements of RAAS; copeptin informs secretion-related activity rather than intact AVP clearance. Maternal and fetal values must be aligned by phase rather than assumed to move together. The proposed persistence depends on incomplete recovery, not on the presence of a transient response.

Table 13.2. Conditional Endocrine–Osmotic Patterns Across Maternal and Fetal Compartments

PATHWAY (Mechanistic class) Conditional MATERNAL response (AVP / RAAS / Cortisol) Conditional FETAL response (AVP / RAAS / Cortisol) NOTES / Distinguishing features
Water-Balance and AVP Pathways
1 – True dilution (Low-TDS / free-water states) If hypotonicity predominates: AVP ↓; RAAS follows filling; cortisol varies with stress. If fetal hypotonicity is demonstrated: AVP suppression is expected unless non-osmotic stimuli prevail; RAAS/cortisol depend on fetal state. Net free-water excess, not low mineral content alone. Cortisol dominance is a proposed additional response, not a defining feature.
2 – Maternal antidiuresis (AVP excess or drug-specific renal action) Sustained antidiuretic action with retained water can cause maternal dilution; RAAS follows filling and cortisol follows stress. A dilutional exposure may suppress fetal AVP; fetal hypoxia or underfilling may recruit it. No necessary maternal–fetal triad. Maternal antidiuresis, fetal exposure and fetal endocrine response are separate steps. Medication-specific physiology and ASD evidence are distinguished in §14.2; exposure alone establishes neither AVP excess nor developmental mediation.
3 – Fetal AVP recruitment, persistence and withdrawal (high-salt diet, IV saline, transient hypertension) If maternal tonicity rises: osmotic AVP recruitment may occur; renin/aldosterone also depend on expansion and renal feedback. If fetal tonicity rises: AVP recruitment is plausible. Persistence after stimulus decline and dilutional rebound require a measured water imbalance. Initial hypertonic stimulus and later recovery are different phases. A copeptin rise alone does not establish overshoot or hyponatraemia.
Sodium-Balance Failure Pathways
4 – Salt-wasting phenotypes With underfilling: AVP and renin may rise; aldosterone requires intact adrenal response; cortisol is context-dependent. A fetal loss or delivery disturbance may recruit defence; maternal salt loss does not impose an identical fetal pattern. Sodium loss, accompanying water loss and compensatory capacity determine sodium concentration and filling. Adrenal failure can prevent the expected hormonal response.
5 – Inadequate RAAS support / possible control reassignment Renin or aldosterone may be suppressed, or mineralocorticoid action impaired; AVP/cortisol depend on the resulting state. A fetal conservation deficit or altered controller balance is a hypothesis requiring fetal measurements. Low renin can reflect feedback to expansion or downstream activity; cortisol substitution is not inferred from low renin alone.
Perfusion-Energetic Sodium Stress
6 – High-RAAS impact / angiotensin-dominant constriction High angiotensin effect can coexist with low renin; aldosterone, AVP and cortisol need not move together. Placental delivery limitation may recruit fetal stress responses; local RAAS activity is distinct from maternal plasma renin. The candidate energetic paradox is strong vasoconstrictor action with impaired transport recovery, not obligatory biochemical hyponatraemia. See §14.6.7.
7 – Hypoxia-induced sodium stress Responses depend on whether hypoxia is maternal, placental or fetal and whether pressure or filling falls. Hypoxia can recruit fetal AVP/stress responses; renal and circulatory consequences determine RAAS recruitment. Fetal anaemia or other oxygen limitation can constrain pump-supported recovery. Serum sodium and maternal endocrine values need not change in parallel.
Cellular Osmolyte-Control Failure
8 – Cytoskeletal volume-control disruption (actin / osmolyte axis) Cell-specific recovery failure does not assign a systemic endocrine pattern; leak or underfilling would add their own signals. Fetal cell volume, transporter localisation and recovery are primary endpoints; AVP, RAAS and cortisol are separate responses. Impaired regulatory volume decrease (RVD) or osmolyte recovery can occur at near-normal extracellular tonicity; it does not establish a pseudo-dilution endocrine signature.
Renal Sodium-Redistribution Pathway
9 – Dietary inorganic phosphate load Phosphaturic and later transport responses depend on dose, timing, renal function and sodium/water intake; no fixed triad. Fetal exposure and renal maturity determine the proposed response; maternal phosphaturia does not specify fetal hormone direction. Segmental redistribution may be compensated or produce net retention or loss. See §14.9 for differing RAAS findings and restoration.
Maternal Exposures and Developmental Response Pathways

Proposed programmed response to a defined challenge, not a demonstrated inherited endocrine triad. Intergenerational programming requires evidence linking the earlier exposure, transmitted change and measured offspring physiology.
Hyperglycaemic translocational states Effective tonicity may rise while measured Na⁺ falls; AVP, RAAS and cortisol depend on the measured state Fetal glucose, tonicity and endocrine responses require separate measurement; no fixed triad Glucose-related water redistribution is distinct from hypotonicity, sodium loss and analytical pseudohyponatraemia. See Sections 18.2 and 19.7.
Maternal Salt Loading If maternal effective tonicity rises, AVP may respond; expansion and renal feedback can suppress renin. Cortisol is context-dependent. 14 Mechanisms of Osmotic Pathways

The nine core mechanisms below develop the systemic and cellular routes mapped in Table 13.1; its additional contexts are developed in §§11, 18, and 19.7. Exposure associations and molecular findings support different claims; listed genetic correspondences remain candidates until variant-specific function is linked to the proposed route. Developmental mediation requires an identified disturbance of local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery in the relevant compartment and window (§2; Table 20.1).

14.1 Mechanism — True Dilution

14.1.1 Initiating condition and the canonical low-AVP geometry

True dilution is the reference case of water intake exceeding excretory capacity relative to solute availability. Low-mineral water alone does not establish that imbalance. Falling tonicity appropriately suppresses AVP, although underfilling or renal constraints can oppose water excretion. RAAS follows filling and renal signals; cortisol recruitment is a separate stress response. Copeptin reflects secretion rather than AVP clearance.

Reverse osmosis can substantially reduce mineral content, but it does not prescribe one final ionic concentration. In point-of-use dispensers studied by Sacchetti et al. (2015), mean total dissolved solids fell from 311 ± 45 mg/L in the incoming water to 43 ± 38 mg/L in unchilled RO output; mean output calcium and sodium were 7.0 and 4.0 mg/L. These are measured concentrations in that installation sample, not universal RO specifications, and dissolved-solids mass alone is not osmolarity. A dilutional signal still requires retained water in excess of the capacity to maintain solute–water balance; the treatment label alone does not demonstrate that state.

14.1.2 The core mechanism — movement toward hypo-osmotic stress

Falling extracellular tonicity drives cellular swelling and volume-regulatory work, including changes in chloride and organic osmolytes. AVP suppression and renal water excretion normally restore the extracellular state; underfilling or limited renal capacity may prolong it. A cortisol-dominant response is a conditional extension, not the defining physiology of dilution.

14.1.3 Water composition and developmental outcomes

Zeng et al. (2014) compared five drinking waters across rat reproduction and offspring development. Purified water produced the lowest pup survival at lactation day 21, whereas unfiltered tap water was associated with longer maze-learning latencies than the other four waters. In the memory probe trial, filtered tap water produced more platform-location crossings than tap water. The day-21 survival result followed day-4 litter standardisation, and earlier survival differences did not follow a simple mineral-content gradient. The purified product had very low dissolved solids, but the paper does not establish that it was distilled or processed specifically by reverse osmosis. Selected contaminants were measured alongside minerals. Their co-variation leaves pollutant, mineral-nutrition and maternal or lactational mechanisms unresolved. Maternal serum zinc correlated positively with offspring memory, without establishing a causal nutrient effect. Maternal and pup blood sodium and osmolality were not reported in the main study. Better maze performance among purified-water survivors does not explain the mortality finding; survivor selection is a possibility, not a demonstrated bias. The experiment raises a substantive question about water composition and early-life outcomes, while leaving osmotic mediation and any relevance to autism untested.

Human evidence distinguishes excess free-water exposure from low mineral content itself. The CDC infant cases involved water given in addition to or in place of formula, including tap water; they do not establish harm from correctly prepared formula made with low-mineral water (CDC, 1994). The German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment found no adverse effects warranting avoidance of very-low-mineral water with a balanced diet and normal drinking quantities, while acknowledging evidence gaps and the importance of total calcium and magnesium intake during pregnancy and lactation (BfR, 2020). The relevant osmotic exposure is the balance of water intake, dietary solute and excretory capacity, rather than the treatment label alone.

Contaminant exposure, nutritional contribution and net free-water balance are distinct questions. Water labels or survival and behavioural differences alone cannot identify a dilutional developmental mechanism. Geographic prevalence variation does not establish a water-chemistry cause. Across 16 US surveillance sites, identified autism prevalence in eight-year-olds ranged from 9.7 to 53.1 per 1,000 in 2022, alongside substantial differences in identification and service practices (Shaw et al., 2025). Apparent alignment with geological or hydrogeologic boundaries remains a hypothesis requiring measured exposure and physiological consequences, with ascertainment, population structure and correlated exposures distinguished.

14.1.4 Secondary interactions — solvent effects and cytoskeletal vulnerability

Low mineral content and contact-material toxicants are separate exposure questions: total dissolved solids do not specify a toxicant dose. A combined route requires demonstrated water–solute imbalance alongside a specified toxicant effect on recovery or regulation (Sections 14.8 and 14.9). Actin-related recovery and phosphate handling provide possible additional amplifiers (Sections 14.8 and 14.9), not consequences of low TDS alone.

14.1.5 Scope clarification of true dilution and solute-driven water redistribution

Non-remineralised household or municipal water can provide little solute, whereas some products supply substantial salt. Neither label establishes the physiological state: total diet, final feed composition and retained water matter. Solute-loading and glucose-related routes are distinguished in Sections 18.2 and 19.7.

14.1.6 Peripartum and early-infancy analogues

Peripartum fluid loading can produce dilutional hyponatraemia; in a prospective labour cohort, total fluid volume, but not oxytocin administration, remained independently associated with this outcome (Moen et al., 2009). Oxytocin nevertheless has a demonstrated antidiuretic action: human infusion reduced urine volume and free-water clearance and increased urinary AQP2 excretion in healthy volunteers and patients with central diabetes insipidus (Joo et al., 2004). V2-receptor dependence and increased apical AQP2 trafficking were demonstrated separately during five-day oxytocin infusion in male AVP-deficient Brattleboro rats (Li et al., 2008). These findings support a water-retention component while distinguishing the human exposure from the experimental renal mechanism. AVP, RAAS and cortisol responses then depend on tonicity, filling, renal function and labour-related stress.

Hypotonic intravenous fluids or peripartum free-water loading enter this route when net delivery exceeds excretory and solute-handling capacity. In infant feeding, the relevant exposure is the final feed and water–solute balance, not preparation-water mineral content alone.

14.1.7 Endocrine adaptation and cortisol-dominant imprinting

Maternal and fetal responses depend on their own filling and tonicity. Appropriate AVP suppression remains protective; a cortisol-weighted developmental response is a further hypothesis.

Prenatal steroid biology provides a relevant observation, but the measured compartment matters. In amniotic-fluid samples from 128 males later diagnosed with autism and 217 controls, a shared steroidogenic factor spanning cortisol and four sex steroids was elevated (Baron-Cohen et al., 2015). This was not a measurement of maternal cortisol, dilution or cortisol-mediated sodium defence, and it did not identify which maternal, placental or fetal source generated the difference. It supports investigating the prenatal steroid environment without assigning the sodium–volume route in advance.

Hypothesis. During a demonstrated sodium–volume challenge, glucocorticoid-dependent support could preserve circulation while changing the balance of renal and vascular regulation. Whether it expands effective volume or suppresses renin depends on the exposure and tissue response; these effects do not establish increased fetal cortisol. In five isolated term human placentas, inhibition of 11β-HSD activity increased cortisol transfer to the fetal circuit, demonstrating a regulated transmission step (Stirrat et al., 2018). The proposed chain therefore requires both altered maternal physiology and a measured change in fetal exposure, rather than an assumed loss of placental protection.

A lasting fetal change would involve altered receptor availability, occupancy or downstream responsiveness after the initiating disturbance resolves. It need not imply changed receptor identity or permanent cortisol dominance; later water, clearance or glycaemic challenges could reveal the proposed altered response.

True dilution begins with net water excess. Appropriate AVP suppression and water excretion can restore balance; the developmental proposal concerns constraints that prolong the disturbance or leave cellular recovery incomplete. This provides the comparator for the subsequent osmotic routes.

14.2 Mechanism: Maternal Antidiuresis and Excess AVP Action

14.2.1 Initiating condition and maternal–fetal exposure asymmetry

Maternal antidiuresis, from AVP or a drug-induced renal action (Section 14.2.3), may change fetal water–solute conditions through placental exchange. Placental metabolism and limited peptide transfer separate maternal AVP from fetal dose: the exposure need not involve maternal hormone crossing. The fetus responds to its own conditions, so suppression during dilution can be appropriate; persistent exposure–response mismatch is the additional developmental hypothesis.

14.2.2 The core mechanism — signal mismatch and compensatory recruitment

Maternal and fetal endocrine states can diverge because their filling, tonicity and regulatory capacity differ. Fetal RAAS or cortisol recruitment requires fetal need, not merely maternal AVP excess or fetal AVP suppression. Where fetal hypotonicity coexists with circulatory threat, Section 10.3 supplies the mixed-cue AVP prediction.

14.2.3 Empirical support: distinct pharmacological disturbances of water–sodium balance

Drugs can disturb sodium and water handling through distinct renal mechanisms, including actions that do not require increased AVP. In adults, oxcarbazepine reduced water-load excretion without an accompanying rise in circulating AVP (Sachdeo et al., 2002). Oxytocin produced V2-mediated antidiuresis in AVP-deficient rats (Li et al., 2008), and sertraline increased AQP2 abundance and trafficking through V2R–cAMP–PKA signalling in rat collecting-duct preparations without AVP stimulation (Kim et al., 2021). Thiazides affect renal sodium transport and water excretion; a hydrochlorothiazide–amiloride rechallenge caused a greater sodium fall in susceptible patients without a greater measured AVP response than in controls (Friedman et al., 1989). These are distinct mechanisms and experimental settings, not a common maternal hormone signature. Their relevance to this fetal pathway depends on a maternal water–solute disturbance producing a corresponding fetal exposure. This preserves a concrete convergence claim: different perturbations may place similar demands on defence and recovery, even when the initiating hormone profiles differ.

The ASD inference faces a separate test. In 1,580,629 Swedish offspring, Sujan et al. (2017) found that the first-trimester SSRI association fell from an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.66 (95% CI 1.46–1.89) to 0.81 (0.58–1.14) in sibling comparisons. For all antidepressants, the sibling estimate was 0.83 (0.62–1.13). Timing-of-exposure and paternal comparisons also supported familial confounding, while analyses using different exposure definitions yielded a consistent pattern. These findings weaken a causal interpretation of the population association. They do not negate sertraline’s experimental renal action, but that action cannot establish maternal dilution, fetal exposure or ASD mediation. The hypothesis therefore requires a measured physiological intermediary, rather than medication use as its proxy. Section 18.1.2 distinguishes this pregnancy-exposure contrast from the separate maternal-baseline proposal and explains the relevant design limitations.

14.2.4 Proposed secondary amplification: acetaminophen and AVP persistence

Impaired termination of an appropriate antidiuretic response is a possible point of amplification. AVP is a disulfide-bridged nonapeptide; rat proximal-tubule studies suggest a reduced-glutathione-dependent reduction step before further peptide cleavage, and human renal brush-border experiments demonstrate glutathione-sensitive AVP degradation (Carone et al., 1987; Fjellestad-Paulsen & Lundin, 1996). Once AVP has been filtered from plasma, slower luminal degradation could increase intact urinary peptide without prolonging its circulating action. Renal removal is nevertheless broader than filtration: isolated perfused rat kidneys cleared immunoreactive AVP at 1,145 ± 47 µL/min against a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 515 ± 37 µL/min (mean ± SE), indicating a substantial peritubular component (Rabkin et al., 1979). That experiment did not establish the component’s reduced-glutathione (GSH) dependence or whether loss of immunoreactivity equalled loss of biological activity. The proposed persistence mechanism requires reduced net removal of biologically active circulating AVP, assessed separately from tissue degradation or urinary peptide recovery.

Therapeutic-dose human studies supply a measured glutathione component. In a randomised crossover study enrolling 12 healthy adults, two 15 mg/kg acetaminophen doses six hours apart lowered plasma GSH on a sulfur-amino-acid-free diet (paired n = 9), but not on the adequate diet (n = 10; Mannery et al., 2010). A separate 24-person crossover reported decreased whole-blood GSH after 1 g four times daily for four days with N-acetylcysteine placebo, whereas GSH was maintained with N-acetylcysteine (Pickering et al., 2019). Both arms of the latter study received acetaminophen. These findings support context-dependent GSH effects, but measured neither renal-site availability nor AVP clearance. They do not establish the proposed sequence in pregnancy.

Reduced local GSH could constrain renal AVP processing, but prolonging intact circulating AVP also depends on other clearance pathways and compensatory secretion. Antidiuresis and dilution additionally require renal responsiveness and available water. Therapeutic acetaminophen producing this sequence remains unestablished; illness, oxidative stress and dosing are candidate modifiers. Section 19.7 distinguishes GSH-sensitive processing from zinc-dependent LNPEP/IRAP cleavage and systemic GSH depletion. Neither clearance route is established as the physiological bottleneck in this setting.

Acetaminophen epidemiology constrains this proposal. Among 2,480,797 Swedish children, the adjusted association with autism was small (hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 1.02–1.08) and was absent in sibling comparisons (0.98, 0.93–1.04; Ahlqvist et al., 2024). Exposure measurement did not resolve every dose, duration or developmental window, and the study did not measure AVP clearance. The proposed clearance mechanism requires evidence that a therapeutic exposure prolongs active AVP action. A developmental contribution additionally requires a consequential disturbance and altered local recovery; the epidemiological measurement limits supply no evidence for either step. Postnatal findings are separate: Bittker and Bell (2018) reported an acetaminophen association in a retrospective parent survey; the estimate remained positive but did not reach statistical significance in a model also including ibuprofen. Exposure reports were not independently verified, and the study did not measure AVP or recovery mediation.

D’Antonio et al. (2026) likewise found no association with autism in their sibling-comparison synthesis, which was dominated by the same Ahlqvist cohort and therefore provides overlapping synthesis rather than an independent replication.

14.2.4.1 Neonatal randomised evidence and the formulation question

PreParaS randomised 48 infants born before 32 weeks to early intravenous paracetamol or placebo. The regimen began within 24 hours of birth with 20 mg/kg, followed by 7.5 mg/kg every six hours for four days (Härkin et al., 2016). The trial registry identifies Perfalgan 10 mg/mL (EudraCT 2013-001842-33). At two years, 44 infants were assessed: Griffiths developmental results were similar between groups and no signs of autism were reported (Juujärvi et al., 2019). The five-year parental survey included 39 children and found neurological or neuropsychiatric symptoms uncommon, without an adverse pattern in the paracetamol group (Juujärvi et al., 2022).

Perfalgan product information lists mannitol among its excipients (Bristol-Myers Squibb, 2010). This identifies a formulation variable, not an established protective effect. Whether the excipient altered water or electrolyte handling in PreParaS requires confirmation of the administered mannitol dose and measured effects under that neonatal regimen. A concentration reported for another intravenous paracetamol product cannot establish the trial’s excipient exposure.

These small follow-ups constrain developmental-harm claims for the neonatal regimen studied; they do not provide a precise ASD-specific risk estimate or test prenatal exposure. An unmeasured mannitol effect cannot explain away their reassuring findings. The proposed persistence mechanism still requires direct evidence of altered active AVP exposure and consequential recovery disturbance. Neither this proposal nor the observational medication associations justify changing indicated treatment to prevent autism.

14.2.5 Hypothesis-level extension: endocrine imprinting during repeated defence

Hypothesis. Repeated discordant fetal osmotic and circulatory cues, or incomplete recovery, could alter receptor responsiveness, stress-axis reliance or later regulatory thresholds. The proposed imprint concerns function after the initiating exposure resolves, rather than maternal hormone concentration or appropriate acute fetal suppression alone.

Maternal antidiuresis is an upstream water-balance exposure; fetal mismatch is a further step. Maternal water retention may change fetal water–solute conditions, but fetal response and recovery determine whether developmental recalibration follows. Maternal and fetal hormone concentrations cannot substitute for one another.

Table 14.1. Pharmacological disturbances of water–sodium balance and conditional fetal exposure

Mechanism Examples Possible consequence and missing link
Drug-specific impairment of water excretion or sodium transport Oxcarbazepine; oxytocin; thiazides; sertraline (renal experimental evidence) Possible maternal water–solute disturbance; fetal exposure requires evidence of transmission. AVP excess does not follow from exposure alone.
