Teratogenic comparator Valproate Sodium–volume mediation unestablished here; receptor and osmotic intermediates require direct evidence.

14.3 Mechanism: Fetal AVP recruitment, persistence and withdrawal

14.3.1 Initiating condition: fetal AVP recruitment

Fetal AVP recruitment is a measured response to challenge: acute hypoxaemia increased AVP in chronically instrumented sheep fetuses, with gestational-age and pressure dependence and without a concurrent rise in plasma renin activity (Raff and Wood, 1992; Section 10.3; Table 20.1). This recruitment is distinct from the proposed failure to terminate antidiuretic action after its stimulus resolves. Maternal sodium loading alone does not establish fetal hypertonicity; the osmotic branch requires a demonstrated fetal stimulus.

14.3.2 The core mechanism — time-lagged equilibration and delayed dilution

A dilutional rebound requires antidiuretic action to persist while the initial solute stimulus declines and water remains available. Its timing depends on AVP secretion and clearance, renal responsiveness and maternal–fetal exchange; neither salt loading nor a glucose fall makes rebound automatic.

14.3.3 Endocrine response: conditional responses during recovery

RAAS responses differ between expansion and underfilling, while cortisol follows additional stress inputs. The proposed sequence therefore has phase-dependent endocrine responses rather than one fixed hormone signature.

Adult experiments show that volume-regulatory sodium excretion can accompany continuing antidiuresis. After oral water loading in three patients with SIADH and five healthy participants given intranasal desmopressin, plasma atrial natriuretic factor and urinary sodium excretion increased during water retention, with a later aldosterone decrease (Cogan et al., 1988). A separate saline-loading experiment in eight healthy adults on a low-sodium diet found natriuresis with RAAS suppression without increased mean arterial pressure, GFR or ANP (Rasmussen et al., 2003). The recruited effectors therefore depend on the challenge. Paired water and sodium balances distinguish corrective excretion from net depletion; these adult component findings do not establish a fetal sequence or developmental effect.

14.3.4 Candidate endocrine imprinting after incomplete recovery

Hypothesis. Repeatedly mistimed AVP action or additional endocrine recruitment could change later renal V₂ responsiveness, osmotic thresholds or sodium–volume defence activation. The proposed imprint arises from unstable recovery dynamics rather than brief compensated dilution and must persist beyond the initiating episode.

14.3.5 Testing AVP recruitment and recovery

Cord copeptin could contribute to testing fetal AVP secretion, interpreted alongside sampling time, fetal tonicity, filling and birth-related stress. It does not by itself establish a preceding salt exposure, distinguish all proposed pathways or measure intact-AVP clearance. A diagnostic signature for this proposed recovery mechanism has not been established.

This route concerns a mismatch between a resolved osmotic stimulus and continuing antidiuretic action. When available water permits subsequent dilution and recovery remains incomplete, repeated episodes could recalibrate later responses; timely termination and full recovery interrupt the proposed sequence.

14.4 Mechanism — Salt-Wasting Phenotypes

14.4.1 Initiating condition: sodium loss exceeding conservation

True salt wasting is net sodium loss beyond replacement and conservation. Unlike dilution, it removes solute; associated volume loss depends on water balance. The defence triad may respond appropriately without every component reaching a maximum or closing the deficit.

14.4.2 Core physiology — coupled electrolyte loss and impaired recovery

Salt-wasting can combine sodium depletion with potassium or magnesium disturbance, but the coupling is specific to the cause. In sodium-depleted rats, concurrent potassium depletion prevented the usual ENaC activation, despite increased abundance of upstream sodium transporters (Frindt et al., 2011). This is a trade-off between conservation tasks, not a rule that potassium deficiency abolishes sodium reabsorption. At the cellular level, TauT/SLC6A6 transports taurine with sodium and chloride (Uchida et al., 1992). The proposed recovery problem is that impaired gradients or transporter regulation could delay replenishment of osmolytes lost during defence. A specific magnesium-dependent TauT defect and its effect in developing neurons or astrocytes require direct evidence. The retained prediction is coupled recovery demand: restoring circulating balance and rebuilding cellular osmolyte reserves may impose different constraints after the same episode.

Infant urinary infection and uropathy provide a defined renal salt-wasting initiator. Six infants aged nine days to seven months with E. coli urinary infection and urinary tract abnormalities developed hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, with increased fractional sodium excretion despite markedly elevated aldosterone (Rodríguez-Soriano et al., 1983). This clinical pattern supports transient tubular aldosterone resistance, termed secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism. Treatment largely normalised the measured disturbances. A later four-infant series, including two girls and two boys, documented recurrence with infection after previously observed hydronephrosis had resolved in one infant, supporting an infection-associated contribution without persistent obstruction (Nandagopal et al., 2009). These selected cases establish a clinically important phenotype, not its frequency among all infants with UTI.

The proposed sequence is conditional: impaired renal sodium conservation can increase replacement and circulatory-defence demands; persistent depletion, altered water balance or recurrent episodes could then constrain local neural or glial ionic and cell-volume recovery during a sensitive interval. Timely treatment and successful renal recovery could interrupt the proposed sequence. The clinical reports establish neither molecular ENaC blockade nor a male distal-reserve deficit, and the hyperkalaemic phenotype must be kept separate from the potassium-depletion/ammoniagenesis branch in Section 33.1.2. Existing clinical records and longitudinal cohorts could distinguish the salt-wasting subgroup from uncomplicated infection using paired electrolyte, renal and recovery trajectories, followed by developmental observations. Normal serum chemistry alone would neither demonstrate nor exclude compensatory work; the proposed developmental contribution still requires the local recovery intermediary, rather than treating peripheral renal dysfunction as its substitute.

Infection histories provide a separate epidemiological question. In a record-based comparison of 403 children with ASD and 2,100 controls, first-month infection diagnoses were more frequent in the ASD group (22.6% versus 18.7%), while genitourinary diagnoses were more frequent across the first two years despite fewer children having any recorded infection over that whole interval (Rosen et al., 2007). The neonatal comparison concerned any infection, not specifically UTI; the genitourinary finding concerns a different exposure interval.

The Danish cohort analysed hospitalised perinatal/neonatal infection from birth through 28 days separately, with adjusted ASD HR 1.16 (95% CI 0.97–1.39). Childhood infection began after 28 days, and its first age stratum extended from 29 days to 17 months. Childhood UTI estimates were 1.14 (0.87–1.49) overall, 1.13 (0.82–1.58) in boys and 1.10 (0.70–1.74) in girls, without a demonstrated sex interaction (p = .76). Broad childhood-infection associations also showed no significant modification across the tested age strata (p = .46). Noninfectious somatic admission was associated with ASD diagnosis, HR 1.76 (1.68–1.86), keeping illness selection and ascertainment among the alternatives (Atladóttir et al., 2010).

The narrower renal hypothesis concerns a documented salt-wasting episode and its recovery during a specified developmental interval. The nine-day to seven-month range in the Rodríguez-Soriano et al. (1983) series spans both Danish exposure windows; early infancy was not simply omitted. Those broad categories did not isolate tubular aldosterone resistance, sodium balance or neural recovery. A comparison of infants with UTI and measured salt wasting against similarly ill infants with preserved sodium conservation could test the proposed distinction using existing records or cohorts. Age pooling does not demonstrate a hidden effect, and the sex-specific estimates do not support an older-girl dilution explanation. Maternal pregnancy infection remains a separate exposure (Section 18.5).

14.4.3 Clinical archetype — hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)

Hyperemesis can combine sodium and water loss with potassium or magnesium disturbance and metabolic stress. The resulting state depends on losses, intake, replacement and renal compensation, rather than a compulsory joint AVP–RAAS–cortisol rise.

14.4.4 Mechanistic spectrum — causes of true sodium loss

Table 14.2 separates mechanisms of net sodium loss from dilution and redistribution comparators. Depletion develops when replacement and available conservation cannot close the loss.

Table 14.2. Causes of sodium loss and distinct dilution or redistribution comparators

Mechanism / Context Primary Driver Conditional response in the affected individual Clinical consequences and fetal inference
Hyperemesis gravidarum Vomiting → Na⁺ & volume loss Unreplaced losses can recruit AVP and RAAS as effective filling falls, if the axes respond; cortisol is assessed separately. Maternal depletion may occur when losses exceed replacement; fetal stress requires independent fetal evidence.
Renal tubular loss (e.g., Bartter/Gitelman analogues) NaCl transport defects; Mg²⁺ loss Renin and aldosterone can rise despite ongoing renal loss; defect, treatment and developmental phase matter. No fixed AVP/cortisol direction (Laghmani et al., 2016). Fetal renal polyuria can cause polyhydramnios in antenatal Bartter disease; maternal tubular disease does not imply the same fetal phenotype.
Adrenal insufficiency: specify the deficient hormone(s) Mineralocorticoid deficiency can impair sodium conservation; glucocorticoid deficiency can impair water excretion. In primary disease, renin can rise despite deficient aldosterone; AVP can remain active during hypotonicity when cortisol is deficient (Oelkers et al., 1992; Kamoi et al., 1993). Sodium loss, water retention or both are possible; identify lesion, balance and replacement before inferring fetal effects.
Prematurity: neonatal renal adaptation Immature reabsorption High renin/aldosterone can coexist with neonatal sodium loss; renal effectiveness and timing matter (Sulyok et al., 1979). No fixed AVP direction. Deficient sodium intake relative to losses can impair growth; assess balance and concentration separately (Al-Dahhan et al., 1984).
Iatrogenic causes Separate diuretic sodium loss from retained hypotonic-fluid dilution. Responses depend on drug, filling and tonicity; hyponatraemia alone does not establish increased AVP (Friedman et al., 1989). Maternal or neonatal depletion, dilution or overlap must be distinguished; a fluid load is not itself net sodium loss.
Proposed placental/amniotic redistribution Redistribution may change exposure without net fetal sodium loss; total compartment balance is decisive. Fetal AVP and RAAS responses depend on demonstrated changes in tonicity and filling, not an isolated amniotic concentration. Amniotic concentration can rise while solute leaves the cavity (ovine experiment: Brace et al., 2004); polyhydramnios alone does not establish fetal depletion.
14.4.5 Endocrine consequence — persistent activation and receptor drift

Hypothesis. Severe or recurrent salt loss with incomplete recovery could leave altered conservation thresholds, receptor responsiveness or autonomic tone after balance is restored, potentially favouring stress-weighted defence. Normal post-recovery regulation would oppose persistence despite substantial acute compensation.

Salt wasting distinguishes net loss despite conservation from antidiuretic action that outlasts its stimulus; both can coexist. Continued or recurrent depletion may impose recovery costs, while a lasting stress-weighted response remains a hypothesis about regulation after the acute deficit resolves.

14.5 Mechanism: Renal handling and adequacy of RAAS support

14.5.1 Initiating condition: inadequate support relative to need

RAAS support is deficient only relative to a measured conservation or circulatory need. Low renin alone may instead reflect volume expansion or effective downstream retention. Control reassignment is proposed where alternative responses compensate for genuinely inadequate support.

14.5.2 Core mechanism: altered renal sodium handling and candidate alternative support

Phosphate–FGF23/Klotho effects on NCC do not imply uniform renin suppression or failed sodium conservation (Section 14.9). Cortisol-weighted support and redox-dependent vascular regulation are distinct candidate modifiers (Section 16.8).

14.5.3 Environmental and clinical candidates for altered RAAS recruitment

Environmental and physiological contributors may alter RAAS recruitment through different routes. The proposed maternal thyroid-related pathway, for example, requires separate assessment of maternal cardiac output, renal water handling and fetal response; it does not establish one shared maternal–fetal hormone pattern.

Table 14.3. Candidate changes in RAAS support: measured responses and developmental questions

Scenario and evidence status Mechanism or directional evidence Cortisol interpretation Developmental implication and boundary
Measured component: phosphate / FGF23 Recombinant FGF23 in adult mice: NCC-mediated Na⁺ retention; aldosterone decreased, plasma renin activity unchanged (Andrukhova et al., 2014). Separate candidate support, not established cortisol substitution. Altered maternal sodium handling could change fetal exposure; the mouse experiment does not establish human dietary or fetal mediation.
Candidate extension: low-TDS / RO water Retained water relative to total solute intake and renal clearance determines the proposed challenge; processing method alone assigns no RAAS direction (§14.1). Low mineral content does not establish cortisol recruitment. The candidate route depends on maternal imbalance and a consequential fetal exposure.
Candidate extension: cortisol excess and persistence Effects depend on dose, renal receptor action, volume balance and distinct renin/aldosterone responses. Functional support during exposure differs from altered responsiveness persisting after recovery. Maternal cortisol excess alone establishes neither transmitted exposure nor persistent fetal mis-tuning.
Measured component: high-K⁺ / low-Na⁺ diet DASH study in nine adults: mean aldosterone rose from 8.3 to 17.8 ng/dL by day 5, then fell to 11.5 by day 11 (Bielopolski et al., 2022). No obligatory cortisol substitution; this is a directional counterexample to suppressed aldosterone. Dietary adaptation is not evidence of fetal stress; transmission depends on maternal balance.
Measured component: clinical hypothyroidism Five adult patients: impaired water excretion and absent AVP suppression after water loading improved with thyroid treatment (Ota et al., 1994). Altered water clearance does not establish compensatory cortisol or a particular RAAS response. Maternal flow or water-handling changes could alter fetal exposure; no fixed fetal defence-triad signature follows.
Measured receptor component: BPA; developmental extension untested BPA inhibited aldosterone-induced activity in a human MR ligand-binding-domain reporter: IC50 2.28 µM (95% CI 1.38–3.57; Toso et al., 2025). The cell assay establishes neither renal sodium loss nor compensatory cortisol dominance. The reporter assay supplies no gestational exposure threshold and does not establish impaired signalling by the intact receptor or renal dysfunction.

Table 14.4. Distinct routes to altered sodium and water handling

Regulatory context Candidate modifier Mechanism or measurement Consequence and interpretation
RAAS and distal transport Phosphate / FGF23; cortisol; low-mineral water (distinct routes) Low renin may reflect feedback, downstream retention or inadequate recruitment; the listed exposures are distinct. FGF23 can promote NCC-mediated sodium retention in mice (Andrukhova et al., 2014); low renin does not establish salt loss.
Filtration / tubular handling Hydration, fructose, caffeine Separate filtration from tubular reclamation; the listed exposures do not share an established afferent-dilation mechanism. Net sodium balance depends on intake, excretion and replacement; increased filtration alone does not establish depletion.
ANP / BNP signalling Cardiac loading; vascular stiffness as a candidate modifier Atrial stretch recruits ANP in dogs; loading, peptide release and renal action are distinct endpoints (Edwards et al., 1988). A natriuretic response may be protective. Stiffness or peptide elevation alone does not establish inappropriate sodium loss.
Drug-specific renal action Caffeine; SSRIs, with sertraline tested experimentally Caffeine can reduce fractional sodium reabsorption; experimental sertraline increases AQP2 without AVP stimulation. The tested actions differ: acute natriuresis versus antidiuretic signalling. Neither implies a shared AVP direction or fetal outcome.

In eight healthy men, 400 mg caffeine increased fractional sodium excretion without changing GFR (Shirley et al., 2002). Sertraline's V2R/cAMP/PKA-linked AQP2 effect was measured in rat collecting-duct preparations (Kim et al., 2021). These findings establish distinct routes to altered renal handling, not chronic depletion or developmental harm. The proposed shared problem is a measured mismatch between renal handling and sodium–volume requirements, followed by incomplete recovery; successful compensation remains the comparator.

Developmental exposure can alter adult fluid-challenge responses after exposure ends. Nuñez et al. (2022) exposed four rat dams per group to 5 or 10 mg/L BPA in drinking water during gestation and lactation, then provided ordinary water to offspring after weaning. At three months, exposed offspring showed sex- and dose-dependent changes in saline drinking after deprivation or depletion, while sodium balance after furosemide remained comparable. The small litter count limits inference, but the withdrawal design supplies a concrete developmental response finding. It did not measure an AVP secretion–osmolality curve or renin, and does not establish a lower AVP release threshold.

A separate mouse study shows that endocrine-active exposure can alter the developing AVP system itself. Gestational BPA at a reported maternal dose of 2.25 µg/kg/day increased female paraventricular AVP-positive neuron counts towards the male pattern, with count differences observed to four months (Zheng et al., 2024). In separate recordings at postnatal days 30–40, exposed female AVP neurons were less intrinsically excitable than controls. Increased neuron numbers therefore cannot be translated directly into increased secretion. This supports developmental modification of regulatory circuitry, while leaving osmotic secretion thresholds, renal antidiuresis and sodium–volume mediation untested. The receptor, behavioural and neural findings here are distinct components, not one demonstrated endocrine cascade.

14.5.4 Candidate persistence and altered RAAS responsiveness

Hypothesis. Low input and high gain are distinct properties. Matched Ang II exposure must produce an amplified tissue response before a low-renin state can be called sensitised; receptor abundance, post-receptor signalling and vascular effects are separate. Persistence after the initiating state resolves could amplify a later stimulus, whereas normal feedback could restore responsiveness.

When RAAS support is inadequate for the measured need, alternative endocrine or vascular support may restore stability. The developmental proposal concerns persistent demand, incomplete recovery or altered subsequent responsiveness, rather than low RAAS activity alone. Section 16.10 develops the broader question of alternative effector support and the thyroid recovery evidence.

14.6 Mechanism — High-RAAS impact

14.6.1 Definition and relationship to low-RAAS baselines

Excessive Ang II action can arise from sustained input or independently demonstrated high tissue responsiveness, including in a low-renin state. The proposed consequence is restricted microvascular delivery and redox or ATP-supported transport stress. Hormone concentration, receptor responsiveness and functional effect must therefore be distinguished; low renin alone establishes neither excessive gain nor deficient conservation.

Low renin and enhanced Ang II responsiveness are separate measurements. Demonstrating the latter requires a matched stimulus and tissue-specific response; renin concentration does not specify Ang II formation, receptor abundance or response gain.

Human challenge studies support this distinction. Wisgerhof and Brown (1978) found enhanced adrenal Ang II responsiveness in low-renin hypertension under their sodium-loading and dexamethasone protocol. In a larger study, Fisher et al. (1999) found comparable adrenal responses on a high-sodium diet, but reduced adrenal responsiveness during sodium restriction, even as the pressor response was greater in the low-renin group. Thus vascular and adrenal gain need not move together. These findings support tissue- and condition-specific response testing; they do not establish one low-renin phenotype, a fetal response or persistent developmental programming.

Immune and endocrine context may modify gain, but the direction depends on tissue, mediator and phase. Neither an inflammatory diagnosis nor population identity guarantees heightened Ang II action.

14.6.2 Trigger pathways: sustained activation and inflammatory amplification in high-gain, low-renin RAAS architecture

Sustained Ang II-mediated constriction may limit capillary delivery and oxygen availability. A transport constraint follows only when metabolic compensation cannot sustain the ATP needed for ionic regulation.

Alternatively, an independently demonstrated high-gain tissue response could magnify a modest stimulus. Production, receptor/post-receptor responsiveness and local buffering are separate determinants; inflammation or low renin alone cannot establish this branch.

14.6.3 Microvascular consequences: arteriolar constriction, uteroplacental resistance, and fetal oxygen delivery

Microvascular constriction can make delivery heterogeneous despite preserved arterial pressure. The proposed bottleneck is insufficient oxygen or metabolic support for local transport, not pressure or circulating sodium alone.

During pregnancy, excessive Ang II-mediated uteroplacental or placental-tree constriction could constrain fetal delivery. Normal pregnancy is relatively buffered against this response; inflammatory, endothelial or hypertensive disturbance becomes relevant when that protection is lost in the affected circulation.

The placenta could retain a record of repeated endocrine or osmotic challenge through altered receptor expression or coupling. The proposed high-resistance branch predicts greater AGTR1- or AVPR1A-mediated constriction after a defined exposure, persisting when the initiating ligand and physiological disturbance have resolved. Existing human evidence constrains the AVPR1A direction: Gao et al. (2019) found reduced AVP contractile sensitivity and maximal response, with lower AVPR1A and PKCβ expression, in isolated fetoplacental arterial branches from pre-eclamptic pregnancies. Diabetes was excluded. This is contrary evidence to a blanket placental gain-up claim, not a demonstration of maternal uterine or fetal-brain responsiveness. It leaves a specific test: does a prespecified exposure produce a sustained increase in placental vascular response, and does that increase reduce perfusion under matched conditions? Receptor abundance alone cannot establish either step.

Structural, thrombotic, implantation-related or other maternal vascular disorders can also impair delivery without Ang II being the initiating mediator.

14.6.4 The energetic bottleneck: oxygen constraint and low effective sodium

Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase consumes ATP, not oxygen directly. The direct recovery comparison in Section 14.7.2 shows successful sodium restoration after anoxia in cultured neurons and its prevention by pump inhibition (Sheldon et al., 2004). This establishes a local transport requirement, without identifying Ang II or placental dysfunction as the initiating cause. Reduced oxygen delivery constrains sodium-dependent work only when ATP production and reserve fail to meet demand; neural and renal transport may then become vulnerable.

Transport failure can impair intracellular sodium and chloride gradients despite adequate extracellular sodium. “Low effective sodium” here describes impaired sodium-dependent function, not necessarily low serum sodium or extracellular hypotonicity. Endocrine recruitment requires the affected compartment to generate an appropriate systemic signal.

14.6.5 The energetic paradox: louder sodium defence, weaker sodium execution

A reinforcing loop requires both a local transport constraint and a signal that recruits further defence, such as reduced filling or renal perfusion, sympathetic activation, or endothelial and immune inputs. Additional constriction could preserve pressure while worsening delivery. Conversely, restored delivery, metabolic compensation or appropriate feedback can terminate the response; local gradient failure alone does not compel systemic AVP–RAAS activation.

14.6.6 Receptor-level adaptation: protective desensitisation and the test for persistence

Repeated hormone exposure can change responsiveness, but the direction and recovery depend on the receptor and tissue. In isolated rat skeletal-muscle resistance arteries, a second Ang II challenge 30 minutes after the first produced less constriction; caveolin-1-dependent regulation limited sustained signalling (Czikora et al., 2015). In transfected cells, V1a and V2 receptors followed different post-internalisation trafficking routes (Innamorati et al., 2001). These are concrete examples of response regulation, including protection against excessive stimulation. They do not establish a common loss of sodium control or durable developmental imprinting.

The persistent extension concerns altered receptor trafficking, responsiveness or termination after the acute need resolves, not receptor “fatigue.” Defence might then recruit more readily, stop more slowly or respond inadequately. Normal matched post-recovery responses would weaken this hypothesis.

14.6.7 Nitric oxide in High-RAAS: secondary amplification via Ang II-linked oxidative stress

In this High-RAAS pathway, reduced nitric-oxide (NO) bioavailability is a possible amplifier downstream of Ang II, preserving the Ang II-first ordering. In cultured bovine aortic endothelial cells, Ang II-induced oxidant signalling reduced dihydrofolate reductase, depleted tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) and promoted endothelial NO synthase uncoupling; restoring dihydrofolate reductase protected NO production (Chalupsky & Cai, 2005). This supports a hormone-to-redox amplification mechanism in that preparation, rather than proving that every High-RAAS state follows the same sequence.

Redox dysfunction can also precede Ang II-mediated stress (Section 16.8). Reduced NO is not itself evidence of increased Ang II action or of a Klotho-mediated lesion.

If impaired vascular regulation produces a measured non-osmotic stimulus, recurrent AVP recruitment could contribute to compensation. Pressure and filling feedback can instead restrain conservation, and direct renal or central NO effects can alter the observed response. Acute systemic NO-synthase inhibition in healthy adults reduced sodium and water excretion while renin fell and AVP did not rise (Al Therwani et al., 2014). Section 16.8 separates these possibilities; additional AVP or cortisol recruitment is a testable part of the proposed pathway, not its automatic outcome.

14.6.8 Cortisol reliance and MR/GR allocation: a hypothesis-level synthesis

Glucocorticoid support may compensate for unmet circulatory or metabolic need. Its effect depends on tissue MR/GR availability, local steroid metabolism and downstream responsiveness; it does not simply replace aldosterone or Ang II. Persistent disproportionate dependence is the proposed cortisol-weighted extension.

MR-to-GR bias would mean a demonstrated shift in the relative contribution of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid receptor signalling in a specified tissue. It is not synonymous with cortisol occupying MR. Local glucocorticoid inactivation helps confer aldosterone selectivity on epithelial MR (Funder et al., 1988). In a patient with deficient cortisol-to-cortisone conversion, hydrocortisone caused sodium retention, potassium loss and renin suppression, illustrating cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid action rather than proof of a switch to GR (Stewart et al., 1988). The proposed developmental bias therefore requires receptor-specific functional measurements; serum cortisol, aldosterone or their ratio cannot identify it.

14.6.9 Adrenal remodelling and compartment-specific developmental limits

Adrenal remodelling provides a candidate mechanism for persistent changes in defence capacity. Mouse lineage tracing demonstrates zona glomerulosa (ZG)-to-zona fasciculata (ZF) conversion during normal renewal and regeneration (Freedman et al., 2013); it does not establish irreversible loss of human mineralocorticoid capacity. The developmental proposal is that repeated recruitment could leave a reproducible change in zonal composition or stimulus–output relationships after the initiating disturbance has resolved. Section 34 distinguishes that proposed persistence from adaptive remodelling during exposure and from experimentally reversible changes in steroidogenic phenotype. A lasting cortisol bias must be measured, rather than inferred from ordinary lineage conversion.

Maternal low renin does not identify fetal or central Ang II signalling or neural WNK function. Renal salt conservation and local cellular variants are separate routes (Section 23.7). Likewise, falling maternal glucose does not establish a fetal dilutional rebound without the relevant water–solute balance.

14.6.10 Immune-mediated cytokine activation as a compound osmotic–endocrine stressor

Immune activation can engage endocrine defence, but it does not impose one RAAS direction. TNF and IL-1 stimulated renin release from rat renal cortical slices (Antonipillai et al., 1990), whereas TNF-α inhibited renin transcription in the mouse As4.1 cell line and attenuated stimulated renin expression in primary mouse juxtaglomerular cells (Todorov et al., 2002). These experiments differ in preparation and endpoint; neither gives a universal illness sequence. A three-hour recombinant IL-6 infusion increased cortisol in healthy adults without increasing mean arterial pressure or heart rate (Steensberg et al., 2003), directly supporting cytokine–endocrine coupling without establishing prior RAAS failure.

An early increase in Ang II or aldosterone action followed by inadequate support is a phase-specific hypothesis. Renin suppression after restored filling can be appropriate; receptor occupancy does not demonstrate injury, “fatigue” or lasting loss of responsiveness after inflammation subsides.

Additional glucocorticoid support may follow inadequate mineralocorticoid action, but cortisol acting through MR differs from GR-dependent support. Tissue steroid availability and 11β-HSD2 matter; inflammation alone identifies neither mechanism (Section 14.6.8). The mismatch is support relative to need, not cortisol being intrinsically imprecise.

Persistent AVP action alongside inadequate sodium conservation could promote dilution where water remains available and underfilling continues. Additional glucocorticoid support is one possible accompanying response. Each arm may remain protective; their phase-specific overlap must be established rather than assigned from illness history.

A positive developmental precedent comes from neonatal immune challenge. Shanks et al. (1995) gave Long-Evans rat pups Salmonella enteritidis endotoxin at 0.05 mg/kg intraperitoneally on postnatal days 3 and 5. The dose produced a sustained physiological response without mortality. In adulthood, exposed animals had greater ACTH and corticosterone responses to restraint, weaker dexamethasone suppression and reduced brain GR density. Thus a finite early inflammatory exposure can leave altered endocrine feedback. The study did not establish an aldosterone-overshoot/MR-fatigue sequence, adrenal zonal conversion, sodium-mediated causation or an autism outcome.

14.6.11 Sex differences, phenotypic modifiers, and developmental context

Sex could modify immune–endocrine responses, but an early Ang II phase followed by reduced mineralocorticoid support and greater glucocorticoid contribution is not an established male pattern. Section 40 separates sex, illness severity, developmental stage and response-state alternatives.

The developing compartment must experience the proposed disturbance. Maternal cytokines alone establish neither fetal exposure nor delivery- or ATP-limited transport; altered local response and recovery provide the necessary link.

The neonatal endotoxin experiment supports susceptibility in a defined model, not general reprogramming by ordinary infections. The hypothesis predicts greater persistence after poorly recovered challenges than after comparable challenges with full recovery, with severity, timing, treatment and current illness distinguished.

14.6.12 Developmental implications: placental hypoxia timing, neurodevelopmental sodium handling, and persistent imprinting

During sensitive windows, Ang II-related delivery constraints could leave fetal ATP-supported ionic recovery incomplete, affecting excitability, synaptic development or volume regulation even while endocrine defence remains recruited. The developmental cost requires an actual recovery deficit; protective circulation and metabolic adaptation can prevent that transition.

A second proposed consequence is endocrine–autonomic imprinting: altered receptor responsiveness or recruitment thresholds after insufficiently recovered challenges. Experimental programming precedents (Section 36.3) do not establish the full Ang II–delivery–recovery sequence or persistent cortisol reliance.

Persistence means altered function after filling, oxygen delivery, local ionic recovery and ligand exposure have recovered, not merely after serum sodium normalises. Normal subsequent response and recovery would oppose a residual regulatory change despite substantial acute compensation.

Immune activation may alter sodium–volume defence and its recovery. The persistent proposal is changed regulation after the original need has passed; cytokine–endocrine coupling and neonatal programming do not make RAAS amplification, reduced mineralocorticoid support or cortisol substitution obligatory.

14.6.13 Boundary conditions and deferrals

This is one candidate route to fetal delivery and recovery stress, not clinical guidance or an ancestry-based assignment of physiology. Population comparisons cannot substitute for individual endocrine and vascular measurements.

14.7 Mechanism — Hypoxia-Induced Sodium Stress

14.7.1 Initiating condition: energetic constraint on sodium handling

Hypoxia can enter this pathway when oxygen delivery limits ATP production enough to constrain transport, despite available sodium and adequate endocrine signalling. The defining mismatch is between metabolic support and regulatory demand; oxygen extraction, glycolysis and reserve may preserve transport during a compensated reduction in delivery.

14.7.2 The core mechanism: ATP supply and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase work

Neural sodium recovery depends on the balance between continuing influx and active extrusion. In cultured postnatal rat hippocampal neurons, five minutes of chemical anoxia with glucose available increased intracellular sodium, which returned to baseline within approximately 6–10 minutes after reoxygenation. Blocking Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase during this interval exposed continuing sodium entry and prevented recovery (Sheldon et al., 2004). The recovery interval therefore carries active transport work after oxygen returns.

In the proposed route, reduced oxygen delivery becomes consequential when ATP production and reserve cannot support that work. Residual sodium loading could then alter sodium-dependent transport and excitability, with the response determined by cell type, developmental stage and the prevailing ionic gradients.

A renal sodium-loss branch would depend on impaired reabsorption relative to the filtered load; whole-body balance and tonicity also depend on intake, filtration and water balance.

14.7.3 Bidirectional vulnerability: the hypoxia–sodium-instability loop

A sodium–water disturbance that reduces effective filling, or sufficiently severe cellular swelling that disrupts tissue delivery, could deepen an energy-limited recovery deficit. This proposed delivery–recovery loop remains conditional: oxygen extraction, metabolic adaptation and restored perfusion can break it.

14.7.4 Endocrine consequence: compensation under energetic constraint

Endocrine responses follow the affected filling, pressure, renal and osmotic signals rather than a fixed hypoxic signature. Preserved pressure alone cannot identify the local energy or recovery state.

14.7.5 Developmental implication: energetic bottlenecks during critical windows

During sensitive windows, repeated delays in sodium-gradient restoration could prolong changes in excitability and sodium-dependent transport while developmental processes are being organised. The proposed lasting effect is altered circuit or endocrine regulation after the acute ionic and energetic disturbance has resolved, linking this route to the cell- and stage-specific tests in Sections 18.1.7 and 23.7.

14.7.6 Endocrine imprinting: the energy-constrained baseline

Hypothesis. Recurrent energy-limited recovery could leave altered response thresholds after oxygen delivery normalises. A cortisol-weighted baseline is one possible configuration; persistent functional change, rather than the severity of the acute response, defines this extension.

This route begins when reduced oxygen delivery limits ATP-supported transport. Compartment-specific compensation may restore gradients; incomplete recovery could amplify the disturbance and affect development. The defining constraint is insufficient metabolic support for otherwise needed regulation.

14.8 Mechanism — Cytoskeletal Volume-Control Disruption

14.8.1 Initiating condition: mechanical impairment of cellular recovery

A cytoskeletal recovery defect can prolong an ordinary challenge without increasing its initial size. Impaired volume control, transporter organisation or osmolyte replenishment predicts slower or less complete recovery after a matched perturbation.

14.8.2 The core mechanism: impaired RVD and the proposed osmolyte debt

Cytoskeletal perturbation can change both volume-sensitive currents and regulatory volume decrease (RVD), but those outcomes need not have one fixed relation. In human HT-3 cells, actin disruption with cytochalasin B increased chloride conductance and prolonged RVD; actin stabilisation inhibited the swelling-induced current and also delayed volume recovery (Shen et al., 1999). The Sodium Struggle proposal adds a distinct recovery step: excessive osmolyte loss or inadequate replenishment could leave an osmolyte debt after volume has partly recovered. This requires concurrent measurements of cell volume, relevant channel flux, intracellular osmolyte content and replenishment. Delayed RVD alone does not show prolonged VRAC opening or loss of every compatible osmolyte.

14.8.3 Physiological consequence: amplification through delayed resolution

An osmolyte deficit could reduce reserve for the next challenge even after extracellular conditions improve. Consequences for potassium handling, glutamate clearance and excitability remain functional predictions. Delayed cellular recovery could extend endocrine defence only through a connecting osmotic, circulatory or stress signal.

14.8.4 Environmental Exposures Affecting Cellular Mechanics and Ionic Regulation

Chemical and physical exposures can alter cellular mechanics or ionic regulation, providing candidate initiating disturbances or constraints on later recovery. Direct volume-control evidence comes from neonatal-rat astrocytes: 10 µM methylmercury inhibited RVD after hypotonic swelling, with increased sodium uptake and reduced taurine release (Vitarella et al., 1996). Replacing extracellular sodium with N-methyl-D-glucamine restored recovery to control levels. The implicated sodium-entry route is distinct from demonstrated actin injury.

Specific toxicants can also impair cytoskeletal function. Nivalenol and deoxynivalenol (0.5–2.5 µM, 24 h) reorganised actin and slowed wound restitution in rat intestinal epithelial cells (Bianco et al., 2012). That is a functional cytoskeletal effect, although restitution is not RVD. Table 20.1 separates these findings from lead-sensitive pump activity, compound-specific pesticide effects and PFOS/monophthalate barrier experiments. The proposed convergence is functional: an exposure can reduce the capacity to restore ionic or cellular-volume conditions, even without making the initial osmotic challenge larger. The proposed developmental extension requires a measured recovery deficit in the relevant compartment; neither chemical-class membership nor altered actin alone establishes that extension.

Physical stimulation can alter both cytoskeletal mechanics and ionic signalling, although the connection between those endpoints remains untested here. In human airway smooth-muscle cells, 30 s of 1 MHz ultrasound (20% duty cycle) reduced contractile force: recovery took about 200 s at 170 kPa, whereas 290 kPa disrupted actin and left incomplete recovery during observation (Mizrahi et al., 2012). This was mechanical recovery, not RVD. Separate experiments demonstrated ultrasound-evoked CFTR chloride currents in transfected HEK293T cells (0.8 MHz, 0.20 MPa; Wen et al., 2024) and increased astrocyte-dependent tonic inhibition through GABA-A receptors in mouse hippocampal cultures (5 MHz, 100 kPa, twenty 2-s sonications; Mishima et al., 2024). Neither established actin-dependent chloride or volume recovery. The hypothesis retains a specific mechanical entry route: an exposure that perturbs actin could prolong recovery from a subsequent matched osmotic challenge. That missing link requires direct measurement; these experimental protocols do not establish developmental risk from routine diagnostic ultrasound.

Ionising radiation provides another cellular example, with a distinct exposure context. In murine MC3T3-E1 preosteoblasts, 0.5 or 5 Gy X-rays altered F-actin; after 0.5 Gy, the initial reduction at 2 h was followed by increased F-actin at days 1 and 3 and return towards control by day 5 (Huang et al., 2020). These findings establish dose- and time-dependent remodelling, not a measured RVD defect or a developmental effect of diagnostic imaging.

THz effects likewise depend on the preparation and waveform. Irradiating purified actin at 0.46 THz for 20 min increased polymerisation, whereas 30 min of intense 4 THz pulses (80–250 μJ/cm² per micropulse) disrupted actin in submerged HeLa cells (Yamazaki et al., 2018, 2020). The latter study implicated energy transfer through water, with separate demonstration of pressure waves. These are positive demonstrations that physical energy can alter actin, with opposite structural outcomes. They do not establish impaired osmotic recovery or developmental injury.

14.8.5 Secondary amplification: particles, barrier function and endocrine-active chemicals

Particles and associated chemicals could jointly impair recovery, but passage, barrier effects, ionic disturbance and receptor interference are separate endpoints. The BPA human-MR reporter finding (Table 14.3) used no particles and did not establish particle-mediated delivery. Detection or passage alone cannot establish the combined mechanism.

14.8.6 Endocrine imprinting: structural imprinting of recovery dynamics

Hypothesis. Slow cellular recovery could influence later regulatory calibration when it generates a relevant endocrine signal. Persistent cortisol dominance or repeated oscillation is not required; the proposed lasting effect concerns altered response or recovery after the initial insult.

Actin-related disruption can delay volume recovery; extended osmolyte loss or incomplete replenishment is a further possibility that requires measurement. The developmental proposal requires a measured cellular recovery deficit; systemic amplification is an additional branch where a connecting endocrine signal exists.

14.9 Mechanism — Dietary inorganic phosphate load

14.9.1 Exposure and the coordination proposal

Inorganic phosphate additives contribute to the phosphorus content of processed foods, often alongside sodium. In a chemical analysis of paired four-day menus, additive-enhanced foods supplied an average of 606 ± 125 mg more phosphorus and 1,329 ± 642 mg more sodium per day, approximately 60% more of each than lower-additive menus (Carrigan et al., 2014). This was a menu-composition comparison, not a feeding experiment. Phosphorus also contributes to infant feeding solute load, discussed below. Orthophosphate used for drinking-water corrosion control is a separate exposure whose actual dose must be established before comparison with dietary loading (US EPA, n.d.). Sodium-adjusted interventions nevertheless provide evidence that phosphate exposure can alter endocrine and cardiovascular responses beyond the sodium that accompanies it; the relevant protocols and their limits are specified below.

Early life supplies a separate water-balance consideration. Potential renal solute load includes dietary nitrogen, sodium, potassium, chloride and phosphorus; a higher excretory burden can reduce the margin against dehydration when intake falls or losses rise (Ziegler and Fomon, 1989). This is a water-requirement argument, not evidence of hyponatraemia, phosphate-driven oscillation or autism. The relevant exposure is the complete feeding composition and available water during illness or reduced intake, rather than phosphorus considered in isolation.

The proposed phosphate route concerns coordination among phosphate disposal, sodium conservation and vascular regulation through shared transport and endocrine machinery. At a matched filtered phosphate load, greater or more persistent proximal phosphate reclamation could oppose disposal unless appropriately suppressed. The proposed upstream susceptibility concerns whether reducing that reclamation while preserving sodium balance requires greater adjustment elsewhere or prolongs compensation (Sections 32.1.4 and 40.3.2). Dietary effects on these components could increase regulatory work or delay recovery; phosphaturia and hormone changes alone do not demonstrate that burden, sodium loss or dilution.

14.9.2 Intestinal entry and proximal phosphate disposal

Intestinal phosphate absorption includes active NaPi-IIb-mediated transport and a passive paracellular route. In wild-type and intestinal Slc34a2-deficient mice, two days of administered active vitamin D increased active jejunal transport only in wild types, without increasing paracellular flux; both genotypes increased phosphate excretion while maintaining plasma phosphate (Hernando et al., 2021). This establishes a regulated entry pathway, not a fixed relation between vitamin D status, absorbed phosphate and a larger plasma excursion. Any contribution to the proposed renal burden depends on the absorbed dose and the accompanying excretory response.

Filtered phosphate is reclaimed in the proximal tubule through sodium-dependent transporters including NaPi-IIa (SLC34A1) and NaPi-IIc (SLC34A3). Their relative contribution depends on species, loading protocol and sampling time. NaPi-IIa, but not NaPi-IIc, adapted rapidly in one mouse dietary-switch experiment (Bourgeois et al., 2013), whereas both declined within one hour of phosphate gavage in wild-type mice in another protocol (Daryadel et al., 2022). NaPi-IIc should not therefore be assigned a universally minor role, particularly in humans, where SLC34A3 mutations cause renal phosphate wasting (Bergwitz et al., 2006). Parathyroid hormone (PTH) and FGF23 can reduce apical phosphate-transporter abundance and promote phosphaturia, but this sodium coupling does not by itself establish a large net sodium loss. NaPi transport accounts for a minority of proximal sodium reclamation; the broader effects on sodium–hydrogen exchanger 3 (NHE3) and other sodium-reclaiming processes considered below matter more than NaPi stoichiometry alone.

Human infant tissue provides a useful direct comparison. In brush-border membrane vesicles from six male and seven female infant kidney donors, NaPi-IIa accounted for approximately 60% of sodium-dependent phosphate uptake in both sexes, without a significant sex difference in relative transporter contributions (Fernandes et al., 2026). This small, clinically heterogeneous deceased-donor study identifies proximal phosphate transport, not whole-nephron sodium allocation, and a nonsignificant comparison does not establish equivalence. The species-dependent contributions also caution against assigning mouse phosphate-transporter proportions to humans.

A broader proximal sodium effect is experimentally possible, but its source matters. In anaesthetised rats, administered PTH(1–34) redistributed apical NHE3 and NaPi transporters, inhibited sodium-pump activity and increased sodium and water excretion (Zhang et al., 1999). This hormone-manipulation experiment does not establish the same sodium response after a meal. Duodenal phosphate increased phosphaturia rapidly in rats without significant sodium fractional-excretion change in the intact comparison (Berndt et al., 2007). A sodium-controlled human intravenous-versus-duodenal loading study did not find an intestine-specific phosphaturic response (Scanni et al., 2014). These results support testing rapid phosphate sensing while keeping phosphaturia, proximal sodium redistribution and whole-body sodium loss as distinct endpoints.

14.9.3 Timing, sensing and phosphate adaptation

The early response can include rapid transporter redistribution and PTH release, but its timing is exposure-specific. In anaesthetised rats given 0.5 mmol phosphate, PTH rose within 10 minutes after intravenous loading and 25 minutes after intragastric loading, while intact FGF23 did not rise over four hours (Thomas et al., 2017). By contrast, FGF23 increased by four hours after phosphate gavage in the mouse protocol described above (Daryadel et al., 2022). Nor can the slower component be explained by an obligatory increase in Fgf23 transcription. Mice fed 1.2% rather than 0.6% phosphate for two weeks had higher intact FGF23 and skeletal Galnt3 expression without increased Fgf23 expression; FGFR1-dependent glycosylation protected FGF23 from proteolytic inactivation (Takashi et al., 2019). This identifies a regulated processing mechanism, not immediate release from a proven storage pool. Different clocks remain a plausible source of mismatch, but transcription, processing and secretion must be distinguished, and their ordering measured for the particular phosphate challenge.

The human response depends on protocol and sampling. In ten healthy men studied in a randomised crossover trial, a standard diet containing 1,000 mg phosphorus/day was combined with either 750 mg/day supplemental phosphorus or sevelamer for five days. The higher-phosphate condition increased plasma phosphate, urinary phosphate and intact FGF23, and lowered circulating soluble Klotho, without changing PTH, aldosterone or measured catecholamine markers (Scotti Gerber et al., 2025). The intended sodium match was imperfect: the lower-phosphate arm accidentally received 0.8 g/day more sodium. Serum sodium, urinary sodium excretion, urine volume and body weight did not differ significantly. This is evidence of phosphate adaptation under the tested conditions, not evidence of a PTH-first sequence, volume depletion or oscillation. Serum phosphate was 0.87 and 1.00 mmol/L in the lower- and higher-phosphate conditions, respectively. Their difference corresponds to about 0.13 mOsm/L of phosphate particles in an ideal calculation before binding and counter-ion effects; it does not demonstrate hypertonicity. Endocrine and transport effects remain relevant at those concentrations.

The direction of the circulating Klotho response is not uniform across human interventions. In a separate randomised study of twenty healthy adults, six weeks of phosphate supplementation increased serum α-Klotho and urinary Klotho (Mohammad et al., 2018). The differing protocols do not establish why the directions diverge. Neither response establishes a corresponding change in renal membrane α-Klotho or can be equated with genetic Klotho deficiency.

A kidney–bone sensing pathway provides positive mechanistic evidence. Zhou et al. (2023) linked proximal phosphate uptake to glycolysis, glycerol-3-phosphate (G-3-P) production and bone FGF23 regulation using cell experiments and mouse Npt2a/Gpd1 manipulations. G-3-P increased within ten minutes of intravenous phosphate in mice; a three-person oral-loading pilot found an increase within one to two hours. This connects mineral handling to metabolic signalling, but does not impose a universal slow delay or demonstrate sodium–volume overshoot.

Effective tonicity provides another input to FGF23 regulation. In osteoblast-like UMR-106 cells, reducing medium NaCl by 20 mmol/L for 24 hours increased Fgf23 expression and FGF23 detected by a C-terminal assay in the culture medium; mannitol reversed the response whereas urea did not (Radvanyi et al., 2024). This supports a response to effective tonicity rather than measured osmolality alone. Intact FGF23 in the culture medium was below detection. In the same study, six hyponatraemic patients had higher C-terminal FGF23 than six controls, without significant differences in intact FGF23 or phosphate. The culture findings identify a regulatory input, but neither assay result establishes consequent bioactive hormone excess or phosphate wasting. These downstream effects and their contribution to the proposed developmental recovery disturbance remain separate questions.

Renal dopamine is another measured phosphate-adaptation pathway. After 24 hours on 1.2% rather than 0.1% phosphate chow, mice had increased renal and urinary dopamine and phosphaturia; carbidopa blunted phosphate adaptation in a separate rat experiment (Weinman et al., 2011). However, urinary sodium-to-creatinine ratios did not differ significantly between the mouse diets, and the five-day human study found no dopamine change (Scotti Gerber et al., 2025). These data support a dopamine contribution to phosphate handling in the tested rodents, without demonstrating a parallel dietary natriuresis or a universal human response.

14.9.4 Distal sodium conservation and whole-body balance

The conditional sequence is phosphate entry and disposal, with altered downstream sodium delivery if proximal sodium reclamation also falls. Distal sodium conservation can help maintain net balance; effective filling and recovery depend on the integrated response. Phosphaturia alone is not natriuresis.

The distal sodium-conservation component is supported by a separate intervention: recombinant FGF23 increased NCC abundance and sodium retention in mice (Andrukhova et al., 2014; §33). It is not thereby established as the second phase of every dietary phosphate response. If phosphate exposure changes sodium delivery along the nephron, tubular feedback provides a plausible route to altered filtration or renin signalling; distal delivery and those responses would need to be measured in the same protocol.

The renin response cannot be inferred from greater downstream sodium delivery alone. In an isolated perfused rabbit juxtaglomerular preparation, increased luminal chloride inhibited renin release, whereas sodium salts without chloride did not (Lorenz et al., 1991). A subsequent volume-conserving response therefore requires the integrated balance, perfusion and hormonal signals to be established, rather than assuming that increased macula-densa chloride directly raises renin.

RAAS findings differ across the actual interventions. Four weeks of high-phosphate feeding increased blood pressure, renal renin expression and circulating angiotensin II in rats; parathyroidectomy with fixed physiological PTH replacement prevented the pressure rise despite elevated phosphate, supporting PTH involvement in that model (Bozic et al., 2014). In twenty healthy adults randomised to phosphate supplementation or phosphate binding, with sodium supplementation intended to match absorbed sodium, six-week blood pressure and urinary metanephrines rose while renin and aldosterone did not (Mohammad et al., 2018). A separate six-man, fixed-order five-day study found higher systolic pressure, lower aldosterone and higher ANP with high-phosphate intake (Zhang et al., 2021). These are distinct response patterns to specify in advance, not interchangeable evidence that RAAS compensation followed sodium loss.

Whole-body balance remains the decisive comparator. In the six-man sodium-controlled study, high-phosphate intake reduced 24-hour urine volume and produced hormone changes consistent with retention, but blood volume was not measured, 24-hour sodium excretion was unchanged, and calculated postprandial sodium-balance gaps resolved by the next morning (Zhang et al., 2021). Thus neither net sodium loss nor sustained volume expansion can be read directly from phosphaturia or hormone direction. The existing FGF23–NCC retention evidence further opposes a simple phosphate-to-low-sodium chain. Increased variability is a prediction to test, not a replacement conclusion that follows automatically when mean sodium remains stable.

Dilution or volume instability remains an additional outcome to establish during phosphate loading. Stable compensated balance would oppose that branch even where PTH, FGF23 or transport activity changes; hormone adaptation alone does not demonstrate a recovery cost.

14.9.5 Infant mineral-hormone differences as modifiers

Sex-dependent mineral-hormone responses could modify this redistribution and the work required to maintain sodium-volume balance. At three months, girls had higher circulating intact FGF23 than boys in a study of 113 healthy infants (Holmlund-Suila et al., 2016). Combined with the experimental PTH and FGF23 effects above, this motivates a conditional chain: a defined phosphate exposure elicits a particular hormonal response; that response changes proximal reclamation and downstream sodium delivery; compensation then determines balance and recovery. A relatively PTH-weighted response in some boys is one candidate mechanism, rather than a response demonstrated by the basal FGF23 difference. The predicted consequence is greater or more prolonged compensatory recruitment under specified conditions, not inevitable sodium loss. A similar segmental response and prompt recovery in both sexes would constrain this contribution (Sections 33 and 40.3).

14.9.6 Conditional acid-base and nitrogen branch

Phosphate disposal and glutamine-dependent ammoniagenesis are also separable. Urinary phosphate buffers secreted hydrogen ions, while electroneutrality applies to the full mixture of ions rather than a fixed sodium, potassium or ammonium partner for each phosphate ion. Neutral sodium-phosphate loading in adults increased acid excretion mainly through titratable acidity and produced alkalosis (Scanni et al., 2014). By contrast, intravenous sodium phosphate markedly increased urinary ammonia in rabbits with experimentally induced metabolic acidosis (Yu et al., 1976). Thus a phosphate–ammoniagenesis interaction is possible under specified acid–base conditions, but is not an obligatory response to phosphate intake.

Developmental acid-handling demands could modify this phosphate response. In 76 low-birth-weight infants receiving a commercial preterm formula, those below 1,600 g had faster weight gain per kilogram and greater net acid excretion than those above 2,100 g, while excreting less sodium, potassium and chloride (Kalhoff et al., 1994). In a separate human-milk-fed preterm cohort, net acid excretion averaged 0.83 ± 0.47 mmol/kg/day (Manz et al., 1991). These observations connect growth, feeding and maturity with acid-disposal requirements; the lower sodium, potassium and chloride excretion was interpreted as compatible with greater retention for growth. Net urinary acid excretion is distinct from gross endogenous acid production or systemic acidosis; neither study establishes a greater male acid burden under matched conditions.

PTH could add a bicarbonate and potassium component if its proximal effects are sufficiently large and sustained. It reversibly inhibited bicarbonate and fluid absorption in isolated rabbit proximal tubules (Iino and Burg, 1979). Administered PTH increased urinary sodium, potassium and bicarbonate in ten children with short stature, whose responses resembled adult controls (Hochberg et al., 1984). Together with NHE3 redistribution, these findings support investigating whether an infant phosphate response increases distal solute delivery and bicarbonate or potassium loss. Actual depletion depends on intake, replacement, filtration and downstream reclamation. Neonatal rodent tubules also increased acidification during acidosis through NHE3 and developmental NHE8 responses, demonstrating adaptive capacity (Twombley et al., 2010).

An infant with sustained metabolic acidosis or consequential potassium depletion could therefore engage a different renal glutamine response from a healthy adult undergoing neutral phosphate loading. In potassium-deprived rats, urinary ammonium excretion and ammoniagenic enzyme expression increased before hypokalaemia developed; combined potassium deprivation and acid loading produced an additive response (Hossain et al., 2011). This is evidence of a measured adaptive response despite initially normal serum electrolytes, not evidence of an infant phosphate effect. Gastrointestinal bicarbonate or potassium losses provide another possible entry into that state. The phosphate-coupled extension depends on the measured acid-base and potassium conditions, the phosphate exposure reaching the relevant renal compartment, and the duration of compensation. Ordinary growth-related acid demand, PTH release or phosphaturia alone cannot identify the acid-loaded state. Sections 24.3 and 33.1.2 consider whether a sufficiently large or prolonged renal metabolic response could affect systemic substrate availability and local neural recovery.

A renal nitrogen contribution would require measurements of flux as well as circulating concentrations. During experimental acid loading in adult men, increased renal glutamine extraction accompanied net uptake of circulating glutamate and greater urinary ammonia excretion, without a comparable increase in renal-venous ammonia release (Owen and Robinson, 1963). Acid-loaded observations also had lower arterial plasma glutamine than control observations, suggesting a systemic substrate effect without establishing renal extraction as its sole cause. Renal glutamine use therefore need not generate high blood glutamate or ammonia. The nephron-coordination hypothesis does not depend on a universal autism-associated amino-acid profile; any proposed renal contribution must be distinguished from other tissue sources and sample-handling effects.

14.9.7 Vascular and autonomic branch

Vascular and autonomic effects also have direct component evidence. In eleven healthy men, a 1,200 mg rather than 400 mg phosphorus meal reduced brachial flow-mediated dilation at two hours; separate bovine endothelial-cell experiments linked high phosphate to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduced NO signalling (Shuto et al., 2009). In the twenty-person trial, high-phosphate exposure raised 24-hour systolic pressure by 4.1 mmHg (95% CI 2.1–6.1) and urinary metanephrines, but did not change the measured endothelial-function or arterial-elasticity indices (Mohammad et al., 2018). The acute and sustained protocols therefore should not be merged into one vascular outcome. A contribution to regional delivery or recovery remains plausible, with systemic filling, cerebral perfusion and developmental consequences still requiring their own measurements (§16.8).

14.9.8 Integrated prediction and local recovery

Phosphate-sensitive G3P signalling connects mineral handling with metabolism, but does not establish ATP depletion. Repeated phosphate loads are candidate initiating pressures; the proposed developmental contribution depends on whether their physiological effects leave local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery incomplete.

15 Volume Pathway Catalogue

Effective circulating volume describes circulatory adequacy, not total body water or a separately measurable fluid fraction. Central filling, pressure, regional flow and oxygen delivery are distinct: normal blood volume can coexist with a delivery problem, and regional underdelivery need not imply systemic underfilling.

The ten circulation mechanisms below retain their original identities. Table 15.1 organises them into two panels: actual filling or delivery disturbances, and sensing or regulatory disturbances. Its five defined mis-sensing states expand one mechanism rather than adding five independent causes. These routes can interact with the cellular routes in Table 13.1.

Panel A distinguishes external loss, extravascular displacement, intravascular pooling, inadequate forward flow and regional delivery failure. Redistribution describes a distribution state; barrier or oncotic failure is one possible cause. Broad venous containment and regional reservoir shifts describe different scales of intravascular redistribution. Panel B distinguishes directional signalling error, altered gain, mistimed response, shifted reference, discordant integration and endocrine mis-regulation. Redox effects can enter either panel through different measured intermediaries (§16.8). Absolute hypovolaemia, central underfilling, tissue underdelivery and a faulty signal must therefore be identified separately.

Adult hormone manipulation illustrates that plasma volume need not track total extracellular fluid volume. In seven healthy women studied during ovarian-hormone suppression and add-back, oestradiol increased plasma volume while total extracellular fluid volume fell; the plasma fraction increased from 16.1% to 21.0%, alongside reduced transcapillary albumin escape (Stachenfeld and Taylor, 2004). This supports a physiological redistribution mechanism, without establishing a larger sodium store or identifying one vascular cause. The study had no male comparator and does not establish an infant female advantage. Comparable developmental effects on filling and recovery remain candidate modifiers alongside renal allocation (Sections 32 and 40).

15.1 Volume-Loss Pathways

These pathways reduce ECV by removing sodium-bearing fluid from the body.

15.1.1 True Volume Loss (Absolute depletion)

True volume loss occurs when external losses exceed replacement and conservation. Bleeding, hyperemesis, gastrointestinal loss, burns or renal-adrenal salt wasting can reduce the available fluid reserve. Preterm sodium-balance studies illustrate incomplete conservation despite endocrine recruitment, without establishing blood-volume depletion or ASD mediation (Sulyok et al., 1979; Al-Dahhan et al., 1984; §§14.4 and 16.1).

15.2 Volume-Redistribution Pathways

These pathways lower arterial filling by displacing otherwise available fluid into compartments that do not effectively support circulation.

15.2.1 Volume Redistribution (Internal displacement)

Redistribution can reduce central availability while total water remains normal or increased. Interstitial, ascitic or serosal accumulation enters this route only when it compromises return or central supply. Maternal obesity and diabetes provide separately sourced ASD-associated contexts, with different confounding and timing patterns (Gardner et al., 2015; Xiang et al., 2018). Those associations do not measure redistribution; §16.2 and Table 15.1 retain that proposed intermediary.

15.3 Barrier / Oncotic Failure Pathways

These pathways weaken intravascular retention even when water and sodium remain physically present.

15.3.1 Barrier / Oncotic Failure (Retention / leak)

Increased permeability or reduced oncotic retention can shift plasma water out of the circulation. Glycocalyx perturbation altered albumin/water passage in endothelial and rat-vessel preparations (Singh et al., 2013; Betteridge et al., 2017; §35.1). Those components do not establish a common leak mechanism for inflammation, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic loss or impaired hepatic synthesis, or prove that any associated oedema reduces effective filling (§16.3).

15.4 Vascular Containment Failure

These pathways impair the container rather than the fluid itself.

15.4.1 Vascular Containment Failure (Tone / structural failure)

Expanded venous capacitance or impaired recoil can reduce central filling despite near-normal total volume. Hypermobility-associated connective-tissue differences motivate this route, but the mixed adult neurodivergent cohort measured hypermobility and self-reported orthostatic symptoms, not venous compliance or central filling (Csecs et al., 2022; §16.4). Demonstrated pooling would be an actual distribution problem; intact sensing must not be assumed from the diagnosis.

15.5 Splanchnic Pooling / Reservoir Shift

These pathways hide volume within capacitance reservoirs rather than removing it from the body.

Splanchnic pooling is intravascular redistribution: blood retained in a regional reservoir can reduce central return without leaving the circulation. Healthy-adult tilt increased splanchnic segmental volume, whereas lower-body negative pressure decreased it despite similar flow reductions (Taneja et al., 2007; §41). Volume and flow therefore need separate measurements. Meal-related load, histamine-linked states and dysautonomia remain context-specific candidates rather than proof of sequestration (§16.5).

15.6 Microvascular Flow Failure

These pathways uncouple central flow from tissue delivery.

15.6.1 Microvascular Flow Failure (Distribution failure)

Microvascular maldistribution can impair regional delivery despite adequate central filling. Endothelial dysfunction, shunting, heterogeneous capillary flow and microthrombotic states are possible intermediaries. Less continuous skin flow in term newborns with suspected infection supplies a regional component finding, not evidence of brain hypoperfusion or an ASD mechanism (Alba-Alejandre et al., 2013; §§16.3 and 16.6).

15.7 Cardiac Output Limitation

These pathways convert volume presence into effective undercirculation by limiting forward flow.

15.7.1 Cardiac Output Limitation (Pump failure)

Cardiac output limitation can reduce effective arterial filling or tissue delivery despite preserved intravascular volume. Cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia or structural disease enters this route only when forward flow is impaired. Maternal cardiac function/Doppler findings and childhood congenital-heart-disease/ASD associations come from different compartments and studies (Pieper et al., 2013; Sigmon et al., 2019; §16.7); neither supplies the missing local recovery intermediary.

15.8 Redox-Dependent Vascular Regulation and Filling-Signal Integrity

These pathways alter vascular regulation and may affect actual delivery, mechanical transmission or sensory encoding through different routes.

Redox-dependent vascular effects can alter actual delivery reserve, while renal or central NO actions can change regulation through separate routes. Adult diesel exposure impaired vasodilator responses without changing resting forearm flow (Mills et al., 2005); this does not establish fetal underdelivery or a sensory lesion. Section 16.8 separates these components from a proposed error in filling-related signalling and from the exposure associations retained in Table 20.1.

15.9 Volume Mis-Sensing

These pathways concern inaccurate cardiovascular information or an inappropriate response to it; reduced gain, altered timing or a shifted reference is not necessarily an error.

15.9.1 Volume Mis-Sensing (Signal acquisition, interpretation or response)

Table 15.1 Panel B separates directional error, altered gain, mistimed response, shifted reference and discordant integration. These states do not locate a lesion: vessel mechanics, afferent encoding, central interpretation and effectors must be distinguished. Section 16.9 develops those tests, with component evidence in Table 16.1. Adequate volume is not assumed; a real deficit and a sensing failure can coexist.

15.10 Endocrine Volume Mis-Regulation

These pathways concern feedback or effector support that is inappropriate for the characterised need, including possible reliance on alternative support.

15.10.1 Endocrine Volume Mis-Regulation (Control reassignment)

Endocrine mis-regulation requires a mismatch between physiological need, available feedback and the sustaining response. Thyroid, FGF23/Klotho, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid disturbances have different measured consequences (§16.10). For example, FGF23 promoted sodium retention in mice, and hypothyroid water-clearance impairment did not always entail failed AVP suppression (Andrukhova et al., 2014; Iwasaki et al., 1990). Low renin or cortisol weighting alone does not establish inappropriate control.

Table 15.1 uses the same five fields as Table 13.1. Panel A maps actual disturbances of filling and delivery; Panel B maps sensing and regulatory disturbances. These are overlapping entry routes, not independent defended variables. Normal total volume does not establish adequate central filling or tissue delivery. A sensing disturbance can coexist with a real deficit. Table 15.2 retains conditional endocrine patterns, and §§16.1–16.10 retain all ten mechanism identities. Table 16.1 supplies component evidence beneath the map.

Evidence key: [E] identifies the stated empirical observation or association; [S], a measured physiological component; [H], a proposed response or mediation. As in Tables 13.1 and 20.1, these are claim roles, not a strength ranking. Separate studies supporting an ASD association and a physiological component do not establish the intervening chain. Gene-to-route assignments remain candidates unless a specified allele, tissue and endpoint are measured; this table does not change the frozen genetic classification. Every proposed developmental route additionally requires impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery with the specified developmental consequence.
