The associations and physiological components in the table do not yet demonstrate convergence on one fetal recovery disturbance. Compensation may preserve stability; the proposed developmental connection remains to be established.

18.1.3 Fetal Exposure and Developmental Timing

Section 9 groups the osmotic, circulatory, endocrine, inflammatory and cellular inputs that define fetal exposure. Fetal AVP competence has its own developmental timetable (Section 10.3), distinct from the timing of a maternal exposure.

Mixed osmotic, circulatory and stress cues can be integrated successfully. The proposed calibration effect arises when recurrent demand, response mismatch or incomplete recovery during a susceptible window changes developmental conditions and later regulation—not from mixed cues alone.

Exposure timing must be separated from hormone maturation. In 419,425 children, gestational diabetes diagnosed by 26 weeks was associated with ASD, whereas later diagnosis was not (Xiang et al., 2018; estimates in Table 18.1). Diagnosis did not measure fetal exposure onset, duration or magnitude. First-trimester and later-only valproate prescription estimates were similar in another cohort, but the later group contained only 67 children and had a wide interval (Christensen et al., 2013). Neither finding establishes a universal earlier-is-worse rule or an AVP-defined 11–19-week susceptibility window.

18.1.4 Maternal and Fetal Regulation in Specific Exposure Routes

Sections 9 and 10 distinguish maternal regulation of the input from the fetus’s response to placentally transformed exposure. The examples below concern vascular delivery, endocrine filtering and fetal cue integration; the exposure’s magnitude, recurrence and completeness of recovery remain the proposed influences on later thresholds and osmoregulatory behaviour.

18.1.4.1 Placental Vascular and Endocrine Examples

Maternal peptide concentration cannot substitute for fetal exposure. Sections 10.1 and 10.1.1 separate placental transfer, metabolism and maternal turnover; Section 10.3 describes fetal AVP competence and its distinct timetable.

Maternal glucose and water–solute perturbations require measured fetal concentration and timing; transport asymmetry alone does not specify the direction or duration of fetal exposure (Section 10.2). Sections 18.2 and 19.7 develop the metabolic route.

Maternal uteroplacental perfusion can influence fetal oxygen and nutrient delivery without maternal peptide transfer. Maternal and fetal placental vessels remain separate compartments: isolated human fetoplacental arterial branches contracted to AVP, but pre-eclamptic branches had lower responsiveness and AVPR1A expression (Gao et al., 2019; Section 14.6.3). This opposes a uniform gain increase and locates the proposed bridge in altered delivery and endogenous fetal defence.

The resulting fetal exposure may also be prolonged or repeated by renal and amniotic-fluid feedback. Section 10.4 distinguishes the established fluid pathways from that persistence prediction during a sensitive window.

A consequential fetal disturbance could occur without recognised maternal pathology, while infection, fever or dehydration alone does not establish programming. Intrinsic genetic constraints can also initiate fetal ionic or recovery demand without passing through this maternal route.

18.1.4.2 Fetal Cue Integration

Fetal cue integration is tested against the matched challenge in Section 10.3. A smaller AVP response can be appropriate; the proposed adverse branch requires a consequential exposure or recovery disturbance.

Three relationships distinguish the proposed branches:

Osmotic and water–solute timing: establish the fetal tonicity trajectory rather than inferring it from maternal sodium or a presumed transport lag (Section 10.2).

Perfusion and dilution: establish both fetal hypotonicity and the filling or oxygen-delivery constraint; their interaction need not prescribe one hormone direction (Section 10.3).

Endocrine response: assess fetal secretion, removal and tissue responsiveness separately from maternal hormone values (Sections 10.1.1 and 10.3).

Hypoxia can strongly recruit fetal AVP, including during mixed cues. The protective AVP–RAAS–cortisol triad can restore stability without its components rising together. Developmental calibration predicts a later functional change after the disturbance resolves; complete recovery without that change would oppose the persistence branch (Section 21.1).

18.1.5 Mechanistic Pathways: Receptor-Level Divergence and Axis Decalibration

Candidate calibration changes include easier AVPR1A-mediated vascular recruitment, stronger AVPR1B-linked ACTH responses and greater AGTR1 support after recurrent demand. A related neural branch predicts relatively stronger AVP signalling or weaker oxytocin modulation in specified circuits and windows. These are proposed functional directions, not signatures inferred from maternal concentrations. Renal AVPR2, MR/GR balance, adrenal development and thyroid support are additional modifiers (Sections 21.4 and 21.6).

AGTR1 provides a developmental vascular example: deletion in human kidney organoids delayed VEGF-A production and prevented day-14 engraftment beneath the kidney capsule of immunodeficient mice, while day-24 mutants engrafted and matured. Induced VEGF-A rescued day-14 engraftment (Pode-Shakked et al., 2023). This renal-transplantation result does not establish the proposed extension that repeated fetal dilution-underfilling increases reliance on AGTR1 and later Ang II responsiveness.

Thyroid signalling connects endocrine state with water handling and neural maturation through different evidence. Hypothyroid adults showed impaired water-load excretion and absent AVP suppression despite normal serum sodium, reversible with replacement (Ota et al., 1994; Table 18.1). In embryonic-day-16 rat cortical cultures, 15 nM T3 increased KCC2 and accelerated loss of muscimol-evoked calcium responses in non-GABAergic neurons at 15–18 days in vitro; the measured GABAergic subgroups did not show that acceleration, and NKCC1 also increased (Westerholz et al., 2013). Thus thyroid-dependent timing does not imply uniformly lower NKCC1 or altered cell volume. Maternal status, fetal exposure and local recovery remain separate; direct thyroid-dependent developmental effects are an alternative to recovery mediation.

Maternal thyroid hormone and thyroid-directed IgG are also distinct exposures. T4 was detected in human embryonic coelomic fluid at 6–11 weeks, and maternal contribution was demonstrable at term when fetal synthesis was absent (Contempré et al., 1993; Vulsma et al., 1989). Anti-TPO transfer alone establishes neither fetal thyroid dysfunction nor neural pump inhibition; stimulating and blocking TSH-receptor antibodies have separate functional evidence (Table 18.4). Thyroid antioxidant and water-handling modifiers are developed in Section 16.10.2.

The proposed result is a changed relationship among ionic, volume, perfusion and stress signals: previously exposed tissue recruits a response more readily, sustains it longer or recovers less completely. Uniform hypo-osmolality is not required.

These directions remain tissue-specific. Reduced AVP responsiveness in pre-eclamptic placental vessels (Gao et al., 2019) cannot settle the fetal neural prediction, just as renal hormone–WNK–SPAK coupling cannot establish neural chloride effects.

18.1.6 Fetal Osmotic Set-Point Formation Under Threat-Biased or Conflicting Signals

The defensive-calibration branch predicts later recruitment of water or circulatory support at a lower threshold, a longer response or slower recovery under comparable conditions. A single hormone value cannot distinguish it from normal gestational resetting or temporary successful compensation.

Prenatal maternal water restriction shifted neonatal AVP thresholds upward in lambs, but they remained hypertonic and hypertensive at assessment and maternal nutritional restriction accompanied dehydration (Desai, Guerra, Wang and Ross, 2003b). This supports altered calibration after exposure ended, not persistence after complete physiological recovery or the lower threshold proposed for hypotonic or mixed cues. A stored imprint requires the specified later difference after the disturbance resolves; its adequately precise absence would oppose that branch.

After three days of maternal water deprivation from gestational day 18, rat fetal sodium rose from 124.29 to 129.45 mmol/L and osmolality from 288.86 to 324.67 mOsm/kg, alongside increased fetal Ang I and Ang II (Guan et al., 2009). At 7–8 weeks, exposed male offspring had greater pressor responses to intravenous Ang II and reduced baroreflex sensitivity without a detected resting-pressure difference; five offspring from different litters were compared per group. This demonstrates a later regulatory difference without requiring a low-sodium phase. Reduced maternal food intake lacked a pair-fed control, and AVP/corticosterone mediation, neural recovery and autism-related behaviour were not established.

18.1.7 Developmental Consequences: Ionic Handling, Volume Vulnerability, and Delayed Inhibitory Maturation

Fetal changes in intracellular chloride, KCC2 trafficking or expression, NKCC1 activity, WNK–SPAK signalling or metabolic support could prolong recovery and alter inhibitory maturation. Maternal defence alone does not establish these tissue effects; Sections 23, 26, and 27 develop their ionic, calcium and energetic consequences.

The proposed chloride-retentive branch links the following candidate findings, each requiring direct evidence:

  • NKCC1-dominant cation–chloride transport

  • elevated intracellular chloride (Cl⁻)

  • secondary intracellular sodium burden (secondary Na⁺ burden) arising from coupled Na⁺ entry with NKCC1-mediated chloride loading

  • increased Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase demand, required to continuously extrude the sodium loaded alongside chloride

  • reduced extracellular space volume fraction (ECS compression)

  • sustained energetic constraint (energy constraint), as ATP demand rises to maintain ionic gradients precisely when mitochondrial support may be limited by perfusion variability

Cellular water gain can compress extracellular space and raise local concentrations at fixed solute content; altered diffusion or removal is a separate effect. Limited oxygen or substrate can impair gradient restoration when ATP supply and reserve no longer meet demand. Repetition could establish a chloride-retentive, high-work recovery pattern, whereas adequate reserve permits successful recovery.

In embryonic mouse medial ganglionic eminence-derived cortical interneurons, KCC2 manipulation changed the transition from GABA-driven migration to a stop response through membrane voltage and L-type calcium-channel transients (Bortone and Polleux, 2009). This links chloride handling to migration timing in a defined population. The proposed extension is that impaired chloride recovery alters this timing and later circuitry; delayed KCC2 expression alone does not establish it. Depolarising GABA can retain shunting inhibition (§§23 and 26), and hypoxia or swelling findings must be matched to the relevant cell and stage.

Delayed KCC2-mediated maturation could consequently affect circuit refinement that depends on precise interneuron timing, including parvalbumin (PV) networks. The chloride disturbance and its circuit effect remain distinct causal steps.

PV interneurons connect this proposal to network function. Optogenetic PV inhibition suppressed prefrontal gamma oscillations in mice, while PV feedback generated gamma-frequency rhythms in slices (Sohal et al., 2009). In 7–10-month-old mouse prefrontal slices, ten minutes of oxygen–glucose deprivation and fifteen minutes of reoxygenation allowed recovery in 1/7 PV interneurons versus 6/8 pyramidal neurons under current clamp; the difference was not significant under voltage clamp (Povysheva et al., 2019). This is preparation-dependent vulnerability, not a developmental ranking. In mice with impaired glutathione synthesis, degradation of mature perineuronal nets increased PV susceptibility to oxidative challenge and altered fast synchrony (Cabungcal et al., 2013). These studies support recovery and extracellular redox protection as candidate influences on PV function without establishing the developmental sequence.

The predicted consequence is delayed inhibitory maturation and less stable oscillatory recruitment when ionic, volume or energetic disturbance burdens rapidly firing interneurons. Slower KCC2 maturation, altered PV function and impaired refinement are separate endpoints; their persistence after serum sodium normalises must be demonstrated.

The proposed maternal-to-neural sequence is therefore:

maternal sodium–volume demand → placentally transformed fetal exposure → defence and recovery during a sensitive window → altered receptor, transporter or recovery function → possible chloride loading, sodium-extrusion work or extracellular-space change → altered inhibitory maturation, PV function or circuit refinement. Successful restoration can interrupt this sequence; intrinsic fetal constraints can enter without a maternal trigger.

18.1.8 Developmental Effects Without Obligatory Sodium Loss or Dilution

Altered developmental calibration could reproduce specified ionic imbalance, chloride vulnerability or reduced volume resilience without sodium loss or extracellular dilution. Such a phenocopy would concern the specified endpoint, not independence from sodium transport. Maternal exposure must connect to a fetal defence/recovery response and later functional change. The imprint is altered response to demand, not obligatory lifelong hyponatraemia or hormone abnormality; intrinsic transporter constraints provide another entry.

18.1.9 Labour-Phase Sodium–Volume Perturbation

Labour adds a further interval in which maternal metabolic conditions may reduce physiological reserve. In pre-labour myometrium from 40 women with diabetes (18 type 1; 22 gestational) and 68 controls, absolute contractility was lower in diabetes (Al-Qahtani et al., 2012). At 10 nmol/L oxytocin, six diabetic and seven control samples showed proportional stimulation that did not differ significantly, although diabetic absolute force remained lower. Reduced calcium signals, channel expression and muscle content offered downstream explanations; OXTR abundance and affinity were unmeasured, so the single dose did not establish equivalent receptor function. The proposed osmotic–metabolic route concerns reduced contractile reserve or delayed recovery.

Exogenous oxytocin can also affect maternal water handling. Human infusion experiments demonstrate antidiuresis when the urinary concentrating mechanism is preserved, while V2-receptor involvement has been demonstrated in vasopressin-deficient rats (Joo et al., 2004; Li et al., 2008). These findings support a water-retention route without making oxytocin physiologically interchangeable with AVP or desmopressin.

Labour combines changes in fluid balance, contractions and fetal oxygenation. Of 61 women receiving more than 2.5 L of oral plus intravenous fluid, 16 (26%) developed postpartum sodium ≤130 mmol/L; about two-thirds of cohort fluid intake was oral (Moen et al., 2009). Umbilical arterial sodium correlated with maternal postpartum sodium. Total fluid volume remained associated with hyponatraemia after adjustment, whereas oxytocin was not independently significant. This supports a maternal–fetal fluid link without isolating oxytocin or establishing augmentation-related fetal injury.

Cord copeptin varies with delivery mode, acid–base state and gestational age; arterial and venous samples must remain distinct (Wellmann et al., 2010; Schlapbach et al., 2011). It reflects secretion-related activity, with kinetics distinct from intact AVP, not clearance, IRAP function or central release (Fenske et al., 2018). We predict relative attenuation with lower fetal effective tonicity under comparable birth and nonosmotic stimuli, rather than obligatory low copeptin. A low value during stress does not identify dilution, and a birth snapshot cannot establish earlier exposure or persistent calibration.

Reduced contractile reserve could increase augmentation needs, while fluid-balance and contraction-related perfusion changes could alter fetal exposure or recovery. However, in 1,362,950 Swedish births, the induction–ASD association fell from HR 1.19 (95% CI 1.13–1.24) to 0.99 (0.88–1.10) in sibling comparisons (Oberg et al., 2016). Induction is not an isolated oxytocin or fluid exposure. This result weakens causal attribution and supplies no support for an unmeasured osmotic subgroup; indicated augmentation is not intrinsically harmful.

18.2 Gestational hyperglycaemia and phase dependent osmotic stress

Glucose provides a distinct osmotic route within these metabolic exposures: an effective extracellular rise can draw water from cells and lower sodium by redistribution while tonicity rises. As glucose falls, this translocational component reverses when other balances are unchanged; neither phase establishes hypotonic hyponatraemia (Hillier et al., 1999). Table 18.2 separates this physical sequence from pathological possibilities. Section 19.7 develops its quantitative limits and the proposed glucose–insulin recovery mechanism.

Table 18.2. Glucose phase and the limits of osmotic inference

Phase or condition Physical interpretation Interpretive boundary
Extracellular glucose rises Water may move from cells to extracellular fluid; sodium may fall by dilution while effective tonicity rises. Relevant compartment, glucose permeability and interval; sodium amount is not inferred from concentration alone.
Hyperglycaemia persists Glucose remains an osmotic contribution; glucosuria, if present, changes water and solute balance. Intake, urine losses, renal function and volume status determine net effects. No fixed AVP, RAAS or cortisol pattern is assigned.
Glucose declines Glucose-derived tonic support falls and the translocational shift can reverse. Return towards baseline is distinct from overshoot, injury or true hypotonicity.
Recovery is incomplete Persistent imbalance is possible if additional processes delay restoration. Rebound requires a persistent water, solute, cellular or hormonal disturbance; glucose variation alone does not establish it.
18.2.1 Circulatory and endocrine conditions that modify recovery

Impaired placental perfusion or persistent water imbalance could modify a glycaemic excursion. Translocational sodium lowering alone establishes neither a fixed AVP–RAAS–cortisol sequence, receptor fatigue nor fetal hypoperfusion. Redistribution into total extracellular water must also remain distinct from plasma expansion or effective filling.

18.2.2 Maternal fetal transfer and developmental exposure

Maternal glucose and sodium do not specify fetal intracellular conditions; transport differences alone establish neither a sugar-rich, salt-deficient fetus nor low AVP with high RAAS/cortisol. Maternal diabetes–ASD associations do not establish that sequence or fetal recovery mediation (Xiang et al., 2018). Table 18.3 separates the required causal links.

Table 18.3. Causal links and boundaries of a maternal metabolic route to altered development

Proposed link Required causal link Inference boundary
Maternal metabolic state A metabolic disturbance changes maternal tonicity or water–solute balance in its circulatory context. Glucose included in calculated osmolality does not itself create an unexplained osmolal gap.
Fetal exposure A corresponding fetal exposure occurs during the relevant developmental interval. Maternal values do not establish fetal cell volume, hormone direction or a fixed equilibration lag.
Cellular recovery The exposure impairs local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery. Initial hypertonic water loss and later return are not equivalent to hypotonic swelling or persistent injury.
Developmental mediation The recovery disturbance contributes causally to the susceptible developmental process. Association, transient illness or a later metabolic diagnosis does not establish this causal chain.
18.2.3 Comparisons with other disturbances of water and solute balance

Low-solute intake, antidiuresis, placental disease and non-electrolyte exposure should not inherit the same fetal signature as hyperglycaemia. True hypotonic dilution, hypertonic translocational sodium lowering and analytical pseudohyponatraemia are distinct: the last is a measurement artifact, not a physiological dilution mechanism.

18.2.4 Oncotic and nutritional modifiers as separate candidate mechanisms

Plasma proteins can alter intravascular–interstitial distribution without producing glucose-driven translocational dilution or low tonicity. Nutritional, placental and circulatory factors could amplify a metabolic disturbance through altered filling or fetal exposure, but their diagnosis does not prescribe a low-AVP, high-RAAS, high-cortisol state.

18.3 Artificial sweeteners and polyols and the limits of osmotic inference

Artificial sweeteners are not included as positive osmotic contributors in Table 13.1 without evidence of sufficient exposure in the relevant compartment. In 19 late-pregnancy participants given 75 mg sucralose with other sweeteners, mean fetal plasma sucralose was 23.6 ng/mL (95% CI 16.7–30.5); the median intake-to-cord-clamp interval was 274 minutes (Leth-Møller et al., 2023). Using a molecular mass of 397.64 g/mol, this corresponds to a calculated ideal osmolar contribution of approximately 0.00006 mOsm/L, not a measured osmolality or tonicity. Placental transfer therefore does not support a material direct sucralose osmotic load at that sampled exposure. Earlier gestation, other doses and nonosmotic mechanisms remain separate questions. Polyols require their own compound-, dose- and compartment-specific evidence; the sucralose calculation neither excludes nor validates their effects. No sweetener-induced osmotic signal error or developmental recovery mechanism is established here.

18.4 Maternal Salt Loading

Maternal salt loading is an exposure trajectory, not a low-sodium endpoint. A measured fetal hypertonic excursion could recruit water conservation and cellular volume regulation. If effective solute subsequently falls while retention persists, a later hypotonic overshoot could follow, aided by continued nonosmotic drive, altered peptide removal or renal handling. Diet alone establishes neither fetal hypertonicity nor delayed AVP clearance; adult adipocyte and global-mouse IRAP findings do not establish fetal kinetics. Gestational peptide turnover and fetal AVP competence constrain this route (Sections 10.1.1, 10.3, and 19.7).

In Afroz et al. (2021, corrected 2022), both parental C57BL/6 mice received 8% NaCl chow and 1% NaCl water from eight weeks before breeding through offspring weaning; controls received 0.1% NaCl chow and ordinary water. After offspring diet normalisation, exposed males showed more locomotion and marble burying at 8–10 weeks (77.14% versus 59.81% buried; p = 0.04). Significant social-chamber preference within controls but not exposed mice did not establish a between-diet social effect. Maternal, paternal, gestational and lactational contributions were unseparated, litter clustering was insufficiently described, and sodium, osmolality and recovery were unmeasured. Microbiome differences lacked demonstrated mediation. The study supplies a persistent behavioural signal, not autism or a demonstrated fetal hypertonic-to-hypotonic trajectory.

Cellular de-adaptation offers a different mismatch: adaptations established during hypertonicity might withdraw more slowly than extracellular tonicity normalises, leaving altered volume or ion gradients without plasma hypo-osmolality. This prediction is distinct from absolute hypotonic overshoot; one cannot substitute for a failed test of the other.

When hypertonicity recruits inward ion transport, including NKCC1 under permissive gradients, accompanying sodium entry can increase Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase work. The proposed cost arises only if restoration is constrained; persistent chloride elevation, inadequate ATP reserve and delayed recovery are not automatic. The mechanism is added restoration work, not simply pumping against higher extracellular sodium.

Salt-related endothelial or placental impairment could separately threaten filling or oxygen delivery and recruit protective AVP–RAAS–cortisol responses without one fixed hormone pattern. Maternal and fetal vessels, peptide exposure and renal balance remain distinct. Hypertonicity alone also does not establish cellular water gain or extracellular-space compression.

Altered nephrogenesis supplies another continuation without requiring dilutional rebound. Section 32 reviews sodium experiments with differing nephron outcomes; the proposed enduring change in renal structure or regulatory reserve remains separate from its RAAS/perfusion mechanism and any later neural consequence.

Thus direct hypertonic challenge, later hypotonic overshoot, slow cellular de-adaptation, vascular constraint and altered renal development are distinguishable salt-exposure routes. Their developmental convergence remains a claim to establish, not a shared endpoint assigned in advance or a reason to substitute branches after a negative result.

18.5 Maternal Immune Activation and Placental Cardiovascular Responses

Maternal immune activation (MIA) could change the fetal environment and the demands placed on ionic and volume regulation through three overlapping routes: maternal molecular passage; placental or fetal production of mediators in response to maternal signals; and altered placental vascular function, fetal loading or oxygen/substrate delivery. Experimental support for these components and the pooled maternal infection/fever association (Tioleco et al., 2021) do not establish a general human infection-to-autism claim: the association in a large Swedish cohort attenuated in sibling comparisons (Brynge et al., 2022; Table 48.1).

Maternal urinary infection supplies a specific exposure for investigating this proposal. In a Swedish register study, a UTI diagnosis recorded during pregnancy hospitalisation was associated with an offspring inpatient autism diagnosis, adjusted HR 1.89 (95% CI 1.23–2.90; Al-Haddad et al., 2019). This was a hospital-recorded exposure, not an estimate for routine outpatient cystitis. Its adjustment for correlated sibling observations was not a within-family exposure comparison. Brynge et al. (2022) addressed a broader maternal-infection definition in a different population; its sibling attenuation therefore remains a relevant constraint without constituting a UTI-specific reanalysis. Maternal renal disturbance, fetal exposure and local recovery mediation were unmeasured in these associations. Section 18.1.2 explains the sibling-design limits and the distinct question of a persistent maternal physiological baseline.

Transfer depends on molecule and developmental stage. Term human placental perfusions disagree about IL-6 transfer (Zaretsky et al., 2004; Aaltonen et al., 2005), whereas mouse experiments support maternal IL-17A passage into fetal-associated compartments (Andruszewski et al., 2025). Neither defines early human fetal-brain dose: maternal concentration, amniotic-fluid detection and target-tissue exposure are distinct.

Placental relay is experimentally supported: trophoblast IL-6-receptor deletion prevented specified fetal-brain and later offspring abnormalities after mouse MIA (Wu et al., 2017). The mouse placenta also transiently supplies fetal forebrain serotonin from maternal tryptophan; poly(I:C) inflammation increased placental output and fetal forebrain serotonin, with altered serotonergic axon development (Bonnin et al., 2011; Goeden et al., 2016). These are active processing routes, alongside molecular transfer and circulation.

Inflammation can alter the placental glucocorticoid gate. In term human villous explants, IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α, each applied separately at 10 ng/mL, reduced 11β-HSD2 activity to about 23–25% of control by two hours, with further inhibition at 24 hours and unchanged mRNA (Kossintseva et al., 2006). Activity can thus change without reduced expression. If this occurred in vivo it could alter fetal glucocorticoid exposure and recovery; the explant finding does not establish that ordinary maternal stress produces it.

Acute cardiovascular effects were demonstrated after severe maternal intraperitoneal LPS (2.4 mg/kg) at mouse gestational day 14. At six hours, placental congestion and abnormal fetal Doppler measures were observed, with atrioventricular regurgitation in 15/23 surviving exposed fetuses versus 1/25 controls; three exposed fetuses died (Rounioja et al., 2005). The findings supported increased placental resistance and fetal afterload despite no significant induction of assayed fetal heart, lung and liver cytokine mRNAs. Those assays exclude neither transferred cytokine protein nor local inflammatory effects. This severe model establishes a cardiovascular possibility, not typical human infection effects or a later autism outcome.

Inflammation could also modify the maternal environment through renal handling. High-dose LPS in mice reduced blood pressure and GFR, increased fractional sodium excretion and lowered the expression of several sodium-handling transporters; supplementary glucocorticoid treatment attenuated both renal dysfunction and transporter downregulation (Schmidt et al., 2007). This provides experimental component evidence, rather than a measurement in pregnant women with UTI. Increased fractional excretion during reduced filtration does not alone establish negative whole-body sodium balance, and pharmacological attenuation does not demonstrate an obligatory endogenous cortisol rescue. The proposed maternal branch applies where infection produces a consequential sodium or water disturbance that adds to placental or fetal recovery demands. Successful renal compensation and treatment remain alternatives, and the infant aldosterone-resistance phenotype in Section 14.4 is a separate clinical observation.

Compensation changes the developmental interpretation. In intra-amniotic-LPS sheep, reduced arterial oxygen content accompanied increased carotid flow, with no detected reduction in estimated cerebral oxygen delivery (Galinsky et al., 2013). A lower-dose maternal-LPS mouse model showed placental injury without detected uterine or umbilical Doppler-index changes (Fricke et al., 2018). Inflammation can therefore produce different delivery trajectories across preparations.

The proposed adverse branch begins when delivery falls below requirements despite compensation, or disturbances recur before local recovery completes. Developmentally competent fetal AVP–RAAS–cortisol and autonomic responses may preserve circulation. Where oxygen or substrate remains inadequate, ATP-dependent sodium/potassium maintenance could become constrained, affecting chloride regulation and volume recovery. The required link is impaired recovery during a susceptible interval; increased afterload alone does not establish a neural ATP deficit. Section 18.6 develops the local neural alternative.

Antibodies provide cardiovascular comparators distinct from acute infection-triggered MIA. FcRn participates in human IgG transfer; fetal concentrations were relatively low at 17–22 weeks and rose substantially towards term (Firan et al., 2001; Malek et al., 1996). Heart-block-associated maternal IgG altered calcium currents and conduction in cardiac preparations (Boutjdir et al., 1997). Agonistic AT1 antibodies retained activity in human cord blood and produced placental/fetal effects in transfer experiments (Irani et al., 2009). Antibody-driven AT1 activation is not compensatory fetal RAAS recruitment, and convergence on impaired recovery remains proposed (see also Section 19.2).

18.6 Local Neural Effects and Maternal Brain-Reactive Antibodies

Alongside the placental and cardiovascular routes, inflammatory effects on transport, glial support or maturation could reduce local recovery capacity during a sensitive window. They may interact with restricted delivery or initiate the proposed process without systemic hyponatraemia, hypovolaemia or prior AVP recruitment. Their connection to the common process requires impaired ionic or cellular-volume recovery that changes development.

After mouse MIA, Corradini et al. (2018) found elevated neuronal chloride, altered chloride-transporter expression and delayed GABA maturation. Fernandez et al. (2019) found an abnormally depolarising hippocampal GABA driving force already at birth, acutely corrected by bath-applied bumetanide. These establish modifiable ionic state and developmental timing; the additional recovery claim is inadequate restoration after challenge (Section 23.13), with possible consequences for inhibitory maturation (Section 30.4).

Systemic LPS impaired dentate granule-cell chloride regulation in adult mice 48 hours later: a reduced somatodendritic gradient under maintained somatic chloride load indicated weaker extrusion, alongside separate evidence of increased NKCC1 uptake (Kurki et al., 2023). This functional-demand result did not measure post-pulse return or development. We propose that inflammation persisting into recovery could prolong a similar constraint in immature tissue; glucose is a possible duration modifier (Section 19.7).

IL-17A increased cortical folding, thickness and neurogenesis in cerebroids derived from 11–14-week human fetal brain tissue, retaining microglia and vascular cells but lacking systemic circulation (Assir et al., 2026). This demonstrates local developmental susceptibility without establishing recovery mediation. Responses differ across stages and preparations: prenatal IL-17A contributed to cortical and behavioural abnormalities in mice (Choi et al., 2016), whereas IL-17A-dependent signalling transiently improved adult MIA-offspring sociability (Reed et al., 2020). The latter circuit effect is distinct from temperature-mediated fever responses (Section 46.2).

Assir et al. (2026) also found sustained nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) p65 activation in separately studied human iPSC-derived neural progenitors; parthenolide co-treatment reduced cerebroid cortical and neurogenic abnormalities. Treatment during exposure does not demonstrate later reversal of established architecture. The mouse MIA-to-protein-production mechanism in Section 29.2 supplies another comparison. Neither establishes recovery mediation, and accelerated maturation, delayed differentiation and altered coordination remain distinct outcomes (Sections 29.3 and 31.4).

The maternal autoantibody-related autism programme (MAR autism; MAR-ASD) concerns a distinct exposure. Maternal antibodies recognise developing-brain proteins including lactate dehydrogenase A/B (LDHA/LDHB), stress-induced phosphoprotein 1 (STIP1) and collapsin response mediator proteins 1/2 (CRMP1/CRMP2) (Braunschweig et al., 2013). Associated patterns were developed from postpartum samples (Ramirez-Celis et al., 2021) and later found in pregnancy samples (Ramirez-Celis et al., 2022), strengthening temporal order without yielding a universally accurate prenatal test. Selected maternal IgG altered brain growth and social behaviour in rhesus monkeys (Bauman et al., 2013); a maternal contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2)-reactive monoclonal antibody produced cortical and behavioural abnormalities in male mice (Brimberg et al., 2016). CASPR2 was not enriched in a separate human gestational ASD comparison (Coutinho et al., 2017), a different target from the multi-antigen profiles. Specificity, fetal dose and target access define each route; acute MIA need not generate these antibodies.

Folate-receptor antibodies measured in children identify another possible route: restricted substrate delivery at a brain interface (Ramaekers et al., 2005, 2007; Section 30). These are not maternal brain-reactive IgG or prenatal MIA findings. Folate delivery could affect recovery or development through another mechanism.

Complement-associated synaptic handling offers another candidate local interaction. MIA preparations have produced increased or deficient microglial engulfment, so neither excess pruning nor maternal complement passage follows automatically from an offspring signal (Yan et al., 2024; Andoh et al., 2019; Section 48).

The common-process conjecture predicts that immune routes contributing to the neurodevelopmental features of autism converge on the recovery constraint in Section 2. A reproducible developmental effect with adequately demonstrated preserved relevant recovery would challenge that necessity; unmeasured recovery establishes neither convergence nor bypass. Direct developmental alternatives therefore remain part of the comparison (Section 23.13).

Table 18.4. Maternal and placental exposures: transfer, target and proposed recovery mediation

Source/carrier and timing Transfer/relay, target and evidence Systemic step and circulatory role Local recovery mediation
Cytokines; molecule- and stage-specific evidence; human perfusions at term. IL-6 transfer findings conflict (Zaretsky et al., 2004; Aaltonen et al., 2005). Mouse placental IL-6 relay and IL-17A passage have experimental support (Wu et al., 2017; Andruszewski et al., 2025). Possible interacting route; not required for direct culture effects. Resting chloride/GABA abnormalities; recovery mediation NE (Corradini et al., 2018; Fernandez et al., 2019).

Candidate profiles associate with ASD; selected antibodies produce animal developmental effects (Ramirez-Celis et al., 2022; Brimberg et al., 2016). Human fetal-brain dose and target access remain unresolved. Not required by direct-target hypothesis. NE; antigen specificity establishes neither convergence nor bypass.
Anti-Ro/SSA and agonistic AT1 IgG; stage dependent. Heart-block-associated maternal IgG altered currents and conduction in experimental cardiac preparations; AT1 antibodies have cord-blood and experimental placental/fetal evidence (Boutjdir et al., 1997; Irani et al., 2009). NE: strict neural/glial post-challenge ionic or volume-recovery mediation is not established in the cited evidence. The systemic column distinguishes a preceding sodium–volume disturbance from a circulatory contribution; bypassing that systemic step does not establish bypass of local recovery. ‘Not required’ denotes mechanistic possibility, not experimental exclusion. IgG transfer involves FcRn and increases substantially with gestation (Firan et al., 2001; Malek et al., 1996); fetal blood exposure does not establish brain/antigen access. The proposed convergence concerns recovery and its developmental consequence, not identical intracellular changes or hormone responses. Sections 7 and 19 distinguish intrinsic initiation from interactions among routes.

19 Convergence and Interaction Among Sodium–Volume Defence Pathways

The systemic and intrinsic routes considered separately above may converge on a shared recovery disturbance without occurring together. When they do interact, one route may increase or reduce the demand imposed by another, or alter ionic, volume or perfusion recovery. Triad discordance, joint intracellular Na⁺/Cl⁻ elevation, increased pump work and ATP depletion are distinct candidate findings, not obligatory features. Systemic and intrinsic routes converge on the proposed core only through a recovery disturbance that carries a developmental effect.

19.1 Convergence, Interaction and Hybrid States

Dietary, pharmacological, obstetric, infectious and environmental inputs can amplify, counteract or act independently of one another. Convergence means different initiating routes reaching a shared physiological endpoint; they need not occur together. The candidate combinations considered here involve disturbed water handling, hypotonic dilution, hypertonic redistribution, renal sodium handling, delivery threat or cellular recovery. An interaction changes the effect of one input in the presence of another. Adverse amplification is the more specific prediction that a defined combination produces a larger or longer relevant disturbance than its components under matched conditions. Neither a common hormone direction nor an intracellular signature is assumed.

Hybrid states combine pathways through layered or transient mechanisms. One candidate is a cytokine–phosphate/FGF23 sequence with an early RAAS response followed by reduced mineralocorticoid support and greater glucocorticoid contribution, interacting with sensory, energetic or distribution constraints.

The developmental claim concerns the timing and incomplete recovery of such compensation. Immune illness might produce high AVP with inadequate mineralocorticoid support and cortisol weighting, but the defence triad does not prescribe this sequence. “Hybrid” denotes pathway integration, not rarity or persistent hyponatraemia.

19.2 Maternal Alloimmunisation (Rh[D]) and Fetal Haemolytic Hypoxia

Maternal anti-Rh(D) IgG causes fetal haemolysis and anaemia, threatening oxygen delivery where circulatory compensation is insufficient. Inadequate oxygen/substrate support could then impair sodium extrusion or renal reclamation. Fetal AVP can support vascular tone and water conservation during hypoxia without increased renin activity (Raff and Wood, 1992); renin and aldosterone depend separately on renal perfusion, pressure, potassium and developmental stage.

The proposed energetic paradox is appropriate endocrine defence alongside inadequate ATP-supported transport: sodium-conserving signals cannot supply the energy to restore gradients. Additional antibody-mediated membrane effects remain a separate hypothesis, not a consequence of haemolysis alone.

Intrauterine transfusion changes fetal cardiac measures and rheology while the maternal antibody source persists (Herling et al., 2020; Welch et al., 1994). Because it changes oxygen carriage, haematocrit, viscosity, volume and loading together, it is not a selective volume rescue; anaemia itself is not hypovolaemia. This red-cell route complements the cardiac and brain-reactive antibodies in Sections 18.5 and 18.6.

Recurrent hypoxic demand could also calibrate later AVPR1A vascular responsiveness, AVPR1B stress recruitment or AGTR1 support upward in specified tissues. A related branch predicts stronger AVP-linked neural signalling and weaker oxytocin modulation; AVPR2/AQP2 adaptation and AQP4 distribution are additional modifiers. Lasting changes after recovery could affect neurovascular support, stress or social-affiliative function. Acute AVP elevation or receptor expression alone does not establish that persistent functional imprint.

During mixed hypoxia and dilution, hypotonicity can restrain osmotic AVP drive without prescribing low AVP, quiet RAAS or cortisol substitution (Section 10.3). The defence triad responds to actual fetal signals; a shift towards cortisol support requires a changed need and response, not an inference from anaemia, energetic strain or phosphate exposure.

This route links maternal antibody exposure to haemolytic oxygen-delivery limitation, possible ATP-supported transport constraint and developmentally consequential defence or recovery. Successful restoration remains possible. An adequately precise absence or opposite direction of the specified later receptor or recovery difference after resolution would oppose the persistence branch.

19.3 Mechanistic Convergence Across Initiating Routes

Impaired water excretion could combine with inadequate sodium conservation or perfusion. Hypothyroid water-load findings demonstrate impaired excretion with absent AVP suppression (Ota et al., 1994; Table 14.3), and additional free water could deepen dilution if supply exceeded clearance. Low mineral content alone does not establish that imbalance. Nor do low renin or preeclampsia establish failed conservation: downstream retention can remain effective, and maternal state does not specify fetal exposure.

Glucose–insulin physiology can initiate, amplify, oppose or modify recovery from a hydromineral disturbance (Section 19.7). Cortisol, inflammatory, renal and circulatory effects could change the trajectory. Glucose-associated sodium lowering remains distinct from hypotonicity, and IRAP–AVP termination supplies a separate candidate link.

Cellular reserve can modify the response to a systemic challenge. The compound-specific component findings and exposure limits are set out in Section 14.8 and Table 20.1. A dose-relevant cytoskeletal, barrier or volume-recovery defect from a specified PFAS, phthalate or other exposure could amplify measured antidiuresis or hypotonic stress. One-carbon metabolism and betaine supply separate candidate influences on osmolyte reserve. NFAT5 participation and ionic transport direction remain to be established; no shared membrane–synapse effect is assigned to all compounds.

19.4 Endocrine Amplification and Feedback Locking

Inflammatory, endothelial and endocrine responses could prolong a disturbance through cytokine recruitment of AVP/HPA signalling, altered placental perfusion or permeability, and local glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid actions. Cytokine–endocrine coupling has component evidence: IL-6 infusion increased cortisol in healthy adults (Steensberg et al., 2003; Section 14.6.10). The effects of these responses depend on the defended state: continued antidiuresis may impede dilutional recovery, whereas sodium conservation may restore inadequate filling. A raised osmotic threshold delays AVP recruitment, and MR engagement alone does not imply increased HPA output. Feedback locking requires the disturbance to sustain a response that in turn maintains the disturbance; overlapping hormones are insufficient. Persistence after normalisation is a further proposed change in receptors, thresholds or recovery capacity.

19.5 Physiological Outcomes of Convergence

Convergence could combine greater ionic demand with less recovery capacity, changing later AVPR1A/AVPR1B responsiveness or local MR/GR signalling. A separate membrane branch predicts impaired OXTR surface organisation from cytoskeletal or microdomain disruption. Altered barriers might also change fetal exposure to maternal hydration or metabolic fluctuations. These functional effects, their persistence and their developmental consequences must be distinguished from circulating hormone levels. Chloride and GABA consequences remain cell- and stage-dependent (Sections 23 and 26); the proposed lasting link is altered calibration after repeated challenge or incomplete recovery.

Preterm sodium loss supplies a measured component: in seven infants, negative sodium balance developed during the first two weeks despite high plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentrations (Sulyok et al., 1979; Section 14.4). Its combination with antidiuresis or an additional epithelial or energetic constraint remains a hypothesis requiring measured effects on water–solute recovery. Prematurity alone does not establish that interaction.

19.6 Clinical and Environmental Realism: Convergent Exposure Clusters

Candidate exposure clusters require distinct causal interpretation. Low-mineral water plus phosphate could alter water–solute balance, but low mineral content does not establish hypotonicity or antidiuresis and FGF23 promoted sodium retention in mice (Andrukhova et al., 2014; §§14.5 and 14.9). Maternal illness plus acetaminophen must be separated from treatment indication; sibling comparisons weigh against the medication association as causal support (Ahlqvist et al., 2024; §14.2.4). Pollution plus a specified cytoskeletal disruptor remains a dose-specific barrier/recovery hypothesis (§§14.8, 16.8, and 21.5). Co-occurrence alone establishes neither amplification nor a common AVP-high, cortisol-high state.

Preeclampsia supplies a vascular context, not a fetal hormone profile; hypoxia is a separate AVP stimulus (§10). Preterm renal losses and fluid practices can produce low, high or changing sodium (§12). Folate, choline and iron may modify osmolyte reserve, barriers or oxygen delivery, but those proposed contributions must be separated from their other nutritional functions.

19.7 Glucose as a candidate extracellular osmotic resource and insulin dependent recovery

Glucose metabolism could influence both the disturbance that recruits osmotic–volume defence and the course of recovery. We propose two separable contributions: temporary extracellular osmotic support from glucose during a hypotonic threat, and coordination of substrate handling, ionic responses and peripheral peptide termination during recovery. The second could operate without a preceding protective glucose rise. GSH-sensitive processing, relative oxytocin exposure and redox or inflammatory feedback provide additional conditional extensions. Each connection requires its own conditions; the section does not propose one obligatory metabolic sequence.

19.7.1 Glucose as a candidate extracellular osmotic resource

We propose that endogenous glucose mobilisation or reduced disposal during a hypotonic threat can temporarily oppose cellular disturbance through glucose’s extracellular osmotic effect. Its physical action motivates the hypothesis. Demonstrating an emergency buffering benefit requires improvement under the relevant conditions beyond glucose’s contribution as fuel.

While glucose acts as an effective extracellular osmole across a specified membrane and interval, its rise can draw water from cells and lower extracellular sodium by redistribution without requiring sodium loss. This does not establish hypotonic swelling. In an acute human experiment, sodium fell as glucose rose and normalised with glucose (Hillier et al., 1999). Subsequent water return towards cells is ordinary recovery. Pathological overshoot requires an additional imbalance in water, effective solute, intracellular osmolytes, transport or hormonal duration; vascular tone, filling and local brain state remain separate endpoints.

The model also constrains the possible effect size. In the illustrative closed adult model (Bell, 2026a), 42 L total water is initially divided into 14 L extracellular and 28 L intracellular water, with extracellular sodium 140 mmol/L and glucose 5 mmol/L. Adding glucose without water, fixing other effective-osmole inventories and allowing redistribution gives, at glucose 10 mmol/L, sodium approximately 138.35 mmol/L, extracellular volume approximately 14.167 L and effective osmolarity approximately 286.71 rather than 285 mOsm/L. The net increment is therefore about 1.71 mOsm/L and the transcellular redistribution about 167 mL. Sodium dilution is already included. The calculation assumes extracellular glucose confinement and no metabolism, intake or renal loss. The 167 mL is neither measured plasma expansion nor water that the kidneys must excrete. A fetal estimate requires its own compartment proportions, solute inventories, permeability and timing; even the concentration increment cannot simply be transferred unchanged.

Epithelial transport helps determine glucose appearance and retention. Small-intestinal sodium–glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1; SLC5A1) couples luminal glucose uptake to sodium entry (§43.1.6). Renal SGLT2 (SLC5A2) supplies the major early proximal-tubule reabsorptive route, with SGLT1 reclaiming glucose further downstream. Expressed human SGLT2 and SGLT1 couple one glucose molecule to one and two Na⁺ ions, respectively (Hummel et al., 2011). In euglycaemic mice, downstream SGLT1 can reabsorb substantial additional glucose when SGLT2 is inhibited or absent (Rieg et al., 2014). Renal reclamation limits urinary loss; it is distinct from intestinal delivery, endogenous glucose production and glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4)-mediated tissue disposal.

Glucosuria can increase water loss without necessarily causing sodium depletion. Sglt2-null mice had glucosuria and increased fluid excretion, but sodium excretion was unchanged in clearance studies; greater drinking accompanied preserved blood pressure, haematocrit and plasma sodium (Vallon et al., 2011). Net effects therefore depend on intake and renal responses as well as filtered glucose and reabsorptive capacity. A fetal extension requires stage-specific evidence for filtration and tubular function, and cannot equate total glucose-reabsorptive capacity with SGLT2 alone.

A protective contribution must improve volume, tonicity or circulation through an osmotic effect, separately from fuel provision and counterregulation; persistent glucose or glucosuria could instead complicate recovery. Severe water intoxication in young mice produced hyperglycaemia with lower insulin (Thurston et al., 1978). In ten men, a 17-hour hypotonic protocol using desmopressin, water and hypotonic saline reduced clamp glucose clearance from 4.4 to 3.3 mL/kg/min (about 25%), with pre-clamp glucose of 4.9 mmol/L in the isotonic condition and 4.7 mmol/L in the hypotonic condition (Berneis et al., 1999). The final two-hour insulin clamp was imposed, not spontaneous recovery. These findings support hydromineral–metabolic interaction, including without glucose elevation, but do not establish protection.

In differentiated H9c2 cells engineered to overexpress intracellular angiotensin II, 40 minutes of hypotonicity reduced insulin-present glucose-analogue uptake and IRS-1 abundance. Losartan pretreatment or repeated hypotonic-medium replacement counteracted the uptake reduction (Gerena et al., 2017). This is a context-specific swelling–transport link; GLUT4 recruitment, redox mediation and benefit to cell integrity were not established.

A selective redox brake is another candidate. In 3T3-L1 adipocytes, 10 µM mitochondria-targeted paraquat for two hours reduced insulin-stimulated 2-deoxyglucose uptake and surface GLUT4 recruitment by about 26%, without detectable respiratory or Akt/TBC1D4 phosphorylation impairment; an inactive analogue did not reproduce it (Fazakerley et al., 2018). L6 myotubes retained AMPK-agonist responsiveness despite impaired insulin-responsive GLUT4 recruitment. Thus transport can be selectively impaired, although no osmotic challenge or IRAP measurement established the proposed sequence.

Osmotic redox inputs depend on challenge direction. In HEK293 cells, 16 hours at 500 rather than 290 mOsm/kg with NaCl increased NFAT5-dependent transcription; mitochondrial inhibitors implicated oxidant signalling, and oligomycin reduced the response without significantly lowering measured ATP (Zhou et al., 2006). This is not evidence of hypotonic GLUT4 restriction. In neonatal rat cardiomyocytes, diluted hypotonic medium increased oxidant signals and injury, while catalase improved volume recovery and survival (Díaz-Elizondo et al., 2006). Harmful redox injury therefore remains an alternative to protective uptake restriction.

After 72 hours at sodium 110–130 rather than 140 mEq/L, neonatal rat cardiomyocyte DCF oxidant-probe signals increased; lipid-peroxidation readouts and vulnerability to an added oxidant challenge increased at 110–120 mEq/L, without detected basal mitochondrial-potential change (Oniki et al., 2020). Mannitol adjustment did not abolish the oxidative changes. This supports an effect beyond low bulk osmolality, but identifies neither mitochondrial superoxide as the source nor selective glucose restriction as protective.

Reduced insulin responsiveness need not mean reduced total glucose entry. Severe hyperosmotic shock with 600 mM sorbitol increased GLUT4 recruitment and glucose transport in 3T3-L1 adipocytes while preventing a further insulin response and impairing Akt activation (Chen et al., 1999). Direction, magnitude and basal transport therefore constrain any extracellular-glucose-retention interpretation.

Epple and Brinn (1976) proposed dual osmoregulatory and intermediary-metabolic islet functions varying across vertebrates, followed by eel pancreatectomy work and a later synthesis (Epple and Miller, 1981; Epple and Brinn, 1987). The present protective-glucose hypothesis was developed independently before this work was identified. It supplies historical precedent, but whole-pancreas removal did not isolate insulin or establish the protective-glucose, IRAP or autism mechanisms proposed here. Useful present-day regulation also does not establish its evolutionary origin.

19.7.2 Insulin and IRAP in AVP termination

The second proposal is that insulin-associated changes in peripheral AVP clearance help coordinate water handling with metabolic recovery. It can be evaluated independently of protective glucose support. Insulin recruits GLUT4 and insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP; encoded by LNPEP) from shared muscle/adipose compartments, increasing glucose-transport capacity and exposing IRAP’s catalytic domain extracellularly. This is surface deployment, not necessarily enzyme release or catalytic activation by GLUT4 transport. Insulin increased adipocyte vasopressin cleavage and accelerated disappearance of intact labelled AVP in mice through IRAP (Herbst et al., 1997; Wallis et al., 2007). Habtemichael et al. (2015) previously proposed TUG-dependent coordination of glucose uptake and AVP inactivation to dispose of oxidation-generated water and relieve vasoconstriction. The present extension concerns recovery as extracellular glucose’s tonic contribution falls.

Wallis et al. (2007) estimated intact labelled-AVP half-lives of about 1.5 minutes in wild-type mice, 1 minute after insulin, and 3 minutes in IRAP-null mice with or without insulin. Knockouts had about twice the circulating endogenous AVP but lower whole-brain AVP content and transcripts: consistent with cross-compartment compensation, not an acquired suppression sequence. Intact labelled oxytocin recovery at five minutes did not differ detectably (n = 5), despite lost N-terminal processing in isolated knockout tissues. Shared substrates therefore do not impose a fixed AVP–oxytocin clearance ratio, and peripheral kinetics cannot identify reduced neural production, altered development or release (Section 36.5).

Insulin’s renal and glucose effects can also dissociate. In six water-loaded participants at maintained glucose, insulin reduced sodium excretion and raised calculated free-water clearance from about 10.6 to 13.0 mL/min, because osmolar clearance fell while urine flow remained unchanged (DeFronzo et al., 1975). This was selective solute handling, not increased urine-water output; AVP was unmeasured and plasma osmolality approximately stable. Insulin also retained substantial antinatriuretic action in obese adolescents with impaired glucose responsiveness (Rocchini et al., 1989). Neither result establishes IRAP-mediated recovery from hypotonicity.

“Insulin resistance” does not specify peptide processing. Human type 2 diabetic adipocytes had about 4.4-fold higher basal plasma-membrane-fraction IRAP despite impaired further recruitment, with GLUT4 reduced across fractions (Maianu et al., 2001). That fraction does not measure exposed catalytic activity. Insulin deficiency, hyperinsulinaemic resistance, trafficking impairment and catalytic IRAP defects therefore remain distinct states (Section 21.2).

The shared cargos can dissociate. In rat adipocytes pretreated with high glucose plus insulin or glucosamine, insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation remained intact while gp160/IRAP recruitment to the plasma-membrane fraction was impaired (Filippis et al., 1998). Lower basal transport nevertheless reduced glucose uptake, and peptide cleavage was unmeasured. The finding establishes trafficking dissociation, not preserved glucose disposal with proven AVP-clearance failure.

Where glucose redistribution and AVP-mediated water conservation occur together, we propose that their relative timing contributes to recovery. The proposed metabolic–osmotic handoff couples falling extracellular glucose to appropriately adjusted water conservation. Net appearance, disposal and distribution determine the glucose trajectory; GLUT4 recruitment alone does not. Insulin and IRAP need not wait for a distinct late phase: IRAP surface recruitment had a half-time of about two minutes in insulin-stimulated 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Ross et al., 1997). The prediction concerns relative timing and magnitude, allowing overlap.

Appropriately timed IRAP termination could limit dilution if excess water retention otherwise continued as glucose fell. But water conservation may remain appropriate during underfilling or shortage. Insulin-dependent cellular hydration can coexist with improved extracellular water balance; the proposal does not require insulin to shrink cells. Benefit depends on the starting state and actual water, tonicity and cellular or perfusion response.

Pregnancy offers a setting for the proposed handoff. Its normal downward osmotic reset is not failed regulation (§10). Insulin sensitivity falls while increased secretion compensates; women developing gestational diabetes showed a lag in that increase (Catalano et al., 1993). We propose an additional, state-dependent sequence during hypotonic challenge: an early extracellular glucose rise supports tonicity, followed by insulin-dependent disposal and appropriately timed peptide termination. This glucose-first, insulin-later coordination is not an established purpose of pregnancy insulin resistance. Glucose-associated sodium lowering must still be distinguished from hypotonicity.

Cell-surface IRAP, placental LNPEP expression, shed circulating P-LAP/IRAP and intact-peptide degradation are not interchangeable. Köse et al. (2025) found lower serum IRAP by ELISA in 40 women with GDM versus 40 controls; Guleroglu et al. (2023) found no significant early difference in 109 pregnancies, 19 later meeting GDM criteria. Assay comparability requires clarification, and neither measured active AVP or oxytocin clearance. Stage, treatment, secretion, tissue access and catalysis matter beyond diagnosis.

Oxytocin studies further separate assay activity from clearance. In ten women assessed late in pregnancy and postpartum, metabolic clearance at the lower matched concentration was 5.7 ± 0.6 versus 1.3 ± 0.1 L/min (Thornton et al., 1990). In 14 pregnant, puerperal and nonpregnant subjects, Takeda et al. (1989) found no significant in-vivo difference despite much greater degradation in pregnant plasma in vitro. These findings constrain a universal multiplier and cannot establish a GDM-specific peptide imbalance or the LNPEP share of clearance. Compensatory supply remains distinct from removal (§10).

A separate observation links osmotic state with peptide-processing activity. In challenged rats, plasma osmolality correlated with plasma cystine aminopeptidase activity while measured CNS activity was unchanged (Silveira et al., 2001). This synthetic-substrate CAP assay cannot substitute for identified cell-surface IRAP or native AVP clearance. Osmotic and insulin regulation therefore remain a proposed convergence, not one demonstrated by combining different activity assays.

The systemic IRAP–AVP prediction is that reduced accessible active IRAP prolongs active peripheral AVP independently of input and delays water or tonicity recovery (Bell, 2026b). Copeptin cannot establish clearance: in 91 volunteers its initial decay during osmotic suppression differed from AVP, about 26 versus 12 minutes (Fenske et al., 2018). These are endogenous protocol-dependent kinetics, not tracer-clearance constants. Global IRAP-null mice showed impaired urinary dilution after a water load of 10% body weight (Zuchowski et al., 2023); this substantial challenge does not isolate acute muscle/adipose action from renal or developmental effects. Peripheral kinetics also do not specify CSF AVP or neural release.

Compensation may normalise concentration without normalising pulse removal. In a first-order model at constant distribution volume, proportionally lower secretion and clearance preserve steady concentration but slow decay of an identical added pulse at fixed subsequent input. This predicts kinetics, not hidden compensation from a normal AVP value. If secretion, alternative clearance or renal responsiveness prevents prolonged active exposure or impaired water recovery, the harmful-exposure bridge is absent.

19.7.3 Conditional GSH and oxytocin extensions

GSH-sensitive processing provides a separate candidate route that could modify the consequences of restricted IRAP termination. Preparation studies demonstrate GSH-sensitive AVP degradation without identifying its relationship to IRAP-mediated clearance. In rat renal brush-border membranes and cortical lysosomal fractions, adding 1 mmol/L reduced GSH enabled AVP degradation measured by HPLC (Carone et al., 1987). GSH-sensitive processing has direct human-tissue support: renal microvilli degraded AVP with added GSH but not without it, whereas oxytocin still degraded without added GSH; crude liver preparations also degraded AVP (Fjellestad-Paulsen and Lundin, 1996). Perfused organs showed peritubular renal and hepatic removal of immunoreactive AVP without identifying either route’s GSH dependence (Rabkin et al., 1979, 1980). These demonstrate multiple removal opportunities, not their physiological shares in active circulating AVP clearance (Section 14.2.4). The enzymes responsible in these older preparations were not identified as IRAP, and these experiments do not establish GSH as an IRAP cofactor.

IRAP separately contains active-site zinc. In CHO-K1 membranes, 40–100 µM added zinc restored chelator-inhibited cystinyl aminopeptidase activity, with renewed inhibition at higher additions (Hermans et al., 2015; Laeremans et al., 2005). The synthetic substrate and chelator-containing buffer define no dietary or serum-zinc threshold for native AVP clearance. IRAP hydrolyses peptide bonds rather than reducing disulfides; zinc-dependent catalysis and GSH-sensitive processing are distinct constraints, not an established serial pathway or demonstrated nutrient limitation in vivo.

Lipid-peroxide demand could weaken membrane protection and AVP termination together if it outpaced GSH recycling and replacement at a relevant renal processing site. Less GSH-sensitive processing might then reduce backup capacity during restricted IRAP termination; that compensatory role remains proposed. Neural, renal and extracellular pools are separate, and renal-preparation findings do not establish lipid-oxidation-induced slowing of active circulating AVP removal (Carone et al., 1987; Fjellestad-Paulsen and Lundin, 1996; Section 14.2.4).

The issue is local availability, not presumed whole-body depletion by AVP disposal. Greater reliance on GSH-sensitive processing need not consume enough GSH to compromise GPX4. Low concentration, poor substrate access or slow regeneration could nevertheless constrain a renal site. For this systemic branch, the effect must reduce active circulating AVP removal, not only filtered-peptide degradation. Secretion adjustment, alternative clearance or renal responsiveness could preserve water balance despite one impaired route. The developmental proposal is that restricted IRAP deployment and limited GSH at a relevant renal processing site could jointly prolong compensation during combined metabolic and oxidative stress. Neonatal blood-cell or plasma findings do not measure that renal pool, and neither a sex difference in infant active-AVP clearance nor compensation for impaired IRAP has been demonstrated.

The substrate differences above motivate an additional compensation hypothesis: selective slowing of AVP removal could increase circulating AVP exposure relative to oxytocin without lowering oxytocin concentration. Reduced oxytocin secretion would require a further feedback step. In rats, AVP or desmopressin pretreatment altered the osmotic threshold for release from oxytocin neurones, inferred from circulating neurophysin measurements, without changing the response slope (Cheng and North, 1989). The authors inferred a largely V2-like feedback influence from the pharmacology. The experiment used administered peptides rather than impaired clearance, and circulating neurophysin measurements do not establish local brain oxytocin release.

This experimental feedback component motivates, but does not establish, a clearance-driven reduction in oxytocin recruitment. The proposed sequence requires reduced oxytocin secretion after demonstrably prolonged active AVP exposure, distinguished from changes in oxytocin clearance and in osmotic or effective-filling conditions. Preserved oxytocin recruitment under a matched challenge despite prolonged AVP exposure would weaken the suppression branch. Its consequences for water and sodium handling depend on the physiological state; a protective renal purpose is not assumed. Any neural extension requires evidence in the relevant circuit (Section 37.1.2).

19.7.4 Proposed feedback between glucose and water handling

One possible feedback loop combines glucose support, peptide termination and GSH-sensitive processing when their necessary conditions coincide. In this scenario, oxidative membrane disturbance increases volume-control difficulty. A sufficient extracellular glucose rise could temporarily oppose swelling without repairing the bilayer, followed by insulin-dependent recovery. Water-intoxication findings establish neither deliberate insulin suppression nor a general high-glucose/low-insulin rule (Thurston et al., 1978); absent GLUT4 recruitment alone does not make glucose impermeant. If inadequate recruitment or a selective IRAP defect delays peptide termination as glucose is disposed of, protection could be followed by a water-handling cost. Acquired insulin resistance is unnecessary, and GLUT4 and IRAP need not fail together (Filippis et al., 1998).

Concurrent GSH-sensitive processing limitation could reduce another AVP-removal opportunity. If active AVP then outlasts the need for conservation, water supply and renal responsiveness could permit antidiuresis to deepen dilution, renewing the challenge to vulnerable membranes. This is the proposed return connection, not an automatic effect of falling glucose. A further return through AVP–lipid-peroxide competition requires enough demand at a shared local site to limit both functions; neither low blood GSH nor separate component studies establishes it. Normal active AVP clearance and water recovery despite verified renal redox limitation would weaken this branch.

Feedback could resolve after prolonging recovery through a sensitive developmental interval, leaving a circuit consequence (Sections 29, 31, and 36.5). Lifelong hyperglycaemia, low GSH or abnormal AVP is unnecessary, but normal later values do not prove an earlier episode. Slow recovery, thresholds and hysteresis alone do not identify this return connection.

19.7.5 Glucose exposure and inflammatory persistence

Glucose could prolong inflammatory conditions independently of the proposed osmotic-support and IRAP sequence, or of insulin resistance. In vascular-cell cultures, high glucose reduced inflammation-induced A20 protein despite preserved early RNA induction; osmotic controls did not reproduce it. O-GlcNAc modification, ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation accompanied the loss (Shrikhande et al., 2010). Reduced A20 could weaken inflammatory restraint, but this experiment did not establish persistence after glucose withdrawal.

Duration has two different experimental precedents. In mouse BV2 microglia, 25 versus 5.5 mmol/L glucose prolonged LPS-associated NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and increased inducible NO synthase expression; high glucose alone did not reproduce the NF-κB response (Hung et al., 2022). Both exposures continued, so post-withdrawal recovery was not established. In aortic endothelial cultures, 16 hours at 30 mmol/L glucose preceded persistent p65-associated chromatin and gene-expression changes over six days at normal glucose (El-Osta et al., 2008). This demonstrates persistence after a substantial pulse, not a threshold for brief infant excursions.

Two proposed consequences could interact: longer neural/glial inflammatory signalling and reduced vascular delivery support. A20-dependent eNOS expression supplies a candidate connection to endothelial reserve (Angolano et al., 2021; Section 16.8.2), distinct from inducible NOS, eNOS coupling or measured NO output. A20 loss has not been shown to explain the microglial or post-withdrawal findings, and these studies do not establish uniform glucose inhibition of TNFAIP3, NFKBIA and NFKBIE. A20 remains the specific experimental example.

Glucose exposure could become a recovery modifier if it extends inflammatory activity sufficiently to delay local ionic or cellular-volume restoration, whatever glucose’s initiating role. The magnitude and duration needed in developing tissue remain unknown. Persistent inflammation with adequate local recovery would limit this proposed route into the Sodium Struggle.

A bounded neonatal exposure can precede later structural change. Streptozotocin on rat postnatal day 1 lowered insulin and raised glucose to 11.9–13.4 mmol/L on days 3–6, with no significant glucose difference after day 7. Early delayed retinal vascularisation, inflammation and apoptosis preceded reduced neuronal-layer counts at day 14; superficial vessel density and Iba1-positive microglial/macrophage counts did not differ significantly at day 21 (Kermorvant-Duchemin et al., 2013). This separates exposure from outcome timing, but concurrent insulin loss prevents glucose-only attribution and ionic/volume recovery was unmeasured.

19.7.6 Physiological benefit and developmental effects

Limited insulin supply, physical-state sensing, signalling or trafficking could precede developmental divergence; repeated demand might instead produce later metabolic impairment, with shared causes or independent comorbidity also possible. Maternal diabetes, post-diagnosis measurements and later type 2 diabetes address different timescales (§48). Early islet autoantibodies establish chronology in selected at-risk children, not insulin deficiency or IRAP impairment in autistic children (Ziegler and Bonifacio, 2012). The shared defence process remains the overarching conjecture; no protective glucose surge, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinaemia or IRAP defect is obligatory in every trajectory.

A developmental contribution requires the relevant exposure to impair local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery during a susceptible interval. Candidate disturbances include impaired astrocytic volume recovery or chloride-gradient restoration; altered extracellular-space conditions or inadequate energetic support could initiate or amplify those disturbances and their effects on inhibitory maturation (Sections 23–29, 30.4, and 31). The prediction is altered maturation or refinement during a sensitive interval, leaving an enduring circuit consequence. Adult peripheral findings establish neither fetal exposure nor PV dysfunction; direct genetic, immune, placental and vascular effects remain alternatives. None of these component studies demonstrates altered OTX2 production, secretion, delivery or capture.

The two principal proposals can fail separately. Adequate evidence excluding the proposed benefit of temporary osmotic glucose support in the specified state would require withdrawal of that adaptive claim. Evidence excluding a useful contribution from IRAP-associated peptide termination or its timing would require withdrawal of the corresponding coordination claim in the specified state. Neither result by itself decides the other. A systemic benefit without developmental mediation remains physiological context. Imprecise nulls are inconclusive, but an unspecified hidden subgroup cannot rescue a well-tested negative result.

These proposals do not justify raising glucose, restricting insulin, altering salt or water intake, or changing medication.

19.8 Chapter synthesis

One disturbance may reduce the capacity to compensate for another, extending recovery into a susceptible developmental window. Endocrine recruitment, osmolyte supply, cytoskeletal integrity and transport capacity provide candidate interaction sites. Successful compensation may instead restore balance or counteract a second disturbance. Convergence on a shared endpoint, adverse amplification, additivity, synergy and threshold behaviour require distinct comparisons; coexisting exposures do not establish any one of them. Section 19.7 illustrates why temporary osmotic glucose support and insulin/IRAP-associated peptide termination must be tested separately, even where they could interact. Section 20 maps the component evidence, and Section 21 examines how a disturbance or its consequences could persist after initiation.

20 Integrated Evidence Map: Contributors, Modifiers and Comparisons

Table 20.1 provides claim-specific source context for the cellular and circulation contributor maps (Tables 13.1 and 15.1). Eight groups identify primary roles in the argument; their roles can overlap, and placement establishes neither causality nor developmental timing. Evidence of a disturbance or recovery constraint can justify retaining a candidate initiating input without proof of the complete developmental route. [E] marks the stated empirical observation or association; [S], a measured physiological component; [H], proposed mediation or an untested response. Each code applies only to its named endpoint. Unless explicitly measured, the final-column connections remain hypotheses: association or component physiology establishes neither the adjacent endocrine pathway nor the required local recovery disturbance and developmental consequence. Rows retain exposure-specific limits and contrary findings; an [H]-only response is not demonstrated by its representative citation.
