Part D From a response to lasting change

21 Developmental Canalisation and Hysteresis in Sodium–Volume Defence

The preceding sections map candidate developmental inputs through osmotic and cellular disturbances (Table 13.1) and through actual circulatory disturbance or altered sensing and regulation (Table 15.1, Panels A and B). This section asks how a transient osmotic, circulatory, sensing/regulatory or intrinsic cellular-recovery disturbance could leave a lasting regulatory or structural consequence. Neither neonatal dilution nor hypovolaemia is required in every route.

21.1 Recovery, persistence and developmental history

The proposed middle layer is developmental canalisation: early stabilisation could change the physiology on which renal, vascular, endocrine and neuroglial development proceeds. Persistence may involve an acquired response bias, altered recovery capacity or a developmental consequence that remains after physiology returns to baseline. These are distinct outcomes, each requiring evidence beyond the initiating disturbance.

During development, repeated reliance on an immediately effective response could change later thresholds, gain or effector allocation. Candidate consequences include altered vascular tone, AVP-linked recruitment, renal handling and splanchnic redistribution. Their direction and persistence must be measured against age-appropriate responses to the same input; repeated recruitment alone does not establish high gain.

A lasting allocation bias could preserve normal resting sodium or pressure while requiring greater effort under demand. Alternatively, normal measurements may reflect complete recovery and ordinary homeostasis. The proposed persistent state is identified by altered response or recovery at matched inputs, not inferred from apparently normal headline values.

Intermittent disturbances could have lasting effects if they alter a regulatory or structural process during a sensitive period. Later normalisation need not erase an established developmental change, but persistence cannot be inferred from the original load.

Fast loops can preserve water balance and perfusion. A lasting transition is proposed when a disturbance or recurrent demand changes later reserve, recovery or effector response; increased transport or signalling alone does not establish it.

Beyond a change in a fast response, repeated demand may leave recovery unfinished or constrain regulatory reserve. The hypothesis proposes that slower structural and compartmental adaptations then assume some stabilisation work, preserving immediate stability while changing developmental conditions.

This requires a demonstrable transfer of work or altered capacity persisting beyond normal recovery, rather than inference from a tissue difference or normal resting sodium and pressure.

Slower anatomical, biochemical or receptor changes could then carry part of the work, supporting viability while reducing later flexibility. Repeated recruitment alone does not demonstrate such structural offloading.

The proposed physiological diversity follows from the interaction between initiating conditions, genetic constraints, available reserve and developmental timing. A shared causal process must be shown at the specified intermediary, rather than inferred from the diversity of possible outputs.

The following examples examine acquired metabolic change, immune training or tolerance, and AVP-linked effector allocation. Each asks whether a specified function changes after exposure and relevant physiological recovery; none defines an obligatory entry route. Slower tissue adaptations and the final cross-system read-outs then connect these examples to later organ and developmental questions.

21.2 Metabolic persistence and functional dissociation

Recurrent hydromineral demand could leave lasting metabolic consequences, with or without an initially protective glucose response. Early limitations in insulin supply, physical-state sensing, signalling or trafficking remain possible initiating routes. Glucose support and peptide clearance, proposed separately in Section 19.7, could participate in metabolic feedback; the question here is whether an acquired functional change persists after the initiating conditions resolve.

Additional gradient-restoration work could constrain metabolic reserve (Sections 23, 26, and 27), but chloride flux does not establish reduced glucose disposal. Vascular access provides another link: insulin recruited skeletal-muscle microvasculature before increased glucose uptake in rats, while NOS inhibition blocked recruitment and partly inhibited early uptake (Vincent et al., 2004). This component result does not establish developmental vascular mediation in autism.

Metabolic imprinting here means an acquired functional change persisting after exposure and relevant extracellular conditions normalise. It differs from repeated fully reversible excursions, incomplete recovery between challenges and independently sustained metabolic disease. Delayed osmolyte restoration or ordinary dysglycaemic fluctuations alone do not establish chronic insulin resistance or a persistently erroneous AVP sensor.

Hyperosmotic stimulation of glucose transport reversed after restoration of isotonicity in small Clone9-cell and 3T3-L1-adipocyte washout experiments (Barros et al., 2001). Thus acute coupling can resolve; persistence requires an additional explanation, and an earlier protective effect cannot be assumed to remain beneficial under later hypertonic conditions.

Selective impairment depends on which functions remain available. Substantial antinatriuresis despite reduced glucose responsiveness (Rocchini et al., 1989), and increased basal membrane-fraction IRAP in type 2 diabetic adipocytes (Maianu et al., 2001), oppose a single insulin-resistance signature. Receptor desensitisation and downstream trafficking are distinct possibilities, and impaired dynamic actin remodelling is not synonymous with weak actin bundles. Fractional abundance does not establish exposed enzyme activity or native-peptide clearance (Section 19.7).

Pattern and status Glucose disposal IRAP-dependent AVP processing
Observed human component comparison, Rocchini 1989 Reduced insulin responsiveness in obese adolescents Not measured
Predicted glucose selective limitation Reduced Preserved despite reduced disposal
Predicted shared trafficking limitation Reduced if GLUT4 deployment is affected Reduced if accessible active IRAP is affected
Predicted catalytic IRAP limitation Preserved if transport is unaffected Reduced despite preserved glucose transport

Table 21.1 describes proposed functional dissociations, not autism subtypes. Significance for one response but not another does not establish dissociation. Glucose-selective impairment could prolong extracellular glucose without prolonging AVP, while an IRAP defect could prolong peptide exposure despite preserved disposal. Whether feedback worsens, compensates for or leaves recovery unchanged depends on secretion, renal response and the initial water–solute and filling state.

IRAP recruitment and peptide clearance remain distinct (Section 19.7). Hypertonic saline and urea inhibited serum synthetic-substrate hydrolysis directly in vitro (Roy et al., 1981, 1982), so assay change need not imply enzyme recruitment. Basal activity, stimulated activity and their increment differ; neither enzyme proxies nor substrate hydrolysis establish intact circulating AVP removal or oxytocin processing.

Applying these proposals to pregnancy requires maternal–placental–fetal exposure assessment: glucose-associated sodium lowering can coexist with higher effective tonicity. Sections 18.2 and 19.7 distinguish these states and the physiological contributions to be tested.

Reduced glucose entry during redox stress may protect or harm cells depending on tonicity, fuel availability and recovery; it is not itself evidence of an osmotic shield (Sections 16.8 and 19.7).

A receptor change that persists after ligand exposure and local physiological recovery could support developmental memory; one resolving with recovery supports continuing-state dependence. AVPR1A/AVPR1B and OXTR branches remain tissue- and window-specific, with function distinct from expression (Section 18).

The conditional birth prediction is lower cord copeptin with lower effective fetal tonicity under comparable nonosmotic stress. A sufficiently precise null or opposite result would weaken it. One cord sample addresses magnitude, not recruitment delay, clearance or earlier gestation; even a positive result could reflect ordinary protection rather than developmental impairment (Sections 10.3 and 18.1.9).

Later metabolic disease cannot identify earlier developmental causation. Shared genetic, placental or inflammatory influences, independent risk and treatment remain alternatives; prospective changes during risperidone treatment illustrate the latter (Scahill et al., 2016). The proposed acquired route is repeated demand followed by altered recovery and metabolic feedback.

21.3 Immune memory: training, tolerance and recovery

Microglia provide a rapid recipient of local extracellular signals. P2Y12-deficient mouse microglia retained baseline motility but showed markedly reduced directional responses to extracellular nucleotides and early process recruitment toward cortical injury (Haynes et al., 2006). Signal concentration, spatial gradient and receptor responsiveness can therefore influence the immediate recruitment response. Extracellular-space compression could modify the initial concentration change for a fixed released amount (Section 25); a lasting change in responsiveness requires an additional cellular mechanism.

An inflammatory history can leave such a persistent cellular record. In adult mice, the second daily peripheral lipopolysaccharide exposure amplified brain cytokine responses, whereas further exposures induced tolerance. Microglial deletion of Tak1 or Hdac1/2 largely prevented the amplified response. Cytokines returned to baseline within 24 hours in the tested cessation conditions, while distinct microglial enhancer profiles remained detectable six months after the initial exposure schedule (Wendeln et al., 2018). This supplies a precedent for transient exposure producing a retained response programme. Training and tolerance are different possible outcomes; repeated challenge need not progressively sensitise tissue.

We propose that recurrent ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty can influence this response history by changing the timing, localisation or repetition of purinergic exposure, with accompanying inflammatory signals recruiting a more persistent programme. Vascular delivery and cortisol timing could modify that response. During development, altered microglial responsiveness could then change the conditions under which circuits are refined. The prediction is a changed threshold, response magnitude or resolution time across a graded series of matched later challenges after the initiating exposure has ended and the relevant ionic and cellular-volume disturbance has resolved. Correcting the earlier recovery disturbance should reduce this later difference under comparable immune exposure. Measuring these response dimensions separately would distinguish sensitisation, tolerance and delayed resolution, and test whether the adult inflammatory-memory precedent extends to the developmental recovery route proposed here.

21.4 Effector Allocation Under a Single-Ligand Constraint

This worked example concerns effector allocation: the relative renal, vascular and endocrine outputs defending filling and tonicity. It does not imply rationing AVP molecules between organs or an obligatory reduction in one output when another increases.

21.4.1 The single-ligand constraint

The single-ligand constraint concerns shared peptide identity, not a single uniform AVP pool. Circulating AVP can couple renal water handling to vascular responses, while pituitary regulation also depends on hypophysial-portal delivery and interactions with corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). In rats, haemorrhage increased portal AVP and other ACTH secretagogues, demonstrating coordinated but multifactor control (Plotsky et al., 1985). Local AVP release has its own calcium-store-dependent regulation, demonstrated in rat supraoptic neurones (Ludwig et al., 2005). Peripheral, portal and neural exposure histories must therefore be distinguished. Effector allocation remains a useful problem wherever multiple responsive targets encounter the same AVP signal.

Within a shared exposure compartment, AVP-responsive pathways have different thresholds and time constants. Helping one target can change another’s operating conditions, creating potential trade-offs. Local access, release, sensitivity and clearance can partly separate their outputs; developmental weighting need not imply simultaneous recruitment or a uniform global broadcast.

21.4.2 Minimal receptor map: V2, V1a, and V1b

The multi-effector reach of AVP is implemented through three receptor pathways that are relevant here.

V2 receptors in collecting-duct principal cells support water conservation through aquaporin-2 (AQP2) delivery to the apical membrane. In isolated rat collecting ducts, AVP increased apical AQP2 and water permeability; both declined after AVP withdrawal (Nielsen et al., 1995). This reversible response supplies the renal component of the model. Its effect on urine concentration and serum sodium also depends on the medullary gradient, solute excretion and water intake.

Vascular V1a receptors provide a rapid route from circulating AVP to smooth-muscle contraction. In V1a-null mice, AVP-induced vascular contraction and pressor responses were lost, while circulating volume and baroreflex function also changed (Koshimizu et al., 2006). This supports V1a participation in pressure defence, but also shows why whole-body blood pressure cannot isolate vascular receptor sensitivity. Regional flow and filtration must be measured in the relevant vascular bed.

Pituitary V1b receptors contribute to ACTH release through AVP signalling that interacts with CRH. In V1b-null mice, AVP-stimulated ACTH release was impaired while the response to administered CRH was preserved (Tanoue et al., 2004). ACTH recruits adrenal glucocorticoid production, chiefly cortisol in humans and corticosterone in these mice. Portal AVP exposure, ACTH secretion and the adrenal response are separate steps; peripheral AVP concentration alone cannot identify the contribution of this endocrine arm.

21.4.3 Why neonatal context matters

Development changes the reserve against which a challenge acts. In rats, urine concentration after dehydration and renal AQP2 expression increased between postnatal days 10 and 40, with a marked transition around weaning (Yasui et al., 1996). In clinically stable human neonates studied during quiet sleep, cardiac baroreflex sensitivity increased with postmenstrual age across 28–42 weeks (Andriessen et al., 2005). These are distinct renal and cardiovascular developmental findings, not a single measure of global immaturity. They explain why adult responses cannot simply be assigned to a newborn and why comparisons must match developmental stage.

A response that works during development could become part of the later starting state. There is a measured precedent: after prenatal maternal water restriction, lambs studied at 23 ± 2 days had an AVP-release osmotic threshold of 290 ± 2 mOsm/kg, compared with 280 ± 2 in control singletons and 285 ± 1 in control twins (Desai et al., 2003b). Maternal nutritional restriction accompanied dehydration, limiting attribution to tonicity alone. The exposed lambs remained hypertonic and hypertensive at testing. This supports developmental change in a regulatory threshold, but not persistence after complete physiological recovery or persistent weighting of V2, V1a or V1b. That allocation hypothesis requires pathway-specific responses after the initiating exposure has ended.

21.4.4 Allocation trade-offs and burden placement

Allocation can support effective arterial filling, sensor-site tonicity, microvascular fluid exchange and local cell-volume regulation through different combinations of renal, vascular and endocrine work.

A V2-weighted allocation relies more on renal water conservation to support filling. Dilution requires a positive water balance relative to exchangeable solute, not V2 activation alone. There is also direct evidence for a renal consequence beyond concentration: desmopressin increased urinary albumin excretion reversibly in rats and approximately threefold after acute infusion in healthy human subjects (Bardoux et al., 2003). The human experiment was pharmacological and acute; the rat reversibility argues against treating the response itself as permanent damage. These results justify testing a renal cost of sustained V2 recruitment, but concentrated urine alone establishes neither that cost nor a developmental consequence.

V1a-weighted vasomotor support can defend pressure and distribution. Persistent endothelial injury, glycocalyx loss or rarefaction would be additional costs, not consequences established by the receptor-specific contraction evidence above.

A V1b-weighted endocrine allocation requires a demonstrated AVP contribution to ACTH and glucocorticoid recruitment. Metabolic involvement is experimentally supported: V1b-null mice showed increased insulin sensitivity in a hyperinsulinaemic–euglycaemic clamp (Fujiwara et al., 2007). However, V1b also acts outside the pituitary, including pancreatic and adipose pathways, so that whole-body knockout cannot assign the effect to cortisol. Persistent metabolic expenditure or substrate-handling changes caused specifically by developmental pituitary V1b recruitment remain predictions.

21.4.5 Stable allocation regimes and hysteresis

A candidate memory mechanism is altered receptor-pathway effectiveness or downstream function after exposure. Increased responsiveness, reduced responsiveness and delayed recovery are different predictions; receptor abundance alone cannot identify functional gain. Section 36 distinguishes these changes from current exposure, acute desensitisation and rebound.

An attractor-like allocation pattern would repeatedly re-emerge under specified conditions. Hysteresis additionally requires history-dependent responses at matched current inputs; persistence alone establishes neither an attractor nor a particular feedback dynamic.

21.4.6 Illustrative allocation regimes

To make the allocation logic concrete without asserting fixed subtypes, two illustrative regimes can be outlined.

A V2-weighted regime predicts greater renal water conservation for a given perturbation, through greater AVP exposure, renal sensitivity or AQP2 trafficking. Dilutional cost additionally requires intake and solute balance to produce positive water balance; concentrated urine alone does not identify it.

A vascular/endocrine regime predicts greater V1a-linked vasomotor or V1b-linked ACTH/glucocorticoid responses to the same challenge. These arms can vary independently and need not displace renal conservation; reduced vascular flexibility or lasting metabolic cost is an additional proposed consequence.

These are proposed stabilisation regimes with potentially different long-term costs. The discriminating prediction is that a measured allocation pattern changes a specified developmental outcome under comparable demand and reserve.

The later organ sections develop how this allocation could affect nephron reserve, splanchnic recruitment, matrix sodium buffering, neuroglial microdomains and membrane restoration.

21.5 Secondary stabilisation: contributors and tissue layers

21.5.1 Convergent upstream contributors as control stressors

AVP-dependent retention, epithelial barrier injury and altered vascular regulation could increase stabilisation demand through different routes. Section 16.8 evaluates smoke, traffic-related pollution and candidate mould exposures separately: impaired vasodilation alone does not identify permeability, underfilling or high-gain AVP control.

Early respiratory morbidity offers another possible source of non-osmotic AVP recruitment, with sex-associated exposure differences considered in Section 40.2. In twelve ventilated premature newborns with respiratory distress syndrome, AVP remained elevated despite normal sodium and osmolality, and recovery-associated diuresis occurred without AVP normalisation (Zanardo et al., 1989). In a separate series of twelve infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, acute hypoxaemia and air trapping accompanied increased ADH; concentrations fell with respiratory improvement, while three infants developed hyponatraemia (Rao et al., 1986). Altered atrial filling was proposed in the latter study, rather than isolated as the causal mechanism. Respiratory distress, hypoxaemia, mechanical support and filling changes are distinct variables.

These observations support a respiratory route into compensatory demand while preserving successful adaptation. Elevated circulating AVP can coexist with normal chemistry; normal measurements alone neither establish pathological compensation nor exclude regulatory work. For the proposed neural developmental route, the additional requirement remains disturbed local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery and its developmental consequence. Parallel peripheral consequences require separate assessment and do not substitute for that intermediary. Neither respiratory illness nor raised AVP alone establishes persistent developmental mediation.

Antioxidant defence could also limit the initiating disturbance, before sustained osmotic–volume compensation is needed. The proposed GSH contribution spans three separable functions: peroxide and membrane protection, preservation of the endothelial glycocalyx, and support of GSH-sensitive AVP processing (Sections 19.7 and 35.1). The neonatal observations in Section 40.4 motivate a sex-dependent modifier of injury and compensatory demand, independently of sodium stores. Demonstrating one component would not establish the others; successful protection and complete recovery remain possible outcomes.

Nephron endowment and transport allocation could also modify an initiating sodium–water or mineral disturbance and the demand for compensation. Section 32 distinguishes this upstream role from renal responses to a disturbance originating elsewhere and from persistent changes that modify later episodes; Section 40 considers the sex-dependent developmental proposal.

21.5.2 Secondary stabilisation layers
21.5.2.1 Layer A: Tissue sodium buffering and matrix-level capacitance

Tissue sodium partitioning is a plausible secondary stabilisation layer with experimental support. In adult female rats fed less than 0.1% or 8% NaCl for eight weeks, higher skin sodium accompanied increased glycosaminoglycan content and chondroitin-synthase mRNA, supporting matrix-associated storage without directly measuring its binding chemistry (Titze et al., 2004). Genetic disruption provides a functional link: mice with combined heterozygous Ext1/Ext2 loss had lower skin sodium and water, a thinner endothelial surface layer and higher plasma osmolality despite similar plasma sodium; impaired vasodilation was an alternative explanation for their pressure response to sodium loading (Olde Engberink et al., 2019). Matrix architecture can therefore participate in sodium–water homeostasis. Its water balance must be measured: in salt-loaded hypertensive rats, tissue sodium increases were largely accompanied by water and were consistent with extracellular expansion rather than hypertonic storage (Rossitto et al., 2020). Tissue sodium content, bound fraction, interstitial water and effective tonicity are distinct endpoints.

In rats, Schafflhuber et al. (2007) compared sodium per unit tissue mass: growth-associated changes involved bone and carcass, while a four-week dietary contrast (0.1% versus 8% NaCl) principally involved the estimated osmotically inactive skin pool, without lower endpoint serum sodium. Bone values used ash mass. These comparisons do not establish ordered recruitment from tissue exchange to osteoclastic resorption.

Lymphatic support also has a measured regulatory role: macrophage depletion or VEGF-C trapping increased interstitial volume retention and blood pressure during salt loading in rats (Machnik et al., 2009). The hypothesis proposes that matrix partitioning and lymphatic transport could redistribute stabilisation work during recurrent challenges. Calling this plasma buffering requires a smaller or shorter plasma sodium or tonicity excursion after a matched load, attributable to tissue exchange; a larger tissue sodium store alone does not show that benefit. The developmental extension is that sustained reliance changes matrix maintenance or recovery capacity sufficiently to affect the local neural or glial recovery process defined in the core hypothesis.

21.5.2.2 Layer B: Vascular and epithelial remodelling with endocrine decoupling under inflammatory load

Repeated barrier strain could shift stabilisation work into slower vascular or epithelial remodelling. Glycocalyx integrity, junctional maintenance and microvascular tone jointly affect fluid retention; their proposed persistent cost is altered vasomotor work, capillary-filtration control or regional flow heterogeneity. This need not appear as a resting leak. Section 35.1 distinguishes the glycocalyx and bilayer contributions.

Inflammation can uncouple endocrine components without imposing a fixed low-renin/high-aldosterone sequence. TNF and IL-1 increased renin release from rat renal slices, whereas TNF inhibited renin transcription in mouse preparations (Antonipillai et al., 1990; Todorov et al., 2002; §14.6.10). Three cancer patients with high IL-6 instead had high renin and low aldosterone; in one, both normalised with successful treatment and became abnormal again with tumour recurrence (Chung et al., 1996). The proposed developmental concern is a mismatch between available support and sodium–volume need, whose direction remains tissue-specific.

Low baseline renin does not establish amplified downstream gain. The proposed distortion requires a measured inflammatory exposure and a disproportionate receptor or effector response under comparable sodium balance and haemodynamics. Under such conditions, mineralocorticoid receptors may experience sustained stimulation that is poorly informative about physiological need. A plausible developmental extension is that prolonged exposure drives durable changes in mineralocorticoid receptor availability and effective gain, including reduced receptor expression, altered nuclear trafficking, shifts in co-regulator balance, or changes in 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 support. The direction and persistence of these changes, and whether they protect cells while compromising systemic sodium–volume defence, remain to be established.

Acute inflammatory changes in MR availability have direct support. In adult mice given 15 mg/kg lipopolysaccharide, aortic MR and α1-adrenoceptor expression fell at 6 and 18 hours; aldosterone co-treatment preserved receptor expression and improved vascular responses. TNF-α also reduced MR expression in human vascular cells (Fadel et al., 2017). This severe acute model supports an inflammatory change in the machinery of vascular support, not persistent renal mineralocorticoid failure. The hypothesis predicts that, in an affected developmental route, reduced functional MR responsiveness remains after inflammation resolves, weakens sodium conservation under a matched challenge and increases reliance on glucocorticoid support. Such redistribution could preserve immediate stability while imposing wider metabolic costs. Persistence, sodium-conserving function and greater glucocorticoid dependence require separate evidence; receptor abundance during illness or normal resting electrolytes cannot establish the sequence.

21.5.2.3 Layer C: Neuroglial water–ion microdomain management

Astrocytic and perivascular water–ion regulation could carry a third share of stabilisation work. Its proposed costs include intermittent swelling, clearance strain and altered perivascular dynamics when restoration remains incomplete. Sections 24 and 30 develop these local mechanisms and their energetic and structural demands.

21.5.2.4 Layer D: Membrane and lipid remodelling

Membrane organisation supplies a fourth candidate layer. Cholesterol can modify permeability and mechanical protection; caveolae can rapidly release surface area without ATP, while rebuilding that reservoir requires ATP (Sinha et al., 2011). Section 35 develops the resulting separation between immediate protection and restoration before another challenge.

21.5.3 The emergence of autism-associated physiology

Secondary stabilisation could connect successful immediate defence to altered developmental timing, precision or flexibility when the adaptation outlasts normal recovery. Its relevance to autism requires a link between that physiological change and the resulting neural effect.

21.5.4 Heterogeneity as a function of burden placement

The burden-placement hypothesis predicts that initiating conditions and reserve profiles may recruit different combinations of matrix, membrane, vascular, endocrine and neuroglial responses. A prespecified allocation pattern should predict a corresponding tissue or developmental consequence. Diverse signatures alone cannot establish a shared process, and retrospective branch selection cannot rescue a failed test.

Section 47 distinguishes lasting developmental consequences from continuing physiological constraints and examines how cellular persistence could modify later expression.

21.6 Cross-system response and persistence read-outs

Box 21.1 Candidate receptor-network read-outs of the proposed shared defence process

AVP/OXT axis: candidate tissue-specific responses include AVPR1A/AVPR1B sensitisation, reduced AVPR2/AQP2-mediated antidiuretic response or reduced OXTR responsiveness after a defined exposure. These are distinct directional predictions; high or low AVP alone does not identify any of them.

MR/GR axis: a proposed shift in glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid signalling could alter AVP recruitment or OXTR response. Enduring calibration requires evidence that the specified change remains after exposure and local physiological recovery, not merely after serum sodium normalises.

RAAS cross-talk: candidate signalling and trafficking interactions require direct measurement of the specified osmotic exposure, receptor response and persistence. Component interaction does not establish RAAS imprinting.

Renal and endothelial persistence: collecting-duct escape from antidiuresis and altered endothelial MR/NO responses are distinct candidates. Antidiuretic escape alone does not establish cell-identity change or incomplete reversibility.

Timing: regional skin-barrier maturation is a candidate exposure window; NFAT5 programming and osmolyte debt require stage-specific measurements. Prenatal and postnatal routes need distinct tests.

The hypothesis proposes a shared sodium–volume–vascular defence process that can be entered through different disturbances and expressed through different receptor and cellular configurations. Neither insufficient sodium nor one AVP direction is required as the initiating observation. High- and low-AVP findings require compartment, timing and receptor-context measurements before a shared mechanism is inferred.

Section 22 maps the remaining applications. Their common question is whether a candidate stabilisation layer leaves altered capacity after recovery, and how that capacity changes subsequent development.

22 From Physiological Responses to Developmental and Later Expression

This roadmap connects the general persistence account in Section 21 to local recovery, developmental change and later expression. Successful immediate sodium–volume compensation could alter later capacity if it changes organ development during a sensitive window. Reduced renal endowment may instead precede the physiological struggle or arise from a shared genetic cause; Section 32 distinguishes these routes. None substitutes for the central requirement that impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carries a developmental effect.

22.1 Roadmap: local recovery, organ reserve and later expression

The groups below follow Parts E–H through the detailed recovery account, organ regulation, later expression and final evaluation. They are not a measured hierarchy of permanence: reversal depends on the tissue, developmental stage, exposure and endpoint. A temporary physiological change can also leave an enduring circuit consequence after the original variable recovers. The developmental-anatomy and intergenerational comparisons in Sections 8 and 11 complement the entry routes in Sections 6, 7, 9, and 10, now brought together in Part B.

Part E Local recovery and developmental conversion

23 Functional NKCC1 Bias, Chloride Recovery, and the Sodium-Driven Energetic Burden

23.1 Scope: an adaptive defence that can become maladaptive

Impaired chloride recovery is a candidate local persistence layer after osmotic, perfusion-metabolic or redox threat. Increased NKCC1 import, reduced KCC2 extrusion or weakened potassium driving conditions may act separately or together. The proposed developmental endpoint is impaired restoration of an age-appropriate chloride state, not simply delayed maturation or a uniform whole-brain chloride abnormality.

During hypotonic swelling, regulatory volume decrease (RVD) can export ions and organic osmolytes, allowing water to leave. Volume adaptation during continuing exposure differs from restoration after that exposure ends. A return of cell volume alone does not show that ionic gradients and solute pools have recovered. Timely restoration of the relevant variables with adequate reserve is the successful comparator. Section 24 develops the full volume and osmolyte account.

AVP recruitment, RVD and transient transporter reweighting can each protect immediate stability. The proposed transition is incomplete local ionic or volume recovery carrying a developmental effect; repetition, osmolyte loss or additional work alone does not establish it.

NKCC1 abundance, phosphorylation, localisation and net flux are distinct; KCC2 failure can raise chloride without NKCC1 gain. Section 23.2 defines the import, extrusion and combined branches before the evidence is considered. Section 23.13 sets out their recovery comparisons and limiting results.

Astrocytic volume, potassium handling and metabolic support could influence neuronal recovery in a perivascular route. The order can also run from neuronal transport, mitochondrial or redox disturbance to greater glial demand; astrocyte-first initiation is branch-specific.

Systemic defence enters this account only where it changes CNS exposure or recovery conditions. A local chloride disturbance does not identify its origin; direct genetic, developmental or redox initiation remains possible.

The metabolic route in Section 19.7 could constrain CNS recovery through altered exposure, substrate delivery or extracellular conditions. Peripheral GLUT4 or plasma/urine measurements cannot establish that neural bridge.

23.2 What “functional NKCC1 bias” means

“Functional NKCC1 bias” is reserved here for a demonstrable NKCC1 contribution to inward chloride transport under the measured ionic conditions. Such a contribution may be local, cell-type-specific and restricted to a recovery window without a uniform increase in total NKCC1 protein. A chloride-loaded phenotype alone is better described as impaired chloride recovery until import and extrusion have been separated.

This neuronal and astrocytic usage must not be transferred unchanged to choroid-plexus epithelium. Developmental stage and ionic gradients alter the meaning of NKCC1 flux; neonatal CSF potassium clearance and adult CSF secretion are separate endpoints (Xu et al., 2021; Fame et al., 2023; Jensen et al., 2025). Section 30 treats this epithelial compartment separately.

Three non-exclusive branches should be distinguished. The import-cost branch requires increased NKCC1-mediated inward flux and its associated sodium-handling demand; phosphorylation and surface availability are supporting regulatory measurements. The extrusion-failure branch requires impaired KCC2-mediated chloride removal because of altered transporter function, stability or driving conditions. The combined branch requires evidence for both. Astrocytic ionic loading or extracellular-space changes may influence these branches but do not identify the neuronal transporter responsible.

KCC2 does not directly consume ATP, but its usual outward KCl transport depends on gradients maintained indirectly by energy-dependent processes. Increased extracellular K⁺ or reduced intracellular K⁺ can weaken outward transport even when KCC2 protein is unchanged. Reversal can occur under suitable gradients and is not necessarily pathological; activity-dependent KCC2 reversal has been supported by hippocampal slice measurements and modelling (Byvaltcev et al., 2023). An extrusion defect can therefore support a chloride-recovery mechanism while falsifying an increased-NKCC1-import explanation for that particular phenotype.

The WNK-SPAK/OSR1 axis can regulate NKCC1 and KCC2 reciprocally, but the relevant phosphosites and functional consequences must be identified. Phosphorylation is not a single on/off state shared by both transporters. KCC2 surface loss can also follow oxidant-sensitive tyrosine dephosphorylation, whereas NMDA or interictal-like activity can engage calpain-mediated KCC2 cleavage in rat hippocampal preparations (Wake et al., 2007; Puskarjov et al., 2012). These distinct mechanisms offer several routes to reduced chloride extrusion.

Elevated extracellular K⁺ is a possible amplifier rather than a universal positive-feedback driver. For a given release and clearance pattern, a smaller extracellular volume can increase local K⁺ transients. Their effects on NKCC1 and KCC2 depend on the complete ionic gradients: stronger inward NKCC1 driving conditions may coexist with weaker outward KCC2 transport, but rising intracellular Na⁺ and Cl⁻, potassium clearance, volume recovery and regulatory feedback can limit the response. The proposed swelling–potassium–chloride loop would amplify only while those stabilising processes remain insufficient.

23.3 Three initiating threats and the controller layer

Three initiating threats are distinguished: osmotic conditions that change CNS tonicity or volume; perfusion-metabolic supply or reserve insufficient for local demand; and excess oxidants or inadequate local buffering. Underfilling is not itself hypotonicity.

These threats may interact bidirectionally through volume, ionic gradients, mitochondrial function and perfusion. Redox strain can follow osmotic or metabolic demand, or initiate recovery difficulty independently.

Systemic entry involves distinct endothelial, arterial-baroreflex, cardiopulmonary and central responses to osmotic, filling, oxygen and stress signals. Endothelial dysfunction is not itself a neural report of underfilling; direct neural or glial initiation need not involve this controller sequence.

Non-osmotic AVP can add water-retention burden to a genuine pressure or filling threat when intake and handling permit it. Section 16.8 develops the vascular redox route; the bridge here is its effect on CNS delivery or recovery, not an assumed AVP rise or chloride load from reduced NO alone.

Angiotensin II or AVP could affect transport through cell-specific receptors or indirectly through pressure, perfusion and tonicity. Those routes remain distinct: elevated hormone or transporter phosphorylation alone does not establish inward chloride flux.

23.4 Timescale and anatomical sequence

Acute defence, restoration and developmental consequences operate on different schedules. Water redistribution and vascular/redox responses may begin within minutes to hours; osmolyte and transporter reset may extend over hours to days; circuit effects may emerge later. These are proposed observation windows, not a universal timetable. Pump work accompanies entry as well as subsequent recovery.

This temporal distinction is essential: acute hypotonic swelling can recruit protective RVD and does not necessarily increase net NKCC1 influx. This recovery branch concerns repeated episodes after which the water threat may have resolved but osmolyte debt, chloride recovery pressure, ATP strain or incomplete transporter reset remains.

A vascular-perivascular route could reach neurons through end-foot function, potassium handling and extracellular conditions. Direct neuronal redox or transporter disturbance can reverse that order and increase support demands. PV cells may be recipients or initiating sites; neither astrocyte-first nor OTX2 involvement is obligatory.

23.5 Immediate defence: swelling, RVD, perfusion triage, and redox buffering

Hypotonic swelling can recruit RVD through loss of KCl, water and organic osmolytes. This cell-specific protective response is not inferred from underfilling without a corresponding osmotic change (Section 24).

Perfusion-metabolic threat can recruit flow redistribution, extraction and metabolic adaptation that preserve ATP supply. Increased glycolysis or lactate is not energy failure; recovery becomes constrained when this support cannot meet local demand.

Redox threat recruits antioxidant, repair and metabolic responses that may initially limit injury. If oxidant production exceeds local buffering, it could affect vascular regulation, mitochondrial support or transporter stability. A direct neural example is the loss of surface KCC2 and a depolarising shift in GABA reversal potential after hydrogen peroxide exposure in mature rat hippocampal cultures (Wake et al., 2007). This establishes a component mechanism in an in vitro injury context, not a low-BH4 mechanism, a universal WNK response or developmental mediation in autism.

The proposed pathology concerns incomplete or unstable recovery when defensive demand exceeds available reserve, rather than recruitment of defence in itself.

23.6 Recovery Time Courses After Hyponatraemia

Recovery asymmetry concerns differences in how quickly the components of a defensive response reset. In rats with severe chronic hyponatraemia, organic osmolyte reaccumulation lagged during correction; rapid correction also produced a brain sodium and chloride overshoot that was not seen with slow correction (Lien et al., 1991). This supports the possibility that ionic and organic-osmolyte recovery follow different time courses. It does not establish osmolyte debt after mild intermittent exposure, which must be measured rather than assumed.

Tejedor et al. (2026) provide an experimental starting point for the osmotic arm. Female Wistar rats received a low-sodium diet and daily desmopressin with water for seven days, with four animals per group. Serum sodium recovered 24 hours after the final dose, but plasma osmolality remained below baseline. Lower whole-brain ADC and increased grey-matter GFAP staining were reported. ADC measures water mobility rather than total brain water; the grey-matter ADC comparison was borderline (p = 0.054). The study therefore does not demonstrate persistent CNS dysfunction after complete systemic osmotic recovery.

The same study found no significant group difference in the measured caudate-putamen osmolytes and did not measure cell-specific chloride, sodium, transporter flux or ATP. Small groups, dietary and caloric differences, and the acknowledged lack of an unchallenged RIH histology control further limit mechanistic attribution (Tejedor et al., 2026). It does not prove an osmolyte deficit, an NKCC1-mediated recovery mechanism or an energetic mismatch during chloride recovery. On subsequent water challenge, the recurrently exposed rats showed a slower, less pronounced ADC decline than controls, contrary to the predicted increase in vulnerability. Recurrence therefore did not produce a uniformly amplified imaging response (Tejedor et al., 2026).

This model leaves persistent extracellular disturbance, delayed cellular recovery and lasting developmental change distinct. Normal serum sodium does not identify which has occurred.

23.7 Chloride Recovery and Energetic Demand

The relationship to the Ben-Ari–Tyzio programme is mechanistic continuity plus an additional causal claim: what limits restoration under demand, and does that recovery difficulty alter development? Comparable resting chloride can coexist with different recovery, while altered resting chloride need not mean recovery failure. Tang et al. (2019) measured a treatment-associated acceleration of chloride extrusion in human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons (Section 6.4). This provides a positive dynamic recovery comparison without establishing recovery as the developmental mediator. Loading, extrusion, extracellular and supply constraints remain candidate causes of recovery failure.

23.7.1 Transport regulation and energetic demand

During chloride replenishment, increased inward NKCC1 transport could add sodium-pump work when energetic reserve is limited. This is the proposed import-cost branch. After RVD, some cells may have a transient chloride deficit or incompletely restored organic-osmolyte pools. Existing transport systems can support rapid ionic recovery, but chloride is not intrinsically a cheaper osmolyte once accompanying cation movements and restoration of their gradients are included. Fast replenishment need not be low-cost replenishment.

Low intracellular chloride can relieve direct inhibition of WNK1, allowing downstream SPAK/OSR1 signalling to favour NKCC1 transport capacity and restrain KCC-mediated extrusion. Rising intracellular chloride provides a brake, rather than continuing to activate this sensor (Piala et al., 2014). In mature hippocampal cultures, chloride-sensitive WNK1 signalling also regulates KCC2 membrane stability (Heubl et al., 2017). Shrinkage-related molecular crowding can sustain WNK signalling despite an inhibitory ionic environment in experimental cell systems (Boyd-Shiwarski et al., 2022). These inputs need not change in the same direction.

Restoration of external tonicity can itself recruit another phase of volume regulation. Boyd-Shiwarski et al. (2022) observed WNK1 puncta in HEK-293 cells during a post-RVD manoeuvre: water-diluted medium at 240 mOsm was followed by sorbitol restoration to 300 mOsm, producing acute shrinkage. Their broader experiments connected crowding-sensitive WNK1 condensation with transport signalling and volume recovery. This supplies a direct cellular precedent for recovery-phase recruitment of the proposed import-cost branch. The post-RVD observation did not demonstrate pathological neuronal chloride overshoot.

Chloride amount and chloride concentration must therefore be distinguished. RVD can remove chloride, but subsequent water loss can raise its concentration while increasing molecular crowding; return to isotonicity does not necessarily release the chloride brake. A separate activation protocol used hypotonic buffer with NaCl and KCl replaced by gluconate salts, leaving approximately 1 mM extracellular chloride (Thastrup et al., 2012). That combined perturbation cannot stand for ordinary hypotonic exposure. The relative contribution of chloride inhibition and crowding requires paired concentration and volume measurements, with WNK isoform, phosphosite and opposing phosphatase effects specified.

The proposed developmental extension is a failure to coordinate or terminate replenishment in a defined neural population. A particular variant or pathway state could prolong inward transport or delay extrusion after restoration, leaving ionic or volume recovery incomplete during a maturation process. Normal replenishment is the essential comparator: increased WNK signalling with adequate recovery remains compatible with successful regulation. Developmental baseline also matters. WNK1-dependent inhibitory KCC2 phosphorylation contributed to chloride regulation in immature rodent neurons (Friedel et al., 2015); this does not assign mature-neuron KCC2 physiology to undifferentiated progenitors. The developmental claim is that impaired recovery changes maturation in cells expressing the relevant transport machinery at that stage. Sections 29–31 distinguish the relevant protein-production, cell-state and developmental-timing questions. A renal effect of a variant can motivate this neural comparison without establishing its result.

WNK3 provides a candidate intrinsic route into the coordination of chloride transport. In Xenopus oocyte coexpression experiments, kinase-active WNK3 stimulated NKCC1 and inhibited KCC2, whereas an engineered kinase-inactive construct produced the opposite effects (Kahle et al., 2005). Human variant assays refine the direction: the three missense variants tested by Küry et al. (2022) reduced WNK3 abundance and inhibitory KCC2 Thr1007 phosphorylation in transfected HEK293T cells, while total KCC2 remained unchanged. This result concerns reduced inhibitory phosphorylation, not demonstrated impairment of chloride extrusion. Transport and post-disturbance recovery were not measured in that assay.

Neuronal experiments show that developmental context can change the outcome of WNK3 loss. Lim et al. (2021) introduced WNK3-targeting shRNA on the first day of embryonic rat hippocampal culture. At days 13–15, GABA reversal potential was more negative, membrane-fraction KCC2 Thr1007 phosphorylation was reduced, and total KCC2, total NKCC1 and NKCC1 phosphorylation were unchanged. No significant GABA reversal-potential difference was detected at days 6–8. Intrinsic excitability and synaptic excitation nevertheless increased in the mature cultures. This was knockdown across culture development, not an acute intervention begun in mature neurons, and a more negative GABA reversal potential did not imply uniformly reduced neuronal excitation.

A constitutive knockout produced a different combination of effects. In juvenile male mice, Sinha et al. (2022) found a more positive GABA reversal potential in medial prefrontal layer V pyramidal neurons, alongside increased inwardly rectifying potassium conductance and reduced intrinsic excitability. Assayed cortical WNK1/SPAK/OSR1 and NKCC1/KCC2 phosphorylation showed no significant differences. Thus, chloride-related responses and net excitability can move in different directions, and the hippocampal-culture and cortical-slice results cannot be collapsed into universal chloride loading or unloading. Neither study measured post-load chloride or cell-volume recovery, and neither established a male–female difference in the response to WNK3 disruption.

Renal findings demonstrate that preserved function is possible after WNK3 loss. Oi et al. (2012) found no significant difference in urinary sodium or potassium excretion in adult male knockout mice, including transitions between sodium diets, and no significant reduction in renal NKCC2 or NCC phosphorylation. Blood pressure was lower during sodium restriction, so the absence of salt wasting did not mean every physiological endpoint was unchanged. These excretion and phosphorylation findings constrain an obligatory renal-loss route; they do not infer compensatory work from normal serum chemistry. Shared expression or regulatory activity in kidney and brain does not establish renal mediation of the human neurodevelopmental phenotype.

The Sodium-Struggle proposal is that a specified WNK3 perturbation could alter the coordination or timing of local ionic recovery during development, either intrinsically or in interaction with a defined exposure. Appropriate experimental models would need to separate starting chloride, transport activity, potassium conductance and cell volume from recovery after matched loading, and relate any recovery defect to a subsequent developmental outcome. Preserved recovery during the relevant interval, or developmental effects independent of the proposed recovery change, would count against that route (Section 23.13). Other WNK3-dependent neuronal effects remain alternatives. Any peripheral renal consequence would require its own measurements and could occur in parallel, rather than mediate the neural effect.

NKCC1 cotransports one Na⁺, one K⁺ and two Cl⁻ without directly hydrolysing ATP. Its net direction depends on the combined sodium, potassium and chloride gradients, not on phosphorylation alone. Rising intracellular sodium and chloride can oppose further inward flux, whereas increased extracellular potassium can favour it if the other gradients permit. Sodium entering through NKCC1 can increase Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase work during transport and recovery. Increased ATP turnover need not lower ATP concentration when supply compensates, and ATP depletion cannot be assumed to produce continuing inward NKCC1 flux. The proposed difficulty is a mismatch between transport-associated demand and available supply (Brumback and Staley, 2008).

Primary injury studies support components of this branch but also constrain it. In cultured embryonic mouse cortical neurons exposed to two hours of oxygen-glucose deprivation and reoxygenation, NKCC1 inhibition or deletion preserved sodium homeostasis and ATP, although reduced pump work was not isolated from other protective effects (Chen et al., 2010b). In P8–13 mouse neocortical slices, bumetanide reduced early swelling and chloride accumulation, but did not reduce swelling and worsened chloride accumulation during prolonged deprivation (Takezawa et al., 2023). These findings support context- and time-dependent transporter involvement. They do not demonstrate a self-sustaining mismatch between transport-associated demand and energetic supply after mild recurrent developmental stress.

23.7.2 Developmental exposures and perinatal signalling

Early experience can also change the developmental trajectory of chloride regulation. In male C57BL/6J mice, maternal separation on postnatal days 1–21 delayed the hippocampal GABA transition assessed through calcium imaging and reduced the developmental increase in membrane-associated KCC2. Reduced KCC2 persisted into adolescence, when behavioural differences were also reported (Furukawa et al., 2017). This provides an exposure-to-transport-development precedent; calcium responses and protein localisation are distinct from recovery after a matched chloride load, and the male-only experiment supplies no sex comparison.

Prenatal hypoxia supplies a different, region-specific precedent. Following maternal exposure to 10% oxygen on gestational days 5–20 and subsequent normoxia, rat pups had lower pontine membrane KCC2 at postnatal days 3–4, but not days 0–1. Between-group NKCC1 abundance and NKCC1/KCC2 ratios did not differ significantly. Transporter blockade altered fictive breathing in isolated brainstem preparations, while GABA-A blockade increased respiratory frequency in both groups at days 3–4 (Caravagna et al., 2022). Thus, reduced KCC2 coexisted with continuing net GABAergic restraint in that assay. These neonatal respiratory findings do not measure cortical recovery or adolescent behaviour.

Stress effects need not point towards delayed inhibition. In a different rat protocol, saline-injected pups separated for six hours daily on postnatal days 4–6 showed more hyperpolarising CA1 GABA responses in both sexes. KCC2 immunoreactivity increased in males only, while the bumetanide-sensitive transport contribution decreased in both sexes (Galanopoulou, 2008). This is a protocol-dependent contrast, not a direct replication of the longer mouse separation experiment.

The proposed connection is that an exposure could change chloride regulation during a sensitive window and thereby alter recovery under subsequent demand. Testing that sequence requires distinguishing transporter abundance, membrane localisation and phosphorylation from chloride extrusion, recovery kinetics, GABA driving force and net network inhibition. The studies above motivate this developmental comparison without establishing AVP or renal mediation. A systemic route and a local metabolic route remain alternatives, and preserved recovery after an appropriately matched load would count against the proposed recovery contribution (Sections 3.3, 23.13, and 40.5).

Tyzio et al. (2006) reported a transient inhibitory GABA shift near delivery in fetal and neonatal rat hippocampal preparations. Maternal oxytocin-receptor blockade prevented this shift, while separate chloride-imaging experiments supported an oxytocin-sensitive reduction in neuronal chloride. Receptor blockade also shortened the latency to anoxic depolarisation during oxygen–glucose deprivation in isolated E21 hippocampi. These findings support a protective birth-window mechanism in that preparation; they do not establish a universal mammalian switch or a human developmental outcome.

Positive developmental intervention evidence comes from two distinct rodent models. In valproate-exposed rats and Fmr1-null mice, Tyzio et al. (2014) reported altered CA3 GABA driving force, excitatory GABA responses and increased glutamatergic activity. Maternal bumetanide given one day before delivery shifted juvenile GABA responses toward inhibition and attenuated early vocalisation and network abnormalities. Maternal oxytocin-receptor blockade in otherwise unexposed animals produced related abnormalities. Following criticism of neonatal vocalisations as an autism proxy, the same group reported improved adult social approach in male valproate rats and reduced excess grooming in male Fmr1 mice (Bambini-Junior et al., 2014; Eftekhari et al., 2014). These experiments support a lasting developmental effect of a brief perinatal intervention. They did not measure systemic sodium–volume defence, recovery after matched ionic loading or a selective neuronal mechanism. The original study disclosed commercial and patent interests; independent replication remains important.

The result does not establish a universal birth-associated GABA defect. Shank3B-null mice had increased CA3 glutamatergic activity with preserved GABA driving force and inhibitory action at the tested ages (Chiesa et al., 2019). Independent work found continuing depolarising GABA in normal perinatal rats and AVP-mediated suppression of hippocampal network events through V1a-dependent interneuron activation in rats and neonatal guinea pigs (Spoljaric et al., 2017). Rat GABA driving force was unchanged by AVP. At the tested 10 nM concentration, oxytocin did not suppress rat network events; this dose and endpoint differ from the 2006 chloride experiments. The findings challenge a universal birth-associated inhibitory switch and support a potentially protective AVP mechanism, although protection from injury was not directly tested. This is not a direct replication of the valproate/Fmr1 intervention. Together these findings require model-specific tests of the ionic intermediary and selective rescue, with litter, sex and developmental stage specified. Rodent vocalisation, grooming and social-approach measures are experimental outcomes, not diagnoses of human autism.

23.7.3 Intervention limits and target engagement

Two phase 3 trials found no broad clinical benefit from bumetanide in established ASD. SIGN 1 (ages 7–17) and SIGN 2 (ages 2–6) each enrolled 211 participants, 422 combined. Neither met its week-26 CARS2 primary endpoint, and secondary results did not establish consistent efficacy. SIGN 1 nevertheless reported more Clinical Global Impression responders with bumetanide (22.7% versus 12.4%). Thirst, polyuria and hypokalaemia were more frequent with treatment (Fuentes et al., 2023). These results constrain therapeutic claims. Prenatal initiation and local chloride-recovery and ATP trajectories were not endpoints and require separate mechanistic tests; their omission supplies no evidence that an early recovery disturbance occurred.

Neuronal NKCC1 and renal NKCC2 actions require separate exposure measurements. Bumetanide inhibits human NKCC1A and NKCC2A expressed in Xenopus oocytes (Lykke et al., 2016); mouse experiments implicate restricted passive entry and active blood–brain barrier transport in low brain accumulation (Römermann et al., 2017). Renal diuresis and potassium loss can coexist with uncertain neuronal engagement. Animal brain-tissue measurements do not establish unbound neuronal exposure in treated children. NKCC1 also operates outside neurons, including in the choroid plexus (Section 30). Section 3.3 adds blood-facing endothelial NKCC1 as another potential site of action, distinct from neuronal target engagement. Renal effects could modify compensatory demand depending on losses, intake and downstream conservation; SIGN adverse events do not identify RAAS, AVP or ammoniagenesis as mediators of failed efficacy.

NKCC1 inhibition can change resting chloride and the load to clear, so bumetanide does not selectively distinguish chloride-state from recovery accounts; negative trials do not favour the latter. Appropriate experimental models can test predicted neuronal chloride changes with verified target engagement alongside predicted renal salt, water or potassium handling changes, measuring net balance and compensatory demand separately. Selective interventions with matched initial ionic loads could distinguish recovery kinetics from starting chloride or systemic support. Section 23.13 separates adequate recovery during the causal interval, prevention of the proposed mediator and later downstream rescue.

23.7.4 Metabolic regulation and vascular recovery

Endothelin-1 is a candidate vascular-to-glial signal. Metabolic strain might also impair KCC2 or its potassium driving gradient without increased import. Lactate elevation identifies neither that transport effect nor the direct oxidant-sensitive KCC2 changes described above.

NFAT5 provides an experimentally grounded connection between metabolic stress and chloride handling. In cultured hippocampal neurons, oxygen–glucose deprivation reduced NFAT5 and increased NKCC1; NFAT5 knockdown under normal culture conditions also increased NKCC1 and reduced chloride-sensitive MQAE fluorescence, consistent with increased intracellular chloride. Neuronal binding assays and promoter-reporter experiments in PC12 cells implicated opposing HIF-1α and NFAT5 regulation of NKCC1 (Yang et al., 2019). This supports a molecular connection, not a measured recovery-time defect: the fluorescence was not an absolute chloride calibration, and a selective NKCC1 rescue of the knockdown’s chloride effect was not reported. Experimental separation of NFAT5 ionic-strength sensing from WNK1 volume/crowding responses further shows why intracellular salt content, concentration and cell size need separate assays (Khandwala et al., 2025). Neither experiment establishes the proposed fetal imprint or its direction under mild recurrent dilution.

Because Yang et al. (2019) jointly removed oxygen and glucose, the experiment does not isolate hypoxia. It supplies a local metabolic route without prior systemic sodium–volume disturbance; recovery mediation and systemic initiation remain separate additional claims (Section 23.13).

A separate vascular experiment makes recovery after challenge particularly relevant. Conditional endothelial Nfat5 deletion in adult mice impaired post-ischaemic reperfusion and reduced arterial Kir2.1 expression despite relatively unremarkable baseline findings (Kunze et al., 2024). This supports testing vascular reserve beyond resting measurements. It does not transfer the injury model to ordinary social demand or establish a fetal sodium-mediated pathway; neuronal and endothelial NFAT5 effects require their own causal tests.

23.8 Why a cortical chloride bias matters disproportionately

A cortical chloride disturbance could intersect with KCC2 maturation, glial support, perfusion/redox conditions and the precision demands of inhibitory circuits. The argument concerns developmental timing rather than the highest absolute NKCC1 expression.

Cortical chloride extrusion changes during development, but GABA depolarisation and inhibition are not opposites. KCC2 contributes to chloride regulation, while the functional effect of GABA depends on reversal potential, conductance, location, resting voltage and firing threshold. Depolarising GABA can remain inhibitory, as demonstrated in neonatal neocortex and adult hippocampal parvalbumin interneurons under the respective experimental conditions (Kirmse et al., 2015; Otsu et al., 2020). Recurrent chloride loading or impaired extrusion could therefore alter the timing of inhibitory maturation where the resulting physiological change disrupts circuit control during a specified developmental window.

Perivascular astrocytic water, potassium and metabolic support supply a further interface. Where cellular expansion reduces ECS, fixed K⁺ or glutamate release can produce larger transients during neuronal chloride maturation (Sections 24 and 25).

Together, these conditions could alter sensory precision, oscillatory timing or stability under load while circuits are refined.

The developmental timing of this intersection matters, but there is no single fetal-to-toddler switch shared by all cortical neurons or species. KCC2 regulation, the effect of GABA and PV-circuit maturation must be matched to the region, cell type and developmental stage studied. The proposed ASD relevance is a lasting alteration of circuit calibration during a susceptible window, which cannot be inferred simply from overlap between broad developmental timelines.

23.9 Consequences for inhibitory polarity, calcium duty cycle, and PV-interneuron vulnerability

A chloride rise shifts ECl positively and can shift EGABA, which also reflects bicarbonate permeability. As above, shunting may preserve inhibition; loss of timing precision requires a functional effect, not transporter abundance or reversal potential alone.

An altered excitation–inhibition ratio can itself help preserve circuit output. Antoine et al. (2019) examined somatosensory cortex in Fmr1, Cntnap2, 16p11.2-deletion and Tsc2 mouse models. Feedforward inhibition onto layer 2/3 pyramidal cells was reduced more than excitation, increasing the conductance ratio, yet synaptic depolarisation and spiking were largely preserved. Conductance modelling indicated that the paired changes stabilised depolarisation near spike threshold; whisker-evoked spiking was not increased in the in-vivo comparisons. This is a concrete example of protective compensation within an autism-relevant circuit. It supports distinguishing a changed regulatory setting from failed function, without establishing either an ionic-recovery defect or hidden developmental injury in those preparations.

The additional prediction is that incomplete recovery after repeated demand reduces fidelity or alters development despite initially maintained output. A developmental effect with recovery preserved throughout its causal interval would challenge that mediation; returning a compensatory excitation–inhibition ratio to control need not improve function.

Calcium entry could increase when GABA-related depolarisation reaches the activation range of available voltage-gated channels or relieves Mg²⁺ block at ligand-bound NMDA receptors during excitation. Strong shunting may instead reduce or leave entry unchanged. Shifting EGABA at fixed conductance differs from comparing excitation with and without GABA; Section 26 develops these distinct branches and their evidence (Owens et al., 1996; Kirmse et al., 2015; Staley and Mody, 1992).

PV interneurons are plausible high-demand recipients of local ionic and metabolic stress, but can also be an initiating site of redox dysfunction. In mice, PV-cell-targeted Gclc deletion reduced PV and perineuronal-net labelling and prolonged visual cortical plasticity into young adulthood (Morishita et al., 2015). That experiment provides a direct cellular redox route without requiring prior astrocytic failure. It did not establish chloride, sodium-pump, BH4 or ATP mediation, and reduced PV immunoreactivity should not be equated with PV-cell death.

Intrinsic PV dysfunction and altered glial support are separate routes to fast-spiking timing differences. Either could affect oscillatory precision, sensory gain or load-dependent stability; astrocytic, ionic and metabolic contributions remain conditional.

Oligodendrocytes can likewise be affected through their own recovery, calcium or metabolic support, or initiate a genetic disturbance themselves. Section 23.10 distinguishes developmental myelination from ongoing axonal support.

The local-support mechanism proposed here can coexist with the extracellular OTX2 mechanism in Section 30.4. Evidence for altered inhibitory timing does not identify whether ionic recovery, signal supply, recipient capture or an independent developmental process was responsible.

23.10 Network-level consequences of chloride-weighted physiology

If reduced local reserve persists, its functional consequences could appear in inhibitory timing, axonal support or vulnerability to hyperexcitable transitions. These are the network-level extensions of the preceding cellular account.

PV interneuron vulnerability and gamma timing. PV-mediated inhibition provides a concrete link to network coordination: optogenetic PV inhibition suppressed prefrontal gamma activity in mice, while PV feedback generated gamma-frequency rhythms in slices (Sohal et al., 2009). The preparation-dependent metabolic-challenge recovery and extracellular redox-protection findings in Section 18.1.7 further support testing PV function under constrained local support (Povysheva et al., 2019; Cabungcal et al., 2013). The proposed consequence is impaired inhibitory precision during repeated demand when ionic or metabolic recovery is inadequate. Impaired local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery must mediate the developmental circuit change. A positive EGABA shift may remain inhibitory, and a larger extracellular potassium excursion depends on release, space and clearance together (Sections 23 and 26).

Oligodendrocyte maturation and axonal support. Oligodendrocyte-lineage NKCC1 expression and calcium-sensitive maturation motivate two distinct possibilities: altered myelin construction and impaired adjustment of metabolic support to axonal demand. A recovery disturbance could affect conduction timing through either route, but neuronal GABA responses do not establish oligodendroglial calcium loading, and uniform demyelination is not required.

A genetic initiating route is demonstrated by Cho et al. (2023). Anks1b-deficient mice showed impaired oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination. Oligodendrocyte-lineage deletion reproduced social-preference and sensory-reactivity phenotypes that were not reproduced by the tested neuronal deletions. Rac1 signalling was dysregulated, and prolonged Rac1 stimulation restored myelin basic protein expression in cultured mutant oligodendrocytes. Clemastine treatment improved social preference and callosal myelination in adult mutant mice. The lineage restriction supports glial initiation; the later rescue shows that some measured outcomes remained modifiable. Neither result establishes an earlier ionic or cellular-volume recovery defect as the developmental mediator, and the drug result is not a treatment inference for human autism.

Looser et al. (2024) identify a different, physiological connection. In adult mouse optic nerves, activity-related extracellular K⁺ signalling through oligodendroglial Kir4.1 coupled axonal firing to glial calcium responses, glycolysis and axonal lactate support. Oligodendrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion reduced resting and activity-evoked axonal lactate and altered glucose metabolism. In approximately three-month-old mice, basal axonal ATP and initial ATP-recovery rates were comparable between genotypes, but rebound was modestly incomplete after glucose deprivation with mitochondrial inhibition or after high-frequency stimulation. Adjustment of conduction speed during recovery was also impaired. Bumetanide did not suppress the activity-evoked calcium response in adult oligodendrocytes under the tested conditions. This support mechanism therefore cannot be assigned to NKCC1-mediated loading, and an ATP-recovery result is not itself a measurement of ionic or cellular-volume recovery.

These studies make glial initiation and activity-dependent support concrete but distinct. The proposed intersection is that local recovery difficulty leaves restoration, metabolite supply and axonal conduction out of step after demand. During myelination, that mismatch could alter how activity is supported while circuits are assembled; neither study establishes this developmental sequence.

Neither study shows ANKS1B regulation of Kir4.1 or obligatory metabolic mediation. Direct cytoskeletal or maturation effects could change demand before recovery becomes impaired. Oligodendroglial Kir4.1 deletion also differs from the astrocytic gain-of-function alleles in Section 6.3; shared channel names do not imply shared dysfunction. Protein production is another possible intermediary (Section 29).

Preserved relevant recovery during the developmental effect would limit this glial route. Upstream genetic or pleiotropic drug rescue cannot identify recovery mediation, and late rescue does not establish initiation.

Seizure vulnerability. Weakened GABAergic control, larger potassium or glutamate transients, or delayed recovery could reduce reserve against hyperexcitable transitions. A positive EGABA shift alone does not establish these conditions. The proposed consequence is greater vulnerability under load in relevant subsets, not universal, autism-specific or continuous seizures.

23.11 Candidate Mechanisms of Persistent Recovery Difficulty

Persistence can reflect continuing exposure, delayed repair, developmental regulation or self-maintaining feedback. Candidate amplifiers must outlast normal termination through restored tonicity/perfusion, chloride-sensitive WNK inhibition, potassium-gradient recovery, transporter reset, osmolyte replenishment and antioxidant buffering.

BDNF/TrkB, cytokine and calcium-dependent pathways remain possible modifiers whose effects depend on developmental and injury context. Calpain-mediated KCC2 cleavage provides an experimentally supported component (Puskarjov et al., 2012). A loop in which a measured chloride and conductance state increases calcium entry, calcium activates calpain and KCC2 cleavage further impairs extrusion is plausible, but the complete loop and its persistence have not been demonstrated by those component experiments.

Other proposed persistence modifiers include delayed KCC2 maturation or membrane stabilisation, PNN disruption, thyroid and glucocorticoid signalling, AVP-related water-handling responses, oxidant burden and recurrent network activity. They need not act together or in the same direction at every age.

Either excess import-associated demand or impaired extrusion could interact with glial volume, extracellular potassium, calcium and transporter stability. The branches defined in Section 23.2 remain distinct even if they converge on delayed chloride recovery.

Energy-first, redox-first and KCC2-first paths remain possible. Prolonged recovery alone establishes neither hysteresis nor a self-maintaining state; persistence requires an identified sustaining mechanism after the initiating exposure and relevant extracellular abnormalities have ended. A lasting circuit alteration after physiological recovery is a separate developmental consequence.

23.12 Modifiers of Recovery Thresholds and Persistence

Constitutional factors could modify threshold or persistence within the three-threat route; primary genetic or developmental mechanisms remain alternatives.

Candidate modifiers include antioxidant and mitochondrial reserve, endothelial/glycocalyx or autonomic function, AVP responsiveness, WNK–SPAK/OSR1 susceptibility, KCC2 regulation and maturation, thyroid/glucocorticoid effects, and PV/perineuronal-net resilience. Sex-dependent perfusion defence, stress-hormone escalation, vascular regulation, WNK plasticity and early buffering could modify entry, persistence or recovery without a sex-specific initiating pathology.

Within this proposed recovery route, chromatin and transcriptional-state regulators are considered as gain-and-reset modifiers; primary regulatory effects remain alternative explanations. Where a chloride and conductance change demonstrably raises calcium entry or duty cycle, repeated calcium signals could interact with chromatin state to influence transporter, cytoskeletal or developmental programmes. This would provide one route to heterogeneity of persistence without making chromatin the origin of the chloride change in that route.

23.13 Recovery mediation and interpretive limits

The distinctive claim concerns what fails to recover and how that changes development. This cellular route proposes altered inhibitory maturation, circuit precision and calibration during sensitive windows; it does not equate autism with generic brain injury or a disease-specific chloride lesion. Similar chloride disturbances occur in other conditions. Their relevance here depends on the local recovery disturbance carrying a defined developmental effect, rather than merely accompanying a stress response.

The Ben-Ari–Tyzio programme already links perinatal signalling, chloride regulation and lasting neural outcomes (Tyzio et al., 2014), and Tang et al. (2019) measured chloride-recovery kinetics in human Rett-syndrome neurons. The present account adds a proposed convergence across initiating routes. Comparable resting chloride values can coexist with different recovery responses; altered resting chloride or failure to establish an age-appropriate gradient does not itself demonstrate impaired restoration. Failure of a later bumetanide trial does not favour this account over an earlier developmental chloride mechanism.

The proposed transport branches remain distinct. Increased NKCC1-dependent inward flux can increase sodium-pump demand; reduced KCC2-mediated extrusion or its potassium driving force can impair chloride restoration without increased influx. Organic-osmolyte loss and glial buffering can create other recovery constraints. Regulatory volume decrease during continued hypotonic exposure and restoration after return to isotonic conditions are different phases, and normal volume need not mean restored ionic composition. Serum or CSF ions cannot substitute for the relevant cellular state. Increased work with adequate recovery remains successful compensation.

Systemic initiation and local mediation are separate claims. Oxygen or substrate limitation can constrain local recovery, while a sodium–volume route additionally requires a contribution from tonicity, effective filling, delivery or their regulation. Yang et al. (2019) studied joint oxygen–glucose deprivation, not isolated hypoxia or post-challenge recovery kinetics. That component result cannot establish the entire systemic sequence. Conversely, direct genetic, immune or metabolic initiation need not first produce a systemic deficit.
