The endothelial route predicts altered blood-to-brain ion transfer, changed local extracellular conditions and prolonged neural or glial recovery under specified conditions (Section 3.3). Appropriate developmental models would measure net transfer, permeability, perfusion and recovery separately. Timely selective prevention of the transfer change, with target engagement and other intervention effects assessed, tests its proposed contribution. Preserved recovery despite the transfer change, or an unchanged recovery defect despite preventing that change, would count against the specified mediation. Cellular uptake alone cannot establish net transfer.

The timing proposal predicts different recovery trajectories when a defined exposure overlaps a specified maturation interval (Section 23.7; Section 40.5). Appropriate models would measure recovery after comparable initial ionic perturbations, separately from starting chloride, transporter regulation, GABA reversal potential and net excitability. A sex-modifier claim requires a prespecified sex-by-exposure comparison of recovery trajectories. An adequately precise estimate excluding the predicted sex difference would constrain that modifier; developmental effects despite preserved relevant recovery would instead challenge recovery mediation.

WNK3 supplies an intrinsic comparison between recovery and other neuronal effects (Section 23.7). For a specified variant, cell type and developmental interval, appropriate models would measure the rate and completeness of chloride or volume restoration after comparable initial perturbations, alongside GABA reversal potential and potassium conductance. The predicted recovery change and its direction would be specified beforehand. Timely selective prevention of that change tests its proposed developmental role (Table 2.1). Broad WNK3 rescue alone would not distinguish recovery mediation from its other cellular actions.

The clinical renal proposal predicts that documented salt wasting and its recovery contribute information beyond an infection diagnosis (Section 14.4.2; Section 46.3). Within a prespecified developmental interval, existing records or cohorts could compare similarly ill infants with measured salt wasting against those with preserved conservation, using intake/replacement, output and serial blood/urine measurements where available. Prematurity, illness severity, treatment and sampling require consideration. A sufficiently precise comparison finding no added relationship between the prespecified physiological trajectory and developmental outcome would weaken that clinical prediction. A positive association would still require temporally relevant neural or glial recovery evidence to support the developmental intermediary; ear-fluid resolution remains a separate peripheral endpoint.

The immune comparison illustrates the distinction. Severe maternal inflammation produced fetal cardiovascular abnormalities in one model, whereas IL-17A altered human cerebroid development without systemic circulation (Rounioja et al., 2005; Assir et al., 2026). Failure of verified cardiovascular correction to restore recovery when local correction succeeds would weaken the specified cardiovascular intermediary while leaving local immune initiation possible. Antibody target specificity identifies an initiating mechanism, not recovery mediation. Similarly, prolonged glucose-associated inflammation matters to this account only if it impairs local recovery; inflammatory persistence alone is insufficient (Sections 18.5, 18.6, and 19.7).

Persistent-defence and metabolic-signalling accounts provide important antecedents, including Naviaux’s cell danger response (Section 26.7). Protein production, glial maturation, folate delivery, sterol signalling, channel-associated cytoskeletal effects and neuromodulation offer interacting or independent explanations (Sections 23.10, 26.9, 29, 30, 35.4.4, and 47.1). Recovery may be upstream, downstream or parallel to these processes. Their co-occurrence, or improvement after a broad upstream intervention, does not resolve that causal order. The proposed recovery contribution must explain something beyond a generic stress signature.

Calcium consequences are also conditional. A positive shift in GABA reversal potential need not abolish shunting inhibition or increase calcium entry. Greater entry relative to a more negative reversal potential is not the same comparison as greater entry than during excitation without GABA. Reduced entry under the relevant conditions limits the increased-entry branch, without deciding other ionic or volume routes. Later low calcium responses cannot be attributed to earlier overload without evidence for that earlier event (Section 26).

23.13.1 What would limit the hypothesis

A developmental effect despite adequately demonstrated preservation of relevant local recovery, or despite timely prevention of its necessary disturbance, counts against recovery mediation in that route. An inconclusive null does not establish preserved recovery. Absence of increased NKCC1 influx limits the import-cost branch; normal chloride recovery alone does not establish normal glial or volume recovery. The relevant compartment, developmental interval and claimed disturbance must be specified in advance, rather than reassigned after a negative result. A credible bypass of the required intermediary would challenge universal participation even if recovery contributes elsewhere.

A transient disturbance can leave a lasting developmental consequence after physiology normalises. Normal later biomarkers and failure of late treatment therefore do not settle an earlier causal question, but neither supplies evidence that an earlier disturbance occurred. Peripheral-cell recovery can characterise a peripheral phenotype without establishing neural development. Cell and animal findings must retain their preparation and developmental context when related to autism. These distinctions preserve a testable common-process conjecture without making any single exposure, AVP direction, transporter response or metabolic branch compulsory.

24 Astrocytic osmotic imprinting: volume regulation, osmolyte debt, and extracellular-space constraints

24.1 Astrocytes as candidate volume responders in early sodium instability

Astrocytes bring several of these recovery processes together through ion, water and transmitter handling that links local activity to vascular support. The developmental proposal is that repeated recruitment leaves altered recovery or reserve on a different schedule from systemic defence; plasma sodium alone establishes neither the original brain exposure nor its recovery.

Astrocytes are not the only cells capable of reversible swelling. In acute mouse brain slices, Murphy et al. (2017) observed rapid swelling of hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons alongside astrocytes during substantial reductions in bathing-medium osmolarity; volume recovered when normal medium returned. AQP4 deletion did not abolish swelling. These conditions do not establish responses to mild fetal exposure, but they rule out the categorical premise that neurons cannot swell and astrocytes must accept water on their behalf. Cell type, developmental stage, exposure and compartment must determine the proposed allocation of volume stress.

Intrinsic transporter variation supplies a complementary local entry point. In mammalian expression systems, SLC1A2 Leu85Pro combined impaired EAAT2 glutamate transport with increased anion-channel function, whereas Gly360Ala, classified in that study as a variant of uncertain significance, primarily increased anion-channel function (Kovermann et al., 2025). These findings in a neurodevelopmental/epilepsy cohort make impaired clearance and altered glial ionic handling concrete candidate routes. Their effects on local recovery and ATP demand require separate measurement, as do any developmental effects relevant to autism.

Experimental hyponatraemia provides a physiological comparator. Fujisawa et al. (2016) found impaired gait and memory, reduced hippocampal long-term potentiation and higher extracellular glutamate in rats given desmopressin and a liquid diet, including a group with serum sodium around 121 mmol/L. Cultured mouse astrocytes showed reduced glutamate uptake under low-NaCl culture and assay conditions, with uptake comparable to controls after gradual medium correction. Corrected rats in a separate cohort also performed comparably to controls on gait and memory tests, consistent with possible recovery. Sodium, chloride and tonicity were not independently isolated, and glutamate mediation of the behavioural effects was not established. These results connect extracellular composition with glial transmitter handling. The developmental proposal is that such changes impair local neural/glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery enough to alter circuit formation; that sequence was not tested.

Human findings provide a functional comparison: gait and attention measures were better during normonatraemia in a small within-person study of adults with chronic hyponatraemia (Renneboog et al., 2006). Such later-life recovery does not determine whether exposure during a sensitive developmental interval can leave lasting effects.

The proposed cost is altered recovery or acquired susceptibility after an initially protective response, without requiring primary neuronal injury or chronic hyponatraemia.

24.2 Osmolyte-based volume regulation under hypo-osmotic stress

This branch concerns measured cellular hypotonic exposure: water entry depends on membrane permeability, intracellular solutes and concurrent transport. Plasma sodium or osmolality alone does not establish the local volume change.

Regulatory volume decrease exports intracellular osmoles, allowing water to leave after swelling. Inorganic ions, including K⁺ and Cl⁻, and organic osmolytes can contribute; organic export does not replace ionic efflux as a universal rule. In primary rat cortical astrocytes, LRRC8A knockdown slowed and reduced the tested volume recovery after hypotonic swelling (Formaggio et al., 2019). This establishes a functional role for the volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) in that preparation, not a fixed division of osmotic work in developing human cortex.

Organic-osmolyte release is nevertheless a concrete part of this mechanism. In primary rat astrocytes, LRRC8 subunit manipulations differentiated swelling-activated taurine and myo-inositol release from release of an acidic-amino-acid tracer (Schober et al., 2017). Channel composition therefore influences which solutes leave. Compatible intracellular osmolytes are not necessarily inert outside the cell, and volume regulation can itself alter extracellular signalling. The developmental proposal concerns the balance between protective solute loss, subsequent replenishment and the local consequences of those fluxes.

LRRC8A/SWELL1, an essential subunit of heteromeric volume-regulated anion channels, also participates in adipocyte insulin signalling and GLUT4 recruitment. β-cell LRRC8 chloride current contributes to glucose-stimulated activity and secretion (Zhang et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2018). These tissue-specific links motivate the metabolic susceptibility route in Section 19.7. The adipocyte signalling effect is not interchangeable with channel conductance or established cortical recovery physiology.

The proposed long-term cost begins where measured loss exceeds restoration before the next challenge. Protective volume recovery and complete biochemical recovery are different endpoints. Whether early repeated exposure separates them is the question addressed by osmolyte debt. Section 40.5 distinguishes brain-water adaptation during continuing hyponatraemia from restoration after its resolution.

24.3 Osmolyte debt as a developmental state variable

Osmolyte debt denotes a measured deficit in specified intracellular organic osmolytes relative to an appropriate cell-type and developmental reference after the external challenge has resolved. Content per cell, concentration and cell volume must be separated. A deficit may record previous defence without implying injury, but it must be distinguished from an adaptive steady state or an unrelated developmental difference. The proposed debt becomes functionally important if it predicts altered response or recovery on the next matched challenge. Its contribution to the core requires impaired ionic or volume recovery; a separate signalling effect with adequate recovery would not satisfy that criterion.

Lien et al. (1991) provide the severe-hyponatraemia precedent for slower organic than ionic restoration (Section 23.6). In a separate acute rat experiment reducing plasma osmolality 15–20%, taurine moved from Purkinje cells towards glia. Saline normalisation reversed that redistribution while total cerebellar taurine remained low (Nagelhus et al., 1993). Cellular redistribution and tissue-pool restoration are therefore distinct. Neither exposure establishes the mild-intermittent developmental proposal; cumulative loss requires replenishment to remain insufficient, while adaptation or lower starting content could limit further loss.

Redox defence supplies a separate possible cost of osmotic adaptation. In male rats, total brain glutathione decreased during 72 hours of desmopressin-induced hyponatraemia and returned towards control after slow correction. Hypo-osmotic adaptation also depleted glutathione and taurine in rat C6 glioma and human SK-N-SH neuroblastoma cells; subsequent peroxide exposure increased cytolytic injury in SK-N-SH cells but not significantly in C6 cells (Clark et al., 1996). These findings connect adaptation with susceptibility to a further oxidative challenge. They do not isolate glutathione from concurrent solute changes or establish a sex difference in brain-water recovery.

Lower organic content need not increase swelling: starting volume, inorganic replacement, permeability and regulation determine the response. The proposed cost is increased restoration work or altered tolerance of renewed load, not ATP demand inferred from the deficit alone.

The prediction is reduced tolerance or slower recovery during repeated, matched challenges in the specified cells, even if resting function is adequate. Normal recovery with adequate measurement precision, or restoration of the proposed osmolyte deficit without the predicted functional improvement, would weaken this branch. Chronic swelling at rest is not required.

24.3.1 Renal and local substrate modifiers

Systemic substrate availability could modify osmolyte restoration alongside local synthesis and transport. The conditional renal route in Sections 14.9 and 33 asks whether a specified acid-base or potassium disturbance increases renal glutamine utilisation enough, and for long enough, to change the substrate environment supporting neural or glial recovery. Renal extraction, circulating concentration, blood-brain exchange and brain-cell metabolism are successive, distinct links. A renal response could be fully accommodated by other tissues, leaving neural substrate availability and recovery intact. The nephron proposal therefore remains independent of a universal low-glutamine/high-glutamate/high-ammonia profile.

Human findings motivate compartment-specific investigation. Shimmura et al. (2011) found higher platelet-poor plasma glutamate and lower glutamine in 23 drug-naïve autistic boys and adolescents aged 8–17 years compared with 22 male controls. This selected sample had IQ scores above 70. These peripheral observations identify a substrate pattern to investigate, without measuring its renal origin or the substrate available to brain cells.

In a separate postmortem series spanning ages 8–29 years, seven autistic donors had 34% lower left anterior-cingulate kidney-type glutaminase (KGA) protein than 13 controls (p = .007). Absolute tissue glutamate (p = .75) and glutamine (p = .11) differences were nonsignificant, while the Glu/Gln ratio was lower (p = .022; Shimmura et al., 2013). Kidney-type names an enzyme isoform present in brain tissue, not a renal source. Protein abundance, metabolite pools and their ratio are distinct from enzyme activity and metabolic flux; neither study paired blood and brain measurements within the same participants.

The postmortem finding was selective among the proteins examined: glutamine synthetase, liver-type glutaminase, glutamate dehydrogenases 1 and 2, GFAP and neuron-specific enolase did not differ significantly. KGA did not correlate with age or postmortem interval, and excluding the donor treated with valproate and topiramate retained the group difference (p = .015; Shimmura et al., 2013). These checks narrow some alternatives without establishing equivalence or excluding agonal effects. Five of seven autistic donors died by drowning, compared with one of thirteen controls, and no donor tissue-pH control was reported.

The positive proposal is that reduced local glutamine breakdown could conserve substrate during altered ionic or substrate conditions. A similar protein pattern could instead reflect substrate-constrained metabolism or intrinsic regulation, with agonal hypoxia remaining a separate explanation. In appropriate experimental models, measuring glutamine supply, cell-specific utilisation and ionic or volume recovery together could distinguish successful adaptation from a limitation that delays recovery. Selective restoration of substrate availability would support a substrate-limited recovery mechanism if the predicted local recovery deficit also improved. Aggregate tissue concentrations alone neither demonstrate that compensatory work occurred nor exclude independently evidenced compensation. The renal-to-neural extension still requires the successive links specified above; lower brain KGA protein does not establish them.

24.4 AQP4 Abundance and Perivascular Localisation

AQP4 provides a second candidate interface between water movement and later vulnerability. It is enriched in astrocytic perivascular end-feet, where localisation can influence exchange geometry. Its expression, membrane distribution and contribution to water flux are distinct measurements. In mouse slices, AQP4 deletion did not prevent acute swelling, but increased astrocytic swelling when medium osmolarity was reduced by 40%, with no such difference at a 17% reduction (Murphy et al., 2017). AQP4 can therefore contribute to limiting swelling without being required for water entry; its role depends on the challenge.

AQP4 polarity denotes domain-specific enrichment and can change without reduced total abundance. Its effects on exchange geometry and recovery depend on function, not localisation alone.

Repeated swelling during end-foot maturation could leave altered AQP4 localisation and later function. Persistence of that exposure-to-redistribution link remains proposed.

Kir4.1-mediated potassium conductance supplies a related interface, but shared localisation with AQP4 does not establish obligatory functional coupling or impaired K⁺ clearance.

The hypothesis therefore predicts that altered AQP4 localisation could redistribute water movement and affect K⁺ clearance dynamics or the spatial precision of vascular signalling. These consequences require separate testing: experimental solute-removal effects depend on both the AQP4 perturbation and the tracer, and do not establish obligatory Kir4.1 dysfunction or altered OTX2 delivery (Bojarskaite et al., 2024).

24.5 Glial signalling and support during recovery

Glial buffering can connect local ionic or volume conditions with circuit function through metabolic support, extracellular signalling and vascular recruitment. ATP used to restore gradients and ATP available to receptors are distinct quantities. The proposed developmental connection is that impaired local recovery changes the support available during later demand, influencing circuit refinement when compensation is insufficient. Sections 23 and 25–30 explain related component physiology; the following subsections connect the volume and osmolyte accounts above to testable later consequences.

24.5.1 Purinergic signalling during recovery

Osmotic challenge can recruit extracellular ATP signalling. Cultured astrocytes exposed to a 20% reduction in osmolarity released more ATP after 15 minutes; Aqp4 deletion abolished that increase. Separate cortical-slice experiments implicated P2 receptors in part of the calcium response (Thrane et al., 2011). This supplies a measured connection between osmotic challenge and extracellular signalling, while leaving the relation between pump expenditure and ATP release to be established.

ATP availability reflects release, extracellular breakdown and accessible volume, while its effects depend on receptor responsiveness. Altered ATP or adenosine timing could consequently change support during recovery without an intracellular ATP shortage. Conversely, additional restoration work can be compensated without abnormal extracellular signalling. The proposed effect on refinement depends on how these changes alter local recovery and subsequent circuit activity.

24.5.2 Glial buffering regime and ECS geometry

Purinergic signalling can support volume regulation. In adult mouse retinal Müller glia, ATP prevented barium-associated swelling during a substantial hypotonic challenge; P2Y1 antagonism or IP3R2 deletion removed that protection (Lipp et al., 2009; Section 26.7). Cortical osmotic calcium responses also vary by astrocytic compartment and challenge magnitude (Eilert-Olsen et al., 2019). These experiments identify protective signalling and local responsiveness that could modify recovery capacity. Both neurons and astrocytes can swell, so the cell bearing the relevant work or water load requires identification (Section 24.1).

Where measured neuronal or astrocytic water loading narrows extracellular space, a given local solute release can produce a larger concentration excursion. Its duration depends separately on diffusion, uptake and removal (Section 25). A buffering constraint arises if restoration of volume or local solute handling remains inadequate before renewed activity; additional transport work alone establishes neither water loading nor reduced reserve.

Altered end-foot geometry or water handling could delay extracellular-space restoration. Coupling might spread that burden through a network, but neither reduced reserve nor a wider tissue-state change follows from one swollen cell.

ECS compression is a further possible consequence, with concentration amplification distinct from diffusion and removal changes (Dmytrenko et al., 2013; Section 25).

24.5.3 Astrocyte-neuron support coupling strain

A separate circuit experiment illustrates the importance of adequate purinergic support. IP3R2-deficient mice had lower extracellular ATP in medial prefrontal cortex, whereas cultured astrocyte intracellular ATP was not detectably reduced. ATP-directed rescue of social and inhibitory-transmission endpoints depended on P2X2 receptors; repetitive behaviours were not rescued (Wang et al., 2021b; Section 26.7). This demonstrates a signalling contribution to circuit function in that genetic model, without an experimentally imposed osmotic challenge or a detected reduction in cultured astrocyte intracellular ATP.

The recovery hypothesis adds a specific connection: preceding ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty changes glial signalling, metabolic resupply or transmitter handling enough to constrain subsequent neuronal recovery. Replenishment after adaptive solute loss provides another possible demand on recovery capacity (Sections 24.2 and 24.3). If compensation is insufficient, reduced support flexibility could limit synaptic maintenance during clustered use. The developmental extension requires that support change to carry an effect during the relevant circuit-building interval. The hyponatraemia experiments in Section 24.1 provide a related transmitter-handling comparator.

24.5.4 Astrocyte-mediated constraints on neurovascular precision

The proposed changes in osmolyte replenishment and end-foot organisation become functionally consequential if unfinished astrocytic recovery reduces the spatial or temporal precision of support during subsequent demand.

Delayed K⁺ clearance, altered calcium-signal spread and impaired flow matching to neural demand are distinct candidate consequences; one does not identify the others.

Comparing brief and sustained demand can test the timing of vascular support.

Astrocytes can contribute selectively to vascular recruitment during sustained demand. In awake mice, suppressing astrocyte Ca²⁺ signals reduced late penetrating-arteriole dilation during 30-second whisker stimulation while sparing the response to 5-second stimulation (Institoris et al., 2022). This establishes a demand-duration-dependent vascular component. Altered end-foot geometry, compartment-specific calcium signalling or endothelial redox regulation could change that contribution and make delivery less well matched to repeated activity (Sections 16.8 and 24.4).

The proposed lasting consequence requires this delivery change to impair local ionic or cellular-volume recovery during development. Where limited delivery combines with incomplete recovery, repeated activity could exceed local reserve and prolong the interval before normal function returns. Resting perfusion alone would not identify such a temporal mismatch, and the acute dilation experiment does not itself establish retained impairment.

Altered water handling without the predicted K⁺-clearance or vascular effect would weaken that functional extension. The proposed connection is that unfinished recovery constrains subsequent support, rather than every glial response representing lost precision.

24.5.5 State-dependent unmasking and slow recovery

Clustered demands could expose reduced reserve that is inconspicuous at rest. The predicted signature is incomplete restoration of a specified local ionic or cellular-volume variable before the next challenge, accompanied by a changed response to comparable demand. A support change supplies a possible mechanism for that delayed restoration. Transport work and water loading can contribute through different routes; altered ATP signalling is a candidate contributor rather than a substitute for the recovery measurement.

Recovery can outlast fast synaptic signalling because gradients, cell volume, extracellular geometry and metabolic reserve follow different trajectories. “Ion-energetic debt” denotes additional restoration work relative to available capacity, not every chloride shift or purinergic response. Adequate compensation can restore prompt function. A persistent physiological imprint requires evidence that a specified disturbance or acquired support change survives the initiating episode. Section 25 develops the physical extracellular-space gain mechanism, separating concentration amplification from changes in diffusion or removal.

25 Extracellular-Space Compression as a Gain Mechanism

Net cellular water loading could add an extracellular consequence to the ionic recovery mechanisms in Section 23 and the volume responses developed in Section 24. Increased transporter flux or ATP turnover alone does not establish such loading.

Where net intracellular osmole gain produces water loading, astrocytic or neuronal expansion can reduce accessible extracellular space (ECS). Astrocytes are central participants in ion and water handling, but a glia-first sequence is a candidate configuration, not a necessary consequence of increased ATP turnover. Mouse-slice experiments found rapid, reversible hypo-osmotic swelling of both pyramidal neurons and astrocytes (Murphy et al., 2017). The proposed gain mechanism therefore requires cell-specific volume measurements alongside extracellular volume fraction; it cannot assign the burden to astrocytes from plasma sodium or transporter expression alone.

For a fixed local amount of released solute, less accessible extracellular volume can increase concentration. Tortuosity and removal need not change in parallel: experimental extracellular-volume reductions have occurred without an increase in tortuosity (Dmytrenko et al., 2013). The proposed gain mechanism must therefore distinguish concentration amplification from altered diffusion, uptake or loss from the region. Its physiological consequence depends on the measured concentration time course and the solute involved.

Concentration amplification could feed back into the chloride–calcium sequence. Larger local K⁺ or glutamate excursions may favour depolarisation or NMDA-receptor recruitment, depending on the measured concentration and circuit state; ATP and proton transients have their own receptor and pH-dependent effects. A more concentrated fixed amount of solute does not automatically require more total transport work. The energetic amplification prediction requires additional flux, altered transport efficiency or recurrent activity to be demonstrated. This preserves extracellular-space compression as a possible gain stage while separating signal amplitude, signal duration and ATP cost.

26 Calcium Signalling in a Chloride-Weighted Ionic Neighbourhood

This section separates voltage-dependent neuronal calcium entry, sodium–calcium exchange and extrusion, ER–mitochondrial handling, glial calcium and purinergic signalling, and intrinsic channel-associated developmental effects. The findings below are read by cell type, compartment, stimulus and developmental stage. Chloride-related entry and glial swelling-to-calcium routes have different conditions; neither establishes the other. Sections 23–25 supply the chloride, cell-volume and extracellular-space foundations, while Section 27 develops energetic support.

26.1 Calcium findings in autism research

Calcium regulation is one route by which impaired ionic recovery could affect developing circuits. Calcium findings in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) models are heterogeneous in direction, cellular compartment and developmental stage. Day-100 cortical excitatory neurons derived from three autistic NRXN1α+/− donors showed more frequent, longer and larger spontaneous Ca²⁺ transients than those from five control donors, alongside transcriptomic enrichment of voltage-gated calcium-channel pathways (Avazzadeh et al., 2019). In contrast, early cortical cultures from six idiopathic-ASD donors showed fewer spontaneous somatic calcium transients than five control lines, with reduced multielectrode-array spiking in most ASD lines (DeRosa et al., 2018). These are different preparations and endpoints, not opposite outcomes of one matched experiment. In 22q11.2-deletion-derived cortical neurons, reduced evoked calcium responses were linked to depolarised resting voltage and reduced calcium-channel availability (Khan et al., 2020; Section 26.4).

A stage-dependent split is especially informative. In two idiopathic-ASD and two control iPSC lines, ATP-evoked peak calcium responses were larger before differentiation, whereas four-week differentiated neurons showed smaller responses to ATP but larger responses to KCl and the group-I metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonist DHPG (AlShawaf et al., 2025). The stimuli were 100 μM ATP, 25 mM KCl and 200 μM DHPG. This small-line study shows why developmental stage and stimulus must be specified; it does not identify chloride as the mediator.

Store-release studies identify another component. Primary skin fibroblasts from fragile X and TSC1/TSC2 syndrome donors showed depressed ATP-evoked and photoreleased-IP3-evoked calcium signals; elementary-event measurements in selected fragile X and TSC1 lines also showed impaired release (Schmunk et al., 2015). A subsequent screen found smaller ATP-evoked, ionomycin-normalised responses in most sporadic-ASD fibroblast lines, although some overlapped controls and one high-response outlier was excluded from the principal comparison (Schmunk et al., 2017). These peripheral-cell findings preserve a cross-diagnosis store-signalling signal without demonstrating the same defect in developing neurons.

Cultured astrocytes from TSC surgical tissue showed fewer calcium-responsive cells after ATP, glutamate or DHPG stimulation, reduced store-operated calcium entry, lower basal mitochondrial calcium and reduced ATP-evoked mitochondrial uptake (Romagnolo et al., 2024). Reserve respiratory capacity was also reduced, while ATP-linked respiration did not differ detectably. The calcium-culture comparison used TSC tissue from patients aged 3–26 years and control tissue from 12–16-week gestations. It therefore links glial calcium handling with metabolic reserve in this preparation, while age, epilepsy and culture context limit attribution specifically to autism.

Dopaminergic cells differentiated from deciduous-tooth stem cells from three autistic and three comparison children showed higher endoplasmic-reticulum (ER)-associated and lower mitochondrial calcium signals. During differentiation, 1 μM melatonin improved mitochondrial calcium, ATP and neurite-outgrowth endpoints; receptor and IP3R antagonism blocked relevant effects (Dong et al., 2023). This supplies a positive pharmacological bridge between organelle calcium distribution and cellular development in a small dental-stem-cell model. It does not establish prior sodium loading or clinical efficacy. Together, these studies make compartment-specific calcium regulation a strong testing ground for the proposed ionic-environment mechanism, without making opposite calcium directions evidence for a common cause.

26.2 Alternative explanations and ionic conditions

Channel/excitability defects, receptor or ER-store pathology, mitochondrial dysfunction and primary calciumopathies can explain different findings. The additional question is whether altered ionic conditions change calcium machinery that is otherwise functional.

Incomplete chloride recovery, additional sodium handling or altered glial/extracellular conditions could change voltage histories and calcium clearance. A calcium phenotype might then arise from the ionic environment without an intrinsic channel lesion; weakened inhibition and increased entry are conditional intermediates.

26.3 Calcium duty-cycle shift in a chloride-weighted ionic neighbourhood

The calcium-entry hypothesis concerns how long and how often a defined membrane compartment occupies states that permit calcium influx during matched activity. A positive shift in EGABA changes the voltage towards which GABAA current drives that compartment; it does not itself reduce GABAA conductance or remove shunting. Strong GABA conductance can stabilise a depolarised voltage below the relevant calcium-channel activation range and suppress excitatory excursions. Increased entry is predicted where the resulting voltage history, channel availability and timing of excitation favour additional calcium current.

Time spent in prespecified calcium-permissive membrane states is a voltage-based proxy for calcium duty cycle, not a measurement of calcium entry. Channel activation and availability are graded and time dependent, so the proxy requires channel-specific validation. Calcium current, integrated entry, concentration transients and clearance remain distinct endpoints. Section 23.13 summarises the conditional calcium interpretation and its limits.

In cultured hippocampal neurons, integrated calcium fluorescence during depolarising GABA paired with postsynaptic spiking exceeded that during hyperpolarising GABA but did not differ significantly from postsynaptic spiking alone (Balena et al., 2010). That result illustrates the need for the matched comparator; it does not demonstrate equivalence or an additional calcium burden relative to activity without GABA.

Earlier excess entry could recruit later changes in channels, extrusion or organelle buffering, but that compensatory sequence requires the earlier phase to be documented. Reduced responses can instead reflect shunting, channel inactivation, receptor/store defects, connectivity or a primary lesion. Opposite findings cannot retrospectively confirm one earlier burden.

26.4 Depolarisation-driven Ca²⁺ entry under altered GABA polarity

Depolarising GABA can recruit voltage-gated calcium entry in particular immature neuronal preparations. In embryonic and neonatal rat neocortical slices, GABAA receptor activation produced depolarisation and calcium rises through voltage-gated channels (Owens et al., 1996). This establishes a positive mechanism when GABA-driven voltage reaches an available channel activation range. In contrast, depolarising GABA inhibited network activity and recruited voltage-gated calcium signals inefficiently in P3–4 mouse neocortex in vivo under anaesthesia (Kirmse et al., 2015). Depolarising GABA conductance also suppressed an NMDA-mediated synaptic component in adult rat dentate granule cells, although calcium was not imaged in that experiment (Staley and Mody, 1992). The relevant question is whether local voltage, conductance, channel availability and coincident excitation jointly permit additional calcium influx.

The proposed chloride-to-calcium bridge consequently has opposing prospective predictions. Entry may increase when depolarisation is sufficient and the conductance permits the required voltage excursion; it may decrease when shunting suppresses excitatory recruitment or sustained depolarisation reduces channel availability. Spontaneous, KCl-evoked and DHPG-evoked calcium responses probe different processes and cannot independently establish this GABA-mediated sequence. In human 22q11.2-deletion neuronal models, depolarised resting voltage reduced evoked calcium responses through voltage-dependent channel inactivation, without a corresponding intrinsic defect in the measured voltage-clamped calcium-channel currents (Khan et al., 2020). That result supports an operating-voltage mechanism but does not establish chloride mediation or earlier calcium overload. A channel-inactivation explanation requires the measured voltage-dependent loss of availability, not a reduced response alone.

26.5 Sodium gradients, NCX strain, and Ca²⁺ clearance

Calcium clearance provides a distinct conditional branch. Increased NKCC1-mediated inward transport adds sodium-handling work, but Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity may preserve the sodium gradient despite that added flux. An NCX consequence therefore requires a measured change in local sodium gradients, membrane voltage or calcium conditions. Where the electrochemical driving force for forward-mode NCX is reduced, calcium extrusion may slow; reversal requires the relevant combined gradients and voltage, not NKCC1 activity alone.

In reduced suprachiasmatic-nucleus preparations from 18–25-day-old rats, removing extracellular Na⁺ slowed the fast component of somatic calcium clearance after high-K⁺ depolarisation approximately threefold (Wang et al., 2015). In acute mouse slices, NMDA evoked sodium increases and local calcium signals in neocortical astrocyte processes; NCX blockers reduced the calcium signal, and modelling supported sodium-driven reversal. Hippocampal astrocytes lacked the corresponding NMDA-evoked sodium response (Ziemens et al., 2019). In solitary astrocytes cultured from neonatal rat visual cortex, mechanical stimulation increased sodium and calcium, while pharmacological results supported a contribution of reverse NCX to calcium signalling and glutamate release (Reyes et al., 2012). These are distinct, positive component mechanisms. Sodium-free substitution, NMDA application and mechanical stimulation do not establish NCX reversal after a modest developmental increase in NKCC1 flux. That extension requires the local sodium, calcium and voltage measurements specified above.

Where calcium flux increases, PMCA, SERCA and the sodium pump supporting exchange could add to ATP turnover. Slower clearance may instead reflect impaired transport. Calcium flux, pump work and ATP concentration therefore remain distinct; preserved sodium gradients with reduced calcium entry would not support the same energetic prediction (Section 27).

26.6 ER and mitochondrial buffering responses

Increased entry or reduced extrusion could shift handling towards ER and mitochondria, changing store filling, release or coupling. Primary receptor, ER and mitochondrial defects can produce similar endpoints, so a compensatory interpretation requires the preceding entry/extrusion change.

The proposed route links ionic-recovery difficulty to increased calcium-handling work and later organelle change. A subsequent ROS increase is another step; reduced mitochondrial calcium alone does not establish earlier overload.

After oxygen–glucose deprivation and reoxygenation in cultured astrocytes, NKCC1 inhibition or deletion reduced mitochondrial calcium accumulation and dysfunction; reverse-NCX inhibition attenuated a sustained calcium rise during a separate severe hypoxic challenge (Kintner et al., 2007). These injury results establish consequential transport-dependent loading, not the developmental sequence. A further neural/glial-to-vascular redox effect could constrain local support through the corridor in Section 16.8, but altered pump work, ATP, ROS and cysteine remain separate steps.

26.7 Astrocyte calcium signalling and osmotic stress

Astrocytes provide a measured bridge from osmotic challenge to calcium signalling. In adult mouse cortical slices, reducing bath osmolarity from 300 to 240 mOsm/L increased Ca²⁺ activity most prominently in subpial and perivascular endfeet. IP3R2 deletion strongly suppressed those endfoot responses but spared the response in fine processes. Dystrophin deficiency, which disrupts AQP4 anchoring, attenuated endfoot responses. TRPV4 blockade reduced the relative increase in spike rate without reducing the increase in integrated calcium-fluorescence signal, and also altered baseline activity (Eilert-Olsen et al., 2019). The same study detected no difference between IP3R2-deficient mice and controls in brain water accumulation after water intoxication; a 10% reduction in bath osmolarity also failed to elicit the calcium response seen with the larger challenge. These findings identify a compartment- and exposure-dependent response, while calcium signalling and regulation of total brain water remain distinct endpoints. Whether astrocytes carry an earlier recovery burden than neurons must be established in the relevant developmental preparation.

A direct volume-regulatory result comes from retinal Müller glia. In slices from adult mice, a solution at 60% of control osmolarity left wild-type somatic size approximately stable for four minutes, whereas IP3R2 deletion or intracellular calcium chelation permitted rapid swelling. ATP prevented barium-associated swelling in wild-type preparations but failed in IP3R2-deficient cells (Lipp et al., 2009). Glial calcium can therefore participate in maintaining cellular volume during an osmotic challenge. The retinal soma-size assay and cortical endfoot calcium assay establish complementary components; they do not establish the same volume-recovery defect across brain regions.

The hypothesis is that recurrent swelling and incomplete recovery alter glial calcium recruitment, local purinergic signalling or transporter organisation in a defined ionic neighbourhood. Persistent changes in anchoring or transporter localisation remain proposed intermediates. A separate causal circuit result strengthens the case for testing this route: IP3R2-null mice and mice with astrocyte-specific deletion induced at postnatal day 60 showed reduced social approach and increased repetitive behaviours (Wang et al., 2021b). Extracellular ATP fell, whereas cultured astrocyte intracellular and total ATP showed no detected difference. ATP or its stable analogue improved social and inhibitory-transmission endpoints; P2X2-receptor knockdown prevented these effects, and repetitive behaviour was not rescued. Thus, impaired astrocyte calcium signalling can alter purinergic support of inhibitory transmission and behaviour without demonstrated intracellular energy depletion. The adult conditional manipulation establishes circuit influence, not prenatal osmotic initiation. Connecting this positive glial result to Sodium Struggle requires the specified local ionic or volume-recovery difficulty to precede and mediate the calcium–purinergic change; an IP3R2 signalling defect alone does not establish that sequence.

Naviaux’s CDR model emphasises extracellular ATP-related signalling and mitochondrial adaptation in persistent defence (Naviaux, 2026a,b). The IP3R2 result shows why excessive extracellular ATP is not a universal requirement. Cellular ATP supply and turnover, extracellular release/removal, receptor responsiveness and concentration changes from altered volume are distinct. Sodium Struggle additionally proposes recovery difficulty changing these signalling conditions, or purinergic change constraining recovery; a developmental effect with adequate relevant ionic and volume recovery throughout the causal interval would challenge obligatory recovery mediation.

This glial swelling-to-calcium route is distinct from neuronal GABA-to-calcium recruitment. Evidence for one does not establish the other, and a positive astrocytic finding cannot rescue a failed neuronal prediction in the same test.

26.8 Extracellular-space compression and network Ca²⁺ dynamics

Net cellular expansion can amplify a fixed solute release by reducing accessible ECS. Altered tortuosity, removal or persistence is a separate consequence (Dmytrenko et al., 2013; Section 25).

The positive physiological precedents are specific. In P4–7 rat hippocampal slices, extracellular volume fraction was 0.41 ± 0.01 in control conditions and 0.17 ± 0.02 after a 90-mOsm reduction. In low-Mg²⁺ solution containing 4-aminopyridine, reductions of 40 and 90 mOsm increased CA3 epileptiform-event frequency by approximately 24% and 40%, respectively (Kilb et al., 2006). In rat CA1, lowering osmolality caused or enhanced synchronous bursts despite blockade of chemical synaptic transmission (Dudek et al., 1990). This was conditional on the preparation: a later CA1 protocol with normal extracellular Ca²⁺ found that 10–20% dilution enhanced synaptic activity but did not generate nonsynaptic bursts (Bikson et al., 2002). In mouse CA1 slices, hypo-osmotic swelling recruited NMDA-receptor-dependent slow inward currents within about one minute. Increased event frequency was detected with a 5% osmolarity reduction in Mg²⁺-free recording solution; a separate 40% dilution experiment retained enhanced firing with Mg²⁺ present (Lauderdale et al., 2015). These acute experiments establish volume-sensitive excitability under defined conditions, not chronic calcium burden or a developmental pathway to autism.

Larger K⁺, glutamate or ATP transients could increase depolarisation, NMDA recruitment or burst-related calcium entry; their duration depends on transport and uptake. Repeated recovery difficulty could thereby alter synchrony and neuron–astrocyte coupling without a lesion in every calcium component. A glia-first order remains one candidate developmental extension of these acute findings.

26.9 Genetic effects on calcium signalling and interactions with an altered ionic environment

Calcium-pathway variants can initiate developmental changes directly or modify a separately demonstrated ionic disturbance. In Timothy syndrome, CACNA1C p.Gly406Arg markedly impaired voltage-dependent channel inactivation, sustaining inward calcium current; patient-derived cortical neurons also showed altered calcium signalling, activity-dependent gene expression and differentiation (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011). ASD-associated CACNA1D p.Ala749Gly and p.Gly407Arg produced gain-of-function gating in expression systems (Pinggera et al., 2015). These are allele-specific findings: other neurodevelopmental CACNA1C variants produced loss, gain or no detected change in the tested channel properties (Rodan et al., 2021). ATP2B2 encodes the calcium-extruding pump PMCA2. A seven-person series with rare heterozygous ATP2B2 variants included neurodevelopmental presentations with autism; expression of the identified variants altered calcium handling in both loss- and gain-of-function directions (Poggio et al., 2023). Increased entry and impaired extrusion are therefore important candidate mechanisms, but neither direction can be assigned from a gene name alone.

An ion channel can also influence dendritic development through its associated signalling machinery. Krey et al. (2013) observed activity-dependent dendritic retraction in Timothy-syndrome rodent models and patient-derived neurons. In rat neurons, the Timothy-syndrome CaV1.2 channel still promoted retraction when additional pore mutations prevented calcium permeation through that channel. Gem overexpression and inhibition of RhoA signalling prevented retraction in the tested preparations. These experiments identify a channel-associated route to cytoskeletal change that cannot be reduced to excessive calcium entry through the mutant channel. They do not establish independence from every ionic process, and they did not test the defined post-challenge recovery intermediary. The measured endpoint was dendritic development, not the complete human autism phenotype. This comparison strengthens the distinction between an ion-channel mutation and the particular physiological process through which it acts.

For this channel-associated route, the additional Sodium-Struggle claim is that impaired local recovery contributes to dendritic change. Retraction with adequate recovery throughout the causal interval would weigh against that mediation. RhoA-directed rescue alone cannot exclude an upstream recovery contribution; the presence of an ion-channel lesion does not identify the mechanism carrying its developmental effect.

Receptor-variant association and receptor function also need to be distinguished. OXTR R376G was found in 6/132 ASD participants and 2/248 controls in a Japanese study (OR 5.83, 95% CI 1.16–29.33; Ma et al., 2013). This small association sample requires replication. The variant-specific functional findings below provide genetic entry points into altered receptor modulation, but do not establish uniformly weakened oxytocin buffering, an AVP/oxytocin imbalance or impaired developmental recovery.

Receptor and store-release findings need the same precision. In transfected cells, OXTR R376G reduced the calcium response to 100 nmol/L oxytocin; its IP3 reduction was significant at 5–30 seconds but not across the complete three-minute comparison (Ma et al., 2013). Another rare variant, R150S, increased oxytocin sensitivity and calcium mobilisation in vitro (Liu et al., 2024). The RYR2 candidate signal from a 41-child ASD CNV study involved an inherited duplication containing additional genes, without a measured channel-function direction (Soueid et al., 2016). A 2025 preprint reported cardiac calcium leak and elevated resting neuronal cytosolic calcium in hiPSC-derived cells from one RYR2 R169P carrier with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ASD. S107 improved the cardiac leak and resting neuronal cytosolic-calcium endpoints. Comparison with a separate healthy control, without a corrected R169P isogenic line, supports a preliminary signal but does not isolate variant causality, demonstrate clinical benefit or establish sodium–volume mediation (Colombani et al., 2025). Within a demonstrated altered ionic baseline, a functionally established gain-of-function calcium-channel allele could increase the consequence of a given depolarisation, a loss-of-function PMCA2 allele could reduce extrusion reserve, and allele-specific OXTR or RYR2 effects could change store recruitment. These are conditional interactions, not evidence that an ionic disturbance precedes the genetic effect. In 22q11.2-deletion-derived neurons, the measured link was from altered resting voltage to reduced calcium-channel availability, with a specific genetic contribution involving DGCR8 (Khan et al., 2020). Chloride elevation and a preceding high-calcium workload were not established. The strong genetic signal makes convergence testable; demonstrating the proposed recovery intermediary remains a separate requirement.

26.10 Integrated physiological synthesis

The integrated proposal is that incomplete ionic or volume recovery changes the operating conditions of otherwise functional calcium machinery during maturation. Chloride-related voltage shifts can increase entry only when excitation, conductance and channel availability permit it; shunting may preserve inhibition or reduce entry instead.

Altered NCX clearance, organelle redistribution, glial calcium responses and ECS amplification are separate branches. Their conditions differ, so one positive result cannot explain every calcium phenotype or establish the others.

Adequate recovery during the developmental interval would challenge this intermediary. Primary calcium-pathway defects remain alternative or interacting causes; heterogeneous calcium findings do not establish common initiation.
