This is not an established common-ASD allele association. Ppargc1a deletion in mice lowered cardiac ATP and reduced the isolated heart’s ability to increase work during chemical or electrical stimulation (Arany et al., 2005). Different genes provide a functional comparison of supply and reserve. The Sodium Struggle prediction is that a specified energetic limitation delays local ionic recovery under demand; neither experiment establishes that mediation in ASD.
Vascular support and responsiveness ASD-associated CUL3 haploinsufficiency has a direct neuronal comparison: a mouse model altered RhoA signalling, cytoskeletal dynamics and cortical development (Amar et al., 2021). The hypertension-associated exon-9-deletion protein CUL3Δ403–459 impairs WNK ubiquitylation; corresponding knock-in mice accumulate renal WNK/SPAK proteins and develop hypertension (Schumacher et al., 2015). A distinct hypertension-associated CUL3 exon-9 deletion reduced endothelial NO production in mouse cells and impaired relaxation in selected arterial beds. Endothelial-mutant mice also showed salt-sensitive hypertension after uninephrectomy and high-salt feeding (Wu et al., 2022). Same gene, different lesions and tissues. The vascular experiment supports a CUL3–NO–salt-handling connection, not the same vascular defect in ASD. An ASD allele’s effect on delivery and local neural recovery must be distinguished from its intrinsic neuronal action. Tables 16.1 and 20.1 retain a separate renal regulatory comparison; shared gene identity does not establish the same allele, tissue, timing or mechanism.
Osmoregulation and solute transport SLC12A5/KCC2 R952H and R1049C slowed post-load chloride recovery in transfected Neuro2a cells (Kahle et al., 2014). ASD association evidence is mixed: the initial screen was null; pooled C-terminal coding-region results were nominally positive, while the non-synonymous subset remained null (Merner et al., 2015; §6). Distinct renal paralogues: SLC12A1/NKCC2 mutations cause type-1 Bartter syndrome, while SLC12A3/NCC mutations cause Gitelman syndrome (Simon et al., 1996a,b). A transporter-family comparison, not shared causal alleles. The neuronal experiment demonstrates a recovery defect; renal salt wasting could supply a separate systemic challenge. Shared developmental mediation remains proposed.
Oxidative stress and redox regulation GSTM1 deletion has inconsistent candidate-association evidence: a small family study reported an autism association (Buyske et al., 2006), whereas a later Nigerian case-control study found no association despite lower reduced glutathione in its ASD group (Oshodi et al., 2017). In ARIC, zero or one GSTM1 copy versus two was associated with incident kidney failure and heart failure over long follow-up (Tin et al., 2017). These genotype contrasts differ from the homozygous-deletion contrast in the early autism study. A candidate same-gene comparison with unequal evidence across phenotypes. GSTM1-dependent conjugation, glutathione concentration and SOD activity are distinct; effects on ionic-recovery cost or duration remain unresolved.

Table 48.2 distinguishes a same-variant multisystem lesion in Timothy syndrome, different CUL3 lesions with neuronal and vascular effects, and SLC12 paralogues with distinct neural-recovery and renal-transport roles. Metabolic and redox comparisons have different evidential strength. These links motivate a recovery question without establishing shared causal alleles, enrichment or mediation; the frozen 42/102 classification remains a component map.

48.6 Developmental timing and synaptic refinement

Timing provides the proposed link between shared physiological constraints and divergent outcomes: a constraint could have different effects during construction, stabilisation or refinement. These windows overlap: ASD genes cannot be assigned wholesale to construction or schizophrenia genes to adolescent pruning. CHD8, PTEN and SCN2A have distinct actions, and the 102-gene classification does not establish a shared timing intermediary.

Pruning has separable selection and execution steps. Activity and complement influenced microglial engulfment in the developing mouse retinogeniculate system (Schafer et al., 2012). Astrocytic MEGF10/MERTK pathways also contributed to elimination there (Chung et al., 2013), while neuronal autophagy provided a distinct pruning mechanism in the models studied by Tang et al. (2014). The hypothesis proposes that altered ionic recovery could change activity-based selection, cellular capacity to execute elimination, or the timing of either. Greater spine density alone cannot identify reduced elimination: increased formation or altered stabilisation can produce a similar snapshot. Section 31.4.1 retains the distinction between human cross-sectional findings and experimental model mechanisms.

Tang et al. (2014) demonstrated pathway dependence: rapamycin improved pruning and social endpoints in Tsc2-heterozygous mice, but normalisation failed when neuronal autophagy was disabled through Atg7 deletion. Growth-pathway regulation and functional removal machinery were therefore distinct requirements. Sections 29 and 31.4.1 propose recovery disturbance upstream of protein production or autophagic function; spine density and static autophagy markers cannot establish those processes.

MIA adds a possible immune interaction. One mouse preparation showed complement changes and increased microglial engulfment, whereas another showed deficient engulfment and excess synapses (Yan et al., 2024; Andoh et al., 2019). These findings do not establish one direction across preparations or developmental windows. Immune exposure could change glial responsiveness while local recovery difficulty changes activity or target-recognition signals. Neither that convergence nor maternal complement transfer follows from offspring complement expression (Table 18.4).

The reduced-elimination branch proposes insufficient reserve for timely removal, but energy limitation does not automatically stop microglial work. During acute glucose deprivation, mouse microglia maintained surveillance and damage responses through glutamine use and mTOR-dependent adaptation (Bernier et al., 2020). This does not establish normal developmental pruning or tolerance of combined substrate and oxygen limitation. It does require the proposed branch to identify an actual cellular limitation and its directional effect on refinement.

Increased elimination requires a different mechanism. Human C4A overexpression increased microglial engulfment and reduced cortical synapse density in mice (Yilmaz et al., 2021), without establishing a sodium–perfusion origin or schizophrenia as the opposite of ASD. Adolescent growth could expose limited reserve, but stature changes hydrostatic pressure rather than proving cerebral hypoperfusion (Figure 44.1). The proposed convergence is a directional interaction between susceptibility, physiology and timing; opposite pruning outcomes cannot both confirm the same pathway.

Refinement changes despite preserved relevant recovery, or despite timely prevention of its defect, would challenge this route. Failed late correction is less informative about initiation. Contact, engulfment and completed removal remain distinct, with neuronal and astrocytic mechanisms alongside microglia (Section 2).

Refinement may catch up after recovery or leave lasting circuit organisation. This distinction gives timing its explanatory role: a brief constraint could alter how a circuit is built without lifelong sodium abnormality. Neither trajectory follows from component compatibility alone.

48.7 Physiological comparisons and water composition

Table 48.3. Reported physiological findings and proposed shared mechanisms

Domain / biomarker ASD findings and limits Cardiometabolic or kidney-disease comparison Proposed sodium-struggle interpretation; mediation unestablished
Effective sodium & water handling Lower CSF AVP in selected early-infant and childhood cohorts; separate reports of polydipsia-associated hyponatraemia with inappropriate ADH secretion in two autistic males aged 17 and 19 (Hiratani et al., 1997). These do not establish one sodium–volume phenotype (Section 36.5). Chronic heart failure: copeptin predicted mortality (Neuhold et al., 2008). Tolvaptan improved fluid-related outcomes and low serum sodium, but not mortality or cardiovascular death/heart-failure hospitalisation in EVEREST (Konstam et al., 2007). Low resting AVP with exaggerated challenge responses is proposed within a specified compartment. Low CSF AVP does not predict peripheral peaks; shared developmental origin remains unresolved.
RAAS signatures Low basal renin with a greater or more persistent challenge response is a proposed configuration, not an established ASD finding. In treated adult resistant hypertension, lower renin predicted greater spironolactone blood-pressure response, with reduced thoracic fluid content (Williams et al., 2018). A separate 12-person crossover trial demonstrated marked blood-pressure sensitivity to dietary sodium (Pimenta et al., 2009). Salt retention, dietary salt sensitivity and endocrine response gain are different endpoints. Low renin or diuretic response alone does not establish low-baseline/high-gain physiology.
HPA / cortisol Exaggerated or prolonged cortisol responses to stress; flattened diurnal rhythms in subsets Cortisol concentration, diurnal timing and challenge recovery are separate comparison endpoints; a cardiometabolic or kidney-disease diagnosis does not establish one shared HPA profile. Candidate cortisol contribution to defence; substitution for aldosterone/MR control is a distinct functional claim.
Autonomic tone (HRV, catecholamines) Task- and context-dependent cardiac autonomic differences; resting RSA and response directions vary (Section 42). Cardiac autonomic indices and directly measured sympathetic activity are separate comparison endpoints; reduced HRV alone does not identify the proposed endocrine configuration. Proposed altered mobilisation or recovery under specified loads; developmental mediation remains unresolved.
Endothelial function & perfusion Regional ASL differences include higher and lower flow (Section 47). Perivascular/glymphatic observations and oxidative markers are separate endpoints, not measurements of delivery reserve. Arterial stiffness, flow-mediated dilation, microvascular density and perfusion under demand describe different vascular properties; none alone demonstrates the proposed developmental recovery pathway. Proposed: repeated vascular defence alters endothelial responsiveness and reduces dilation or recruitment under demand; the exposure-to-functional-limitation sequence remains unestablished.
Insulin and lipids Post-diagnosis HOMA-IR difference in a small treatment-naïve sample (Manco et al., 2021); subsequent T2D association (Chen et al., 2016); metabolic change during treatment (Scahill et al., 2016). Insulin sensitivity and lipid status require separate description; the presence of cardiovascular or kidney disease does not establish both, or a common endocrine triad. Early susceptibility, acquired impairment, feedback, shared cause and independent comorbidity remain alternatives (Sections 19.7 and 21.2).
Oxidative stress & mitochondria F₂-isoprostanes, 8-OHdG and glutathione address distinct redox endpoints. Lower lymphocyte mitochondrial activity in a small comparison study and selected-clinic acyl-carnitine abnormalities are functional and biochemical findings, respectively (Giulivi et al., 2010; Frye et al., 2013), not a measure of cumulative allostatic load. Oxidative-damage markers, mitochondrial respiration and ATP availability are distinct endpoints; their overlap across diagnoses does not establish shared origin or direction of causation. A defined defence response could precede and mediate oxidative or mitochondrial strain; separately reported biomarker overlap does not establish that sequence.
FGF-23/Klotho & mineral metabolism Lower distal-tibial trabecular density and estimated strength in children aged 11–12 (O’Flaherty et al., 2025); fracture patterns vary by site, age and ascertainment. These findings do not identify phosphate, FGF-23 or Klotho mediation. Separate sodium-sensitive and endocrine/autonomic skeletal routes are discussed above; tonicity-sensitive FGF23 regulation is considered in §14.9. In 3,879 adults with CKD stages 2–4, higher FGF-23 predicted mortality and, in specified filtration strata, end-stage renal disease (Isakova et al., 2011). This association does not establish vascular causality or a paired low-Klotho state. FGF23 increased NCC-mediated sodium retention in mice; Klotho-deficient tubules lost its stimulated phosphorylation increment, not proven basal NCC activity (Andrukhova et al., 2014). Soluble Klotho is not a renal membrane measure; human phosphate trials showed opposite circulating responses (§14.9). T3/Klotho and preparation-dependent vascular NO/redox findings are developed in §33.3. Low BMD identifies neither this branch nor local neural/glial recovery mediation.
AQP2/AQP4 and osmotic fragility Clinical water-balance and perivascular observations do not directly measure AQP abundance, localisation or function In post-infarction rats, decompensated heart failure with raised filling pressure and lower serum sodium increased renal AQP2 abundance and apical targeting; compensated infarcted rats did not show the same increase (Nielsen et al., 1997). This is renal AQP2 evidence, not brain AQP4 evidence. Candidate acquired aquaporin-regulatory change persisting after recovery; exposure, functional effect and persistence remain distinct claims.
Nephron endowment and renal functional reserve Developmental nephron deficit and altered renal reserve remain unestablished as general ASD features. Low nephron number can increase susceptibility to compensatory filtration, hypertension and injury; outcomes are not inevitable. Proposed hardware constraint: renal limitation modifies sodium–water recovery and regulatory cost; increased endocrine or vasomotor gain does not automatically follow.

Water composition extends the cross-organ comparison to environmental exposure; it does not establish a dilutional pathway. Softer-water supply was associated with greater arterial stiffness in 144 Slovak adults (Rapant et al., 2019); a retrospective school cohort of 660 children linked very-low-mineral water to higher homocysteine and adverse lipid or oxidative markers but no significant blood-pressure difference (Huang et al., 2023b). Calcium/magnesium nutrition, total dissolved solids and sodium are distinct exposures. A water–solute interaction with limited renal or vascular reserve remains possible, but neither these associations nor low nephron endowment establishes retained water, dilution or an autism mechanism.

48.8 Scope and tests of a shared recovery process

‘Sodium struggle’ is not a synonym for ASD. Genetic susceptibility, developmental timing, the physiological disturbance and cumulative exposure define the comparison. Different ages and tissues encounter different demands and reserves; sodium loss, relative water retention, impaired perfusion and local recovery difficulty do not prescribe one endocrine pattern (Table 14.3). Heat, illness, diet, medications or psychosocial stress may modify an earlier trajectory or leave it unchanged.

Brain, kidney and vasculature may differ in their limiting reserve. A constraint during neural development could affect circuit formation, whereas later renal or vascular challenges could chiefly affect cardiometabolic function. Co-vulnerability could produce overlap, and successful compensation could leave neither outcome. These are candidate trajectories, not histories recoverable from diagnoses alone.

Central AVP, water-balance disturbances, autonomic responses, perfusion and mineral metabolism have largely been studied separately. Their coexistence as a shared defence phenotype remains unestablished, as does one origin for low-renin hypertension, hyponatraemia, FGF23/Klotho findings and stiffness in cardiorenal disease. Table 48.3 keeps observations distinct from candidate mechanisms; Sections 14.9 and 33.3 provide the detailed Klotho account.

The shared-process claim is that a particular limitation changes the work or completion of recovery and thereby affects an organ during a susceptible interval. Tables 48.1, 48.2, and 48.3 distinguish exposure follow-up, biomarkers and genetic or functional comparisons. For a proposed ASD route, that connection must reach the local neural or glial recovery difficulty defined in Section 2; protective physiology alone does not establish developmental harm.

The comparison should distinguish response gain and recovery from resting concentrations, and a sodium-centred mechanism from generic stress or independent disease. Its value is the prediction that the same protective physiology can have different consequences according to where reserve is limited and when that limitation is encountered; no single marker or water-composition association establishes the shared history. Section 49 evaluates these comparisons alongside the complete developmental argument.

49 Discussion

49.1 Evidence and the central recovery claim

The strongest support for this framework lies in experiments that measure a defined physiological process and show what changes it. The manuscript brings together sodium and chloride restoration, cellular-volume regulation, vascular and metabolic support, and manipulable developmental processes. These findings make the proposed connections testable. They do not yet establish the central inference: that impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carries a developmental effect across autistic trajectories. That inference has greater explanatory reach than any individual component result and therefore requires a separate causal test (Sections 2 and 23.13).

Direct recovery assays are especially informative because they measure restoration over time. KCC2 R952H and R1049C slowed chloride-sensor recovery after loading in transfected Neuro2a cells (Kahle et al., 2014). In human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons, KW-2449 shortened the chloride-recovery time constant towards the isogenic wild-type value (Tang et al., 2019). These experiments establish defined recovery phenotypes and, in the latter preparation, a modifiable one. Their epilepsy and Rett-model contexts remain important; the mixed ASD association evidence for SLC12A5 does not change the measured cellular result. Neither experiment establishes recovery-mediated development across autism, and KCC2's structural functions and the drug's other actions prevent a broad rescue from identifying the mediator by itself (Section 6.4).

Successful restoration supplies the necessary positive comparator. Cultured postnatal rat hippocampal neurons restored intracellular sodium after chemical anoxia and reoxygenation, whereas sodium-pump inhibition prevented that recovery (Sheldon et al., 2004; Section 14.7.2). In primary rat cortical astrocytes, LRRC8A knockdown markedly impaired regulatory volume decrease during hypotonic exposure (Formaggio et al., 2019; Section 24.2). The first comparison concerns restoration after an insult; the second concerns volume regulation during continued exposure. Together they show why the measured variable, phase and transport machinery matter. Increased transport work, adaptive solute release or a transient deviation can accompany successful regulation rather than a developmental cost.

Developmental experiments address another part of the argument. Perinatal interventions in valproate-exposed rats and Fmr1-null mice altered juvenile neural physiology and early pup vocalisations, providing a precedent for developmental effects after a brief intervention (Tyzio et al., 2014; Section 23.7.2). Those experiments did not measure recovery after matched ionic loading or isolate selective neural recovery mediation. Likewise, the vascular, oxygen-signalling and lineage-timing experiments in Section 31 establish consequential developmental interfaces while leaving the proposed recovery connection open. The evidence is therefore strongest for particular components and experimental recovery phenotypes; it is less complete at the step linking that recovery to a defined developmental transition, and cannot establish universal participation.

This ranking concerns what the selected findings establish, not a systematic estimate of the literature. The narrative selection described in Section 1.1 is illustrative. Reusing one experiment in an early explanation, a mechanism chapter and this evaluation does not provide independent replication, and the frozen genetic component classification does not establish enrichment or mediation.

49.2 Entry routes and developmental conversion

The systemic and intrinsic routes explain different starting points. A maternal, placental, renal or vascular disturbance can alter the conditions supporting local restoration. An intrinsic transport, metabolic or cellular constraint can begin within neural or glial tissue without a preceding systemic sodium deficit. Immune mechanisms can enter at either level. Underfilling, impaired effective filling despite fluid expansion, hypertonic exposure and genuine overfilling need their own exposure and response descriptions. The AVP–RAAS–cortisol triad organises context-dependent protective responses; it does not assign one hormone direction to every route (Sections 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 15, and 18).

A measured initiating disturbance can justify a place in this account before its full developmental sequence is demonstrated. The additional work is to connect that disturbance to delayed, incomplete or unstable local recovery and then to a specified developmental effect. More pump turnover, lower reserve or prolonged protective recruitment can be fully accommodated. Conversely, a local transport defect can matter without a large systemic abnormality. The explanatory distinction is between the effort needed to restore conditions and whether restoration succeeds at the time development depends on it. Exposure associations, circulating hormones and resting ion concentrations address parts of that sequence rather than substituting for it (Sections 1.1, 2, and 4).

The same distinction applies to persistence. Renal structure, vascular responsiveness, receptor action and controller thresholds could change later exposure or recovery, while continuing ligand exposure could maintain a response without an acquired change in gain (Sections 21, 22, 32, and 34–39). The proposed glucose contribution to extracellular osmotic support and the insulin-associated AVP-clearance route are separable questions; either can be tested without making the other compulsory (Section 19.7). Identifying a sustaining mechanism gives these branches explanatory content beyond the continued presence of a biomarker.

49.3 Lasting organisation and current function

The developmental accounts in Sections 30.4, 31.4, and 31.5 distinguish physiological recovery from lasting changes in circuit organisation. Section 46.2 considers fever-related changes as acute functional comparisons, and Section 46.3 considers middle-ear fluid clearance as a peripheral comparison. Neither identifies the developmental mechanism on its own.

The enduring-developmental proposal concerns a transition that occurs while restoration is constrained: differentiation, inhibitory maturation, synapse stabilisation or circuit refinement. Once that transition has changed, its consequences may remain after the initiating exposure and local physiological disturbance resolve. The continuing-state proposal instead concerns a present limitation in delivery, transport, buffering or recovery that changes current function. Both can operate in one person, but evidence for either does not establish the other. Later recognition, including during the additional demands of upright locomotion, need not identify the timing of origin (Sections 30, 31, and 47).

This distinction changes the interpretation of behaviour and short-term improvement. A physiological explanation becomes informative when a specified limitation precedes a functional change and that function improves as the limitation resolves. Sensory comfort, communication, pleasure, attention, learning and individual agency remain independent explanations of movement and engagement. The cost of participation cannot be inferred from a person's wish to engage, eye contact or repetition. Acute modulation during fever, ordinary recovery during sleep or resolution of a peripheral fluid problem can clarify present function without reconstructing the earlier developmental cause (Sections 45–47).

49.4 Alternative mechanisms and cross-disease specificity

The proposed intermediary adds a particular causal requirement to chloride-state, metabolic-signalling, neuroimmune and direct developmental accounts. A resting chloride difference can change signalling without demonstrating impaired restoration; a recovery defect can occur despite similar starting values. Protein production, cytoskeletal signalling, extracellular developmental signals and altered lineage timing could influence development independently, or could act upstream or downstream of recovery. Their relationship must be resolved within a defined model. A broad upstream rescue that improves several processes cannot determine which one carried the developmental effect (Sections 23.13, 26, 29, 31, and 35).

Cross-disease comparisons sharpen that question when they identify a shared lesion or function precisely. Table 48.2 distinguishes a same-variant multisystem channel lesion from different CUL3 lesions in different tissues and from neural and renal transporter paralogues. Those comparisons have unequal evidential strength. A shared gene name, biomarker or developmental exposure does not establish a common causal path. For a recovery mechanism to explain divergent neural, renal, vascular or skeletal outcomes, its predicted direction must depend on a specified tissue, developmental interval and limiting reserve rather than being chosen after the outcome is known (Section 48).

Parallel organ effects remain valuable comparisons in their own right. A skeletal cost of sodium-sensitive resorption or endocrine signalling could coexist with a neural effect, occur without it, or reflect a different exposure history. Reduced nephron reserve may constrain later renal recovery while compensation preserves function elsewhere. Similarly, prognosis, a fluid response and a survival benefit are different outcomes in the cardiorenal intervention comparisons. The proposed neural route requires its local recovery intermediary in addition to any shared systemic history; unrelated comorbidity and successful compensation remain possible (Tables 48.1 and 48.3).

49.5 What contrary findings change

Contrary findings should narrow the claim they actually test. Preserved GABA driving force and inhibition in the tested Shank3B-null preparation constrain an obligatory chloride-state explanation for that model (Chiesa et al., 2019). They do not establish that every relevant local recovery process was normal. Conversely, attributing the result to another unmeasured compartment would not support the hypothesis. The claimed variable, cell type and developmental interval must be specified before testing. An adequately demonstrated developmental route with preserved relevant recovery, or an effect persisting despite timely prevention of the required disturbance, would challenge universal participation while leaving possible contributions elsewhere (Section 23.13.1).

Other negatives constrain broader interpretations. The recurrent-hyponatraemia model in Section 23.6 showed a slower, less pronounced ADC decline on subsequent water challenge, rather than the predicted amplification (Tejedor et al., 2026). Lower CSF AVP in selected childhood and early-infant cohorts constrains general central AVP excess, while leaving peripheral and local circuit signals separate (Oztan et al., 2018, 2020; Section 36.5). The sex comparisons in Section 40 include preserved renal regulation, null endocrine differences and opposing tissue- or protocol-specific responses. Similar renal outputs neither exclude internal transport differences nor demonstrate them. The modifier claim requires a physiological difference under specified developmental conditions, rather than a universal female reserve advantage or a diagnosis-ratio explanation inferred from adult physiology.

Developmental direction also matters. Section 30.4 retains delayed, accelerated and unchanged findings across distinct OTX2, PV and matrix models. They constrain a universal immaturity account. Opposite outcomes can test a timing-dependent hypothesis only when the relevant preparation, interval and expected direction are specified beforehand; they cannot both confirm an unspecified shared defect. Direct genetic and extracellular-signalling explanations remain available until the recovery connection is measured.

Human associations also change with exposure definition and comparison design. In the neonatal cohorts reviewed in Section 12, the fully adjusted glucose-corrected sodium-range result was nonsignificant, and the grouped psychiatric/developmental endpoint in the asphyxia cohort was also nonsignificant (Gervais et al., 2022; Viitaharju et al., 2026). Neither endpoint was an autism-specific recovery test. Maternal infection associations attenuated in the sibling comparison retained in Table 48.1 (Brynge et al., 2022). These results limit the corresponding exposure inferences without erasing the separate experimental component mechanisms. They also show why collecting compatible associations cannot establish a shared physiological history.

The two phase 3 bumetanide trials did not meet their primary clinical endpoints in established ASD, and treatment produced more thirst, polyuria and hypokalaemia (Fuentes et al., 2023; Section 23.7.3). These findings constrain therapeutic claims and do not favour a recovery account over a chloride-state account. Later treatment failure cannot settle an earlier developmental mechanism when the relevant interval and mediator were not tested; equally, it supplies no evidence for an otherwise unobserved earlier disturbance. The same discipline applies to a positive acute response: improved function does not identify the developmental cause.

49.6 Three discriminating comparisons

Three comparisons would resolve different joints in the argument. They are priorities within the existing experimental and observational approaches developed in Table 2.1 and Section 23.13, rather than three obligatory steps for every route. Each needs a defined preparation or population, developmental interval, recovery variable, alternative explanation and outcome. Normal serum sodium, larger initial loading and altered resting biomarkers cannot substitute for the recovery measurement.

First, an intrinsic recovery comparison can build on the human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons and dynamic chloride assay described in Section 6.4. Compare recovery time, residual deviation and stability under matched initial loading and ongoing demand, while measuring inhibitory maturation or synapse development separately. Then assess whether timely correction of the recovery defect changes that developmental endpoint, with transport-related effects distinguished from KCC2's structural or other intervention effects. Better recovery alone establishes a physiological rescue. A developmental improvement attributable to correction during the relevant interval would support mediation in that route; persistence of the developmental effect despite adequate, timely prevention of the proposed disturbance would count against it (Sections 4 and 23.13).

Second, a systemic clinical comparison can ask whether measured salt-wasting and recovery trajectories add information beyond an illness diagnosis. Existing records, cohorts or archived samples may permit comparison of similarly ill infants with impaired conservation and those with preserved conservation, considering serial blood and urine measurements, intake, replacement, output, prematurity, illness severity and treatment. The question is whether the defined physiological trajectory precedes and predicts a specified developmental outcome. A sufficiently precise null would weaken that clinical prediction; a positive association would still require temporally relevant local neural or glial recovery evidence to support the proposed developmental intermediary. Renal or peripheral outcomes alone cannot complete that inference (Sections 14.4.2, 23.13, 32, and 40.3.2).

Third, the valproate-exposed rat model in Section 23.7.2 provides an existing preparation for a developmental-history comparison across the perinatal chloride-regulation interval and later circuit function. Its GABA and behavioural findings would need to be related to a measured recovery trajectory, distinguishing a retained developmental consequence from continuing physiological impairment. Compare later function after the exposure and relevant disturbance have resolved, at the same chronological age and comparable current physiological and task conditions; record maturation separately so that matching does not remove the timing effect under investigation. Timely selective prevention of the earlier recovery disturbance would test its contribution to the retained difference. The existing broad bumetanide intervention does not provide that selective test. A history-dependent effect reduced by such prevention would support the proposed connection; differences explained by continuing exposure or current load would favour present-state modulation. Normal later physiology and failed late reversal cannot decide this comparison alone (Table 2.1; Sections 21, 31, and 47).

49.7 Scope of the proposed contribution

The framework's contribution is a common causal question across otherwise different physiological and developmental accounts: does a defined limitation impair local restoration at a consequential time, and does that disturbance carry the developmental effect? The breadth of possible entry routes makes this question useful only if its required intermediary remains specific. One supported route would establish a contribution in that setting; several supported routes would strengthen convergence without proving participation in every autistic trajectory. A well-characterised bypass would challenge that universal conjecture. The proposed value therefore lies in comparisons that distinguish successful compensation, incomplete recovery and recovery-dependent development, while allowing parallel peripheral outcomes and independent causes. This physiological synthesis does not establish an intervention or assign an individual's developmental history from diagnosis.

50 Conclusion: The Sodium Struggle as a Physiological Framework

The Sodium Struggle proposes a common developmental process: diverse initiating conditions converge on disturbed local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery during sensitive fetal or early postnatal windows, changing the conditions under which circuits mature. Maternal, placental, renal and vascular physiology can supply systemic entry routes, including altered sensing or regulation; genetic influences can act through systemic regulation, direct cellular constraints, or both. Local routes can begin with impaired transport, energetic support or recovery itself. Maternal immune activation can act through circulatory or local immune mechanisms. Clinical hyponatraemia and preceding systemic defence are not compulsory. Whether this process participates across all autistic trajectories remains a demanding, unestablished conjecture.

Its organising insight concerns compensatory physiology and its developmental consequences: protective responses can preserve apparent systemic stability while local restoration remains constrained. The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad, autonomic support and renal sodium–water responses defend tonicity, effective filling and perfusion. Their recruitment can be appropriate and successful. The sodium paradox concerns the possible coexistence of limited systemic support and substantial cellular restoration work: sodium entry can increase pump demand, while impaired chloride extrusion supplies a distinct recovery constraint. Increased ATP turnover need not deplete ATP, and increased effort with adequate recovery does not satisfy the hypothesis. The developmental claim begins where restoration becomes delayed, incomplete or unstable and changes maturation.

The hypothalamic layer connects this physiology to regulatory calibration. Systemic AVP supports water and circulatory regulation; local dendritic AVP can recruit nearby presympathetic neurons in the rat PVN (Son et al., 2013). These are distinct compartments, not evidence for uniform AVP elevation or recruitment of a shared AVP-producing or CRH population. The proposed shift towards AVP-linked recruitment or weaker oxytocin-mediated modulation concerns a specified circuit and developmental interval. Repeated protective recruitment, together with local recovery difficulty, could alter controller thresholds, receptor weighting or recovery kinetics. A more AVP-weighted, sympathetic and cortisol-supported profile remains a prediction rather than an assigned signature.

Distributed imprinting could involve vascular responsiveness, renal handling, autonomic gain, hypothalamic balance, astrocytic buffering, extracellular-space regulation or cellular transport. These are alternative or interacting sites. Their relevance to this core requires a local recovery disturbance that changes a defined developmental process, potentially affecting inhibitory maturation, synaptic stabilisation or refinement. Enduring circuit organisation may remain after physiology normalises; continuing regulatory differences can separately modify its expression. Later demands, including upright locomotion and its circulatory, sensorimotor and buffering requirements, may expose a limitation that was partly compensated earlier. The timing of recognition need not identify the timing of origin.

Glucose’s possible osmotic support and insulin-associated AVP clearance exemplify separable metabolic proposals (Section 19.7). Redox-dependent vascular dysfunction, membrane injury and endocrine constraints offer other entries or amplifiers. Each candidate contribution requires its own physiological evidence and, for the developmental claim, the specified local recovery effect.

Schrier’s effective arterial blood volume, Guyton’s sodium–volume–pressure physiology, Sterling and Eyer’s allostasis, and Barker’s developmental programming provide the framework’s physiological foundations. They explain functional adequacy, coordinated compensation, adaptive reweighting and lasting calibration; they do not establish a sodium–volume cause of autism. The additional claim here is that different demands or intrinsic constraints converge on local recovery difficulty that carries a developmental effect. Cross-disease comparisons ask whether similar protective physiology operates at other times and sites, without establishing a shared cause.

This contribution connects ion handling, vascular regulation, endocrine control and neural maturation around a defined causal question. The selected evidence is strongest for physiological components and directly measured recovery in experimental preparations; whether the recovery disturbance carries a developmental effect remains unresolved. Genetic and immune findings may support that intermediary or reveal routes that bypass it. Exposure associations, altered resting biomarkers and increased workload cannot decide between those possibilities. Nor can later challenge responses retrospectively establish an unmeasured developmental episode. The framework assigns neither blame nor an intervention. Its explanatory value depends on distinguishing component physiology, recovery mediation and developmental consequence.

Three comparisons give that question practical priorities: recovery and a separate developmental endpoint in human Rett-model neurons; naturally occurring salt-wasting and preserved-conservation trajectories in existing clinical material; and developmental history versus current physiology in the valproate-exposed rat preparation. Section 49.6 specifies their alternative explanations and informative outcomes.

Section 23.13 states the decisive unresolved boundary. A well-characterised developmental route proceeding despite adequately demonstrated absence, or timely selective prevention, of the relevant recovery disturbance would challenge universal participation, even if the process contributes elsewhere. Normal routine serum sodium is not that demonstration, and an unmeasured intermediary is not evidence for the hypothesis. Conversely, an unsupported earlier episode cannot rescue an informative negative result. The hypothesis stands or falls on whether impaired local recovery actually carries the developmental effect, not on how many otherwise compatible observations can be assembled.
